News.title: Met Office weather maps show UK battered by rain on Wednesday - full list of 59 counties soaked
News.content:
Met Office weather maps show UK battered by rain on Wednesday - full list of 59 counties soaked

The Met Office has forecast heavy rain for Wednesday, September 30 with 59 counties across the country expected to be soaked by downpours throughout the day

View 6 Images The UK is expected to be battered by rain on Wednesday (Image: Derby Telegraph)

The UK is expected to be battered by downpours tomorrow as a thick band of rain travels across the nation.

‌



The band of rain will be moving steadily east/northeast across Britain on Wednesday, September 30 with the majority of areas experiencing some form of showers at some point in the day.

‌



According to Met Office weather maps, in the morning, the main band already stretches from southwest England right through Wales, northern England and Scotland.

‌



View 6 Images The heavy rain starts from the morning (Image: Met Office )

At 9am the heaviest rain is expected to fall through western Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern Wales and south west England.

By midday, the band of rain moves slightly east, with many of the same areas being covered, including heavy showers in Cornwall and Devon as well as much of Wales.

‌



View 6 Images The south east of England is expected to be covered by heavy rain at midday (Image: Met Office )

Into the afternoon, the patterns appears to shift with counties further east being struck by showers.

Weather maps appear nearly fully blue at 3pm, with much of the north east of England now also covered.

‌



View 6 Images By the afternoon the band of rain begins to move eastwards (Image: Met Office )

The heaviest-looking section of rain appears to be around central/northern Scotland and northern England, whereas the downpours appear to ease slightly in the south from the morning.

As evening comes the rain is expected to move further east again, with areas that have been soaked all day expecting to get some dry periods.

‌



View 6 Images By 6pm, London and surrounding areas can expect showers (Image: Met Office )

In the south at 6pm, the main band has passed, however rain will hit London and surrounding areas.

By 9pm, much of the rain has cleared apart from dispersed showers in the north east of England.

‌



View 6 Images The rain will have mostly cleared by the evening (Image: Met Office )

Elsewhere, the wet conditions are predicted to have mostly cleared.

The Met Office forecasts "heavy rain" on Wednesday.

‌



The forecaster says: "Heavy rain moves across the UK on Wednesday, bringing a fresher feel. Staying breezy with sunny spells and showers thereafter."

News.title: Labour conference live - Mahmood says 'more to come' on RAF Fairford 'terror attack' as Burnham chairs COBRA meeting
News.content:
The Prime Minister told LBC this afternoon that he wanted to get the 'full picture' of what happened at the base, and added he would share more details about the upcoming meeting

The Prime Minister announced on the sidelines of the Labour Party Conference today that he would be holding a COBRA meeting to address the RAF Fairford incident, with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood confirming after that she expects there to be "more to say in the days to come".

The Home Secretary told a fringe event at the Labour Party Conference that the decision to bail the suspects was a police operational decision. The Home Secretary said: "You will have heard some news from counter-terrorism policing about the release under bail. These are investigations, these are matters for the police, they have got to take the lead on how they use all of the powers at their disposal in cases such as these, but the investigations are continuing.

"So there'll be more to say in the days to come, I'm sure, as how those investigations are progressing. I've just come from a Cobra meeting with other colleagues in government chaired by the Prime Minister, and everyone should know that we are focused on this. You shouldn't read anything into the fact that we're limited in what we can say publicly at this stage except for the fact that nobody wants to compromise any investigation or any future court cases either."

Speaking with LBC's Shelagh Fogarty from Liverpool this afternoon, Andy Burnham said the security situation will be on the minds of many Brits following the arrests of five men in the nearby village of Whelford on on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences on Sunday. He told LBC that he wanted to get the “full picture” on what had happened at the base used by the British and US air forces in Gloucestershire.

Earlier, Wes Streeting gave an update on Britain's national security after five men were arrested over an alleged terror plot at an RAF base. The Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, said our response to any attempt to destroy a two-state solution in the Middle East would be: "we will not let you succeed"

And Chancellor John Healey set out plans to reindustrialise Britain with investment in industry and support for apprenticeships - while pledging that getting young people back into work was not just an "economic must" but a "moral duty". The Chancellor used his speech to the Labour Party conference to seek to reassure financial markets with a commitment to being responsible with the nation’s finances

Follow along live below....

News.title: Wes Streeting asked to probe claims civil servants 'torpedoed' compensation for nuclear test vets
News.content:
Wes Streeting asked to probe claims civil servants 'torpedoed' compensation for nuclear test vets

EXCLUSIVE: Labour peer Kevan Jones has claimed that he has learned alleged briefings from civil servants that 'lawyers were only interested in their fees' were in fact false

View 3 Images Wes Streeting has been asked to look into claims civil servants 'torpedoed' compensation of veterans of the UK's nuclear weapons programme (Image: Jack Taylor/Pool Reuters via AP)

Wes Streeting has been asked to investigate claims civil servants “torpedoed” the government’s compensation deal for veterans of Britain’s nuclear weapons programme.

‌



Labour peer Kevan Jones – a former Veterans Minister and now titled Lord Beamish – has learned his 2009 offer of a £20million payout was never received by lawyers. He said: “I was told they had rejected it out of hand. Civil servants briefed me the lawyers were only interested in their fees, and I made statements to Parliament on that basis.

‌



“I have since learned this was false, and not only were those lawyers keen to settle for the sake of their clients, but my offer was never even delivered."

‌



Family's heartbreaking plea 26 years after Vicky Glass found murdered in stream READ MORE :

Nuclear test veterans' medical records were gathered by secret government lab READ MORE :

View 3 Images Kevan Jones has alleged he was given a false briefing by civil servants (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

“Had my orders been followed, this would all have been put to bed for a reasonable sum. I’ve passed my papers to the Defence Secretary, and I think he should waive the MoD’s client privilege so all documentation and discussion about my settlement offer can be published.”

‌



Solicitor Neil Sampson was representing the 1,011 vets and widows affected by the scandal at the time Lord Beamish drew up the deal. Mr Sampson said the MoD had an offer to make “but before they would tell us, we had to agree to either recommend whatever it was or, if we rejected it, we could not tell our clients”.

He added: “I would have been struck off had I agreed. It was effectively torpedoed. It bought time for the MoD to lodge an appeal, and the case was later thrown out.”

View 3 Images Neil Sampson was representing affected families while Lord Beamish drew up the deal (Image: Steve Bainbridge)

Article continues below

The Mirror ’s Nuke Blood Scandal campaign uncovered evidence of a secret programme of blood tests on troops, hidden behind national security and now the subject of a fresh legal battle and a major crime review by police. Thames Valley Police confirmed it is considering new leads for a full investigation.

A spokesman said: “This is a very complex matter that is receiving our full attention. There are many multifaceted enquiries, which continue, to establish a full assessment of all the facts that have been presented initially and more recently through several sources.”

An MoD spokesman said work continued on addressing veterans’ concerns, and added: “As this work progresses our focus will be on transparency, accountability and building confidence among veterans and their families.”

News.title: Boy, 13, who drowned while 'lake jumping' had told friends he couldn't swim
News.content:
Boy, 13, who drowned while 'lake jumping' had told friends he couldn't swim

Tragic Hayden Jones-Powell had gone to Meynell Lake in Fosse Way, Syston, with a group of friends after school finished early

View 2 Images Hayden Jones-Powell was just 13 (Image: Family Handout / SWNS)

A schoolboy who tragically drowned after he went "lake jumping" with his friends had told them he couldn't swim.

‌



Hayden Jones-Powell was only 13 years old when he died at Meynell Lake in Leicestershire on June 25. The boy was one of 15 children who went to the lake after Wreake Valley Academy closed early that day due to high temperatures, an inquest heard on Friday.

‌



Hayden had told his friends he couldn't swim before going into the water and he was last seen at around 12.45pm. His friends raised the alarm and teachers from the academy rushed to the lake to try to find him but to no avail.

‌



Officers were then called just after 1.30pm and specialist dive teams, Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Service and East Midlands Ambulance Service searched the lake. Later that evening, at 8.15pm, Hayden was found in the water, with a post-mortem examination confirming he had drowned.

Leicestershire Police said there were no suspicious circumstances surrounding the death. Coroner Isobel Thistlethwaite recorded a conclusion of accident, Leicestershire Live reports. Hayden's parents, Ben Jones-Powell and Emily Ambler, paid tribute to their son after his death, saying the boy had a passion for football and a love of animals.

"We want him to be remembered by his big smile," they said. "The world isn't the same without him. His love of animals, his passion towards football and being outside.

‌



"Hayden also had an amazing sense of humour and was extremely quick-witted. We don't know how we will cope without him."

Hayden was a keen West Bromwich Albion supporter with a wide circle of friends. He leaves behind two older brothers and a sister.

His aunt, Charlotte Powell, previously said he was "just a really lovely little cheeky boy." She said: "He wanted to cool off from the heat and enjoy the cool water, getting some respite from the heatwave after school."

‌



View 2 Images A memorial at Syston Skatepark in Hayden's memory (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

She added: "It's horrific, absolutely horrific. It's the thing that happens to other people, doesn't it? It doesn't happen to your family."

Hayden's death was followed by an outpouring of grief across the Leicestershire town as hundreds gathered in Syston's Central Park to release balloons in his memory two days after the tragedy. Many wore T-shirts printed with his photo. Flowers, cards and balloons were also left along a nearby fence in tribute.

‌



Ms Powell said the tributes showed how much he meant to people. "Not one child doesn't know Hayden. They all loved him," she said. "You've only got to look up the fence to see the tributes they've paid to see what an impact that boy had in 13 years. It's incredible."

His friends also shared a memory of his sense of humour. They said he would ask his school's deputy head teacher what was in his sandwiches every single day, without fail.

"He always had a quick wit for something," Charlotte said. "He was so loved, so loved, and that is evidently here today."

Article continues below

Wreake Valley Academy said it was devastated by the loss of one of its students. A spokesperson said: "This tragic accident has deeply affected everyone at our school and we are providing support to students, staff, and families who need it."

News.title: Thames Water: Thousands without water in 18 London and Surrey postcodes - list
News.content:
Thames Water said thousands of homes across London and Surrey were left without water or with low pressure following a 'large burst water main'

Thousands of homes were left without water or with low pressure in parts of London and Surrey following a "large burst water main".

Thames Water said on Monday afternoon that its engineers had isolated the broken pipe in West Molesey, Surrey, and were working on a permanent repair. The company said up to 15,000 properties were initially affected by the issue on Monday morning, but later added that the number had fallen to 6,000.

Customers in the following postcodes were impacted: CR4, KT1, KT10, KT12, KT2, KT3, KT5, KT6, KT7, KT8, SM4, SW16, SW17, SW18, SW19, SW20, TW10 and TW16.

Images showed supermarket shelves stripped bare as residents rushed to stock up on water, while some schools and nurseries in Surrey said they had been forced to close because of the fault.

News.title: Dad and daughter, in her 20s, killed in same 'devastating' workplace incident
News.content:
Dad and daughter, in her 20s, killed in same 'devastating' workplace incident

A man in his 50s and his daughter in her 20s died following a tragic incident in Co Offaly, Ireland, with the company describing the tragedy as 'unprecedented'

View 3 Images The tragic incident happened at Banagher Precast Concrete in Co Offaly

A father and his daughter have both been killed in a horrific workplace tragedy, leaving a tight-knit workforce devastated and in a state of shock.

‌



The man, in his 50s, and his daughter, in her 20s, lost their lives following the incident at Banagher Precast Concrete, Co Offaly, in Ireland, shortly before midday on Monday, September 28.

‌



It is understood the pair are from Romania and had been employed at the Banagher plant for several years. Their deaths have plunged both stunned colleagues and the wider local community into mourning, with the company describing the incident as "unprecedented" and "devastating tragedy."

‌



Gardaí and emergency services raced to the scene at around 11.40am, where the man and woman were pronounced dead, reports the Irish Mirror.

The bodies of the victims were then transferred to Midlands Regional Hospital Tullamore, where post-mortem examinations are due to take place.

View 3 Images The bodies were taken to Midlands Regional Hospital Tullamore (Image: "irishphotos@mirror.co.uk" )

‌



Banagher Precast Concrete described the incident as "a devastating tragedy for everyone connected with our company", adding that employees were "all in deep shock".

In a statement issued to RTE News, the company said its Board of Directors, management team and staff offered their "deepest sympathies and heartfelt condolences" to the families, friends and colleagues of those who perished.

The firm's immediate priority, it stressed, was providing support to the families of the two employees who died. Banagher Precast Concrete also took the opportunity to thank the emergency services and all those who responded to the incident. The full circumstances surrounding the tragic incident have yet to be established.

‌



The company said it would work fully alongside all statutory bodies and offer whatever support is needed as part of the ongoing investigation. The firm stated that the welfare of its workforce has always been a fundamental value, deeply ingrained within its day-to-day operations.

It described an incident of this magnitude as "unprecedented" for the organisation, adding that its employees were "all in deep shock".

The company has urged that the privacy of the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives be respected, and confirmed it would not be releasing any further details at this time.

‌



View 3 Images Tony McCormack TD , Offaly (Fianna Fail)

Fianna Fáil Offaly TD Tony McCormack extended his condolences following the devastating news.

"I was deeply saddened to hear the tragic news coming from Banagher, where two lives have been lost in a workplace incident," he told the Irish Independent.

Article continues below

"My thoughts are first and foremost with the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives. I can only imagine the shock and heartbreak they are experiencing.

"I am also thinking of their friends, work colleagues and the wider Banagher community at this incredibly difficult time. My deepest sympathies go to everyone affected by this terrible tragedy."

News.title: M25-M40 traffic - live: Motorways at standstill after horror lorry crash at junction
News.content:
The incident happened at the junction of the M40 and M25, with traffic on the M40 in Buckinghamshire held in both directions

Traffic is being held in both directions at the junction of two motorways outside London following a serious lorry crash.

The incident happened when a lorry travelling southbound on the M40 crashed and crossed the central reservation, traffic information company Inrix has said. Two lanes are closed in both directions at junction 1A with the M25, with congestion reaching junction 1 at the Denham Roundabout.

Drivers are facing "long delays" in both directions along the M25 on approach to the M40.

News.title: Five men arrested in RAF Fairford incident released on police bail
News.content:
Five men who were arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences near RAF Fairford are being released on police bail, counter-terror police have said.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said officers were exploring "multiple lines of inquiry", including whether proxies or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state were involved.

The five men are all UK nationals in their 20s from London.

They were initially detained on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Counter-terror police said they remained under investigation and their release was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others".

Three of the men live in Westminster, one in Camden and another in Willesden, police said, and they are aged between 23 and 25.

A farmer who called 999 to report the three white vans in the village of Whelford, which lies directly east of the base, told the BBC it was "pure luck" that she spotted them.

The woman, who wished to remain anonymous, said she arrived home to find the driveway and road blocked and saw a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"When they saw me they ran ahead of me - some into the field and some towards the neighbouring village of Kempsford. I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

She said that she called the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford but received no answer. She then rang 999 at 01:36 BST and said "within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she added.

News.title: Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid
News.content:
Andy Burnham is expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid in his first party conference speech as Labour leader on Tuesday.

The prime minister will tell party activists in Liverpool that the new publicly owned company, branded Great British Grid, will speed up grid hook-ups by driving up competition for connection projects.

Burnham is expected to put the proposals at the heart of a new goal to bring UK energy costs in line with other nations in Europe within ten years.

He will promise to have an "honest conversation" with the public and take on the "difficult issues" that have been ignored for too long.

Burnham is expected to bill the creation of the GB Grid as the first significant move in his ambition to provide greater public control of utilities, which he put at the centre of his pitch for power over the summer.

He is expected to say that faster connections to the electricity grid could help fix a "cost crisis" in energy that has proved "crippling for businesses".

Full details of the new body are yet to be set out, but Labour said it would invest in and compete for transmission connection projects alongside the three private companies that currently own and manage the grid in Britain.

The party said it would also make it easier for firms waiting to be connected to the grid to finance connection infrastructure themselves, with GB Grid supporting and potentially co-investing in projects alongside them.

Labour has said that funding for the new body will be found within the existing budget of GB Energy, the public green investment company set up by Labour last year and which is now headquartered in Aberdeen.

News.title: Delays in fitting electronic tags putting victims at risk, report finds
News.content:
Almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements are not fitted on time, with significant delays putting victims in England and Wales at risk, a report has found.

The report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) says some criminals are waiting up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.

Only 55% of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, while 60% of alcohol monitoring tags were fitted promptly, according to the report's findings.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government was delivering the "biggest expansion of tagging in British history" with Â£100 million in funding.

Electronic monitoring is used by the Probation Service to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order.

A total of 27,847 people were given tagging orders with equipment in England and Wales as of June 2026.

"There is a real danger that electronic monitoring creates a false sense of assurance if the technology is not matched by effective professional practice," said Martin Jones CBE, HM Chief Inspector of Probation.

"Expanding tagging programmes without addressing their weaknesses risks overpromising and underdelivering on public protection," he added.

In some cases, there were waits of more than two weeks for the equipment while one in 10 people waited five months to be tagged after the required time.

Some of the reasons for tags not being fitted on time included individuals not making themselves available.

Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman OBE said victims needed to "know immediately" if tagging was delayed because this could give a "false sense of security".

She said a "robust response" was required in the event of breaches but there were "real concerns" over how "overstretched" probation services would be able to handle this.

Data from the tags was often found to be underused with major violations raised and explored in just 46% of relevant cases, the report also found.

Inspectors discovered little evidence that electronic monitoring was being used consistently to promote behaviour change.

There are three types of tags:

curfew tags

location tags

alcohol tags

They include strict controls of an offender's punishment to manage risk, safeguarding and the protection of victims.

Those who breach their orders either immediately return to prison, are given a court order or a formal warning.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "public protection" was the government's priority.

They said: "That's why we are delivering the biggest expansion of tagging in British history, backed by Â£100 million in funding, with tag install rates up by nearly 50% since 2024.

"This is part of our record Â£700 million investment in probation and community services, recruiting 2,300 trainee officers over the last two years and a further 1,300 this year â ensuring dangerous offenders are kept under closer surveillance than ever before."

Plans to significantly expand electronic monitoring were announced earlier this year as part of the Sentencing Act 2026, which aims to ease prison pressures by managing more offenders in the community.

Thousands more prisoners will be released early from October as part of the new law. Most will require tagging.

News.title: Migrants using longer, more dangerous routes across Channel
News.content:
A growing number of migrants are trying to cross the Channel on small boats using longer routes from beaches further south and west of Calais and Dunkirk, French authorities say.

Last week one boat set off from Normandy and spent more than 30 hours at sea, before being intercepted and taken to Dover by Border Force.

Although attempts from Normandy have been rare, authorities in neighbouring Seine-Maritime say there have already been 58 attempts this year, up from 30 last year.

The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings, with figures showing a sharp drop in arrivals this year.

Despite overall crossings dropping, the stretch of coastline used for smuggling appears to be widening.

Earlier this month another migrant boat was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight having set off from the Cherbourg area.

These locations are nearly 80 miles (128 km) from the beaches where many of the small boats have crossed in recent years, with those on board spending longer at sea.

News.title: Temperatures to hit 25C in burst of late September warmth
News.content:
The boost in temperatures will come as a strong southerly airflow develops into Tuesday.

With unusually hot air across France and Spain - where temperatures have widely been in excess of 30C - the southerly wind will bring some of this warmth to the UK.

Temperatures across England will exceed 20C widely with the highest temperatures in south-east England where it will get into the mid-20s Celsius.

Average temperatures across England in late September are around 16 to 19C.

While there could be a lot of cloud with a few showers on Tuesday morning, sunny spells will develop over England and Wales.

It will also be warmer than average across Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland with maximum temperatures on Tuesday of 17 to 22C.

However, after starting sunny here, cloud will increase during the day.

The southerly winds will strengthen with gusts up to 50mph expected in Northern Ireland and western Scotland.

This is linked to a large and deep area of low pressure moving north in the eastern Atlantic toward Iceland.

News.title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
News.content:
The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News.

Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously."

Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK."

Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans.

"In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran."

The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher.

US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.33p on Monday, according to the RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 199.09p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.23p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October.

A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March.

Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel."

News.title: Egyptian officials convicted of kidnapping Cambridge student found dead in 2016
News.content:
Three Egyptian security officials have been convicted by a Rome court over the kidnapping of an Italian student whose tortured body was found in Cairo a decade ago.

The men, who were tried in absentia, denied the charges. On Monday they were sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges of aggravated kidnapping. A fourth Egyptian defendant was acquitted.

Giulio Regeni, 28, was studying for a doctorate at Cambridge University when he went missing while on a research trip in Egypt in 2016.

Days later, his mutilated body was found in a ditch near Cairo. An autopsy later revealed he had been tortured.

Italian and Egyptian prosecutors originally investigated the case together, but reached opposing conclusions.

Egyptian authorities argued criminal gangsters were to blame for Regeni's murder and suggested various other explanations for his death, including a car accident, failed drug deal, or botched robbery.

They also denied any state involvement in Regeni's disappearance or death.

But prosecutors in Rome concluded that the Egyptian national security agency was involved in the crime.

The four defendants were Gen Tariq Sabir, Col Usham Helmi, Col Athar Kamel Mohamed Ibrahim and Maj Magdi Ibrahim Abdelal Sharif. Sabir was acquitted.

Rome's chief prosecutor and a lawyer for Regeni's family welcomed the verdict.

"From today, people around the world can feel safer," Alessandra Ballerini, the family's lawyer, said. "Impunity can be defeated and democracies can place limits on arbitrary power."

Regeni's family have campaigned throughout the decade for justice. As the verdict was read out, there was silence from family members and supporters in court who wore yellow t-shirts and badges, the colour of their campaign, AFP reported.

News.title: Warning more homes will be uninsurable due to flood risk
News.content:
Homes are being built today that could become uninsurable in the future due to the risk of flooding, the boss of insurance giant Aviva has said.

Amanda Blanc said the risk of flooding is "absolutely increasing", but based on current building patterns 115,000 new homes will be built in flood zones in the next decade.

"That doesn't seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built," she told the BBC.

About 6.3 million homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency, and Aviva research found one in nine homes built between 2022 and 2024 are at medium to high risk of flooding.

Blanc told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that England was "for sure" building homes that might be uninsurable at some point in the future.

"It's very well known where these flooding areas are. Let's think very carefully about homes that are being built."

Blanc said construction that borders those flood zones also needs a different approach.

"You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood," she said.

According to Aviva's research, nearly a third of new homes built in 2024 will be at risk of some flooding by 2050, and one in seven would be at medium to high risk of flooding as extreme weather becomes more acute.

Earlier this year the Met Office estimated that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters like the one experienced in the UK in 2023-2024 have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: Slipknot fans hit back after Marilyn Manson announced as support act for UK show
News.content:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

News.title: Mahmood signals rethink on migrants' right to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is willing to rethink plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK.

The home secretary has been under pressure to water down the proposals from a significant number of Labour MPs, including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, and trade unions.

In a speech to Labour's annual conference, Mahmood acknowledged "some have said elements of these reforms are not fair".

And she said the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

Mahmood suggested doubling the time it takes for most migrants to qualify for the right from five to 10 years. Some of those who came to the UK on health and social care visas could wait up to 15 years, under the proposals.

Earlier this year, when Rayner was a backbench MP, she accused the government of "moving the goalposts", branding Mahmood's plans "un-British" - and then stuck with her criticisms when she re-joined the cabinet.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison, said the proposed changes would unfairly penalise overseas care workers.

Home Office sources insist no final decision on changes to the immigration rules have been taken, and Mahmood was setting out the principles that would guide her in her conference speech.

The home secretary told delegates: "As we restore control and fairness to our asylum system, we must do the same for legal migration too.

"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did, and fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young.

"That same principle underpins my reforms to the right to live here indefinitely, ensuring settled status is earned by those who have shown a consistent commitment to this country."

And she vowed to come up with a policy that was fair to those who "came here legally" and to British citizens.

A Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain.

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Speaking earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham denied Mahmood had been forced to ditch the plans because Rayner viewed them as "un-British", saying the reforms would need to "strike the right balance".

Asked whether he was "Team Shabana" or "Team Angela," he told LBC: "I'm both of them, I'm Team Angela and Shabana.

"But it just reflects that there's a consultation, there's different not just opinions from politicians, but obviously there's a range of views that have gone into that consultation, so we're in the process now of looking at that."

News.title: Russian foreign minister questions 'what will become of UK' and future of 'the Celts'
News.content:
Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums.

Sergey Lavrov made the comments at a youth conference where he said he did "not know what will become of the country called Great Britain", according to The Times, external.

The comments come weeks after the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland declared "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and signed an agreement to say it had no right to "block democracy".

In response to Lavrov's comments, Plaid Cymru said Wales' constitutional future was "a matter for the people of Wales", and "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".

In the conference, Lavrov also suggested the west had too much influence in the UN Security Council, external - the five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US.

According to The Times, he said: "The Celts â Wales, Ireland, Scotland â are now seeking to hold referenda.

"We do not advocate the expulsion of any of the permanent members of the security council. Although, of course, the scale of the British Empire, when it first took its seat in the UN security council at the organisation's founding, has, naturally, diminished to the utmost degree."

News.title: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
News.content:
The chancellor has warned against allowing Britain's benefits bill to balloon while not offering young people opportunities.

John Healey told Labour's annual conference in Liverpool that cutting welfare spending was "more than an economic must - it's a moral duty".

"The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage," he said.

He announced the expansion of a Local Apprenticeships Service for mayors in England, which he said would deliver thousands more apprenticeships for young people.

Healey's speech comes as he faces pressure to cut public spending or raise taxes ahead of next month's Budget to bring down government borrowing costs.

In an attempt to reassure the markets, he said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" with him and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "united on meeting the fiscal rules".

Fiscal rules are the government's self-imposed constraints to manage decisions on spending and tax.

The Budget would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space", the chancellor said.

And he admitted that "the money New Labour had in the '90s is simply not there now".

Healey blamed the Conservative Party's time in government for leaving Britain spending more on debt than on the Home Office, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice combined.

Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said in response to the speech that "Labour MPs will never support cutting the out-of-control welfare bill" and "with Labour, it's always more taxes if you work and more benefits if you don't".

Healey praised young people as "digital natives, whip-smart, questioning, ambitious, brave" who could move from "generation jeopardy to generation hope".

But he pointed to the million young people not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - which he said created a necessity to make benefits a bridge into work, rather than a "trap".

"It is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn't offer a future," he said.

Asked how quickly the bill might come down, when he appeared on the BBC's Newscast, Healey would not commit to the benefits bill falling, saying he "won't set a timeline" for the UK's benefits bill coming down by the time of the next election.

News.title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
News.content:
Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.

News.title: UK diesel price hits all-time high, the RAC says
News.content:
The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers.

The Chancellor said on Monday that the the "place" and "time" for the government to deal with questions around rising petrol and diesel prices and fuel duty is next month's Budget.

John Healey told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm acutely concerned and conscious about how hard it is for families. I see that at the pumps myself.

"We can't remove the cost of living pressures, we can't remove the prices that people are having to pay, but where we can we will act and we will give people just a bit of breathing space, and the same goes for the cost to business."

Simon Williams, the RAC's head of policy, said record diesel prices "spell pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans".

"Undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers," he said. Williams said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days".

The price of Brent crude, a benchmark for global oil used to make petrol, diesel and other fuel products, rose over the weekend and is now hovering at around $108 per barrel. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has also implemented an export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply.

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

News.title: Lithium-ion battery caused fire that killed mum and 3 children
News.content:
A house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September.

Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters.

Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire."

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property, at 03:45 BST.

MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom.

A man was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

In search of an island of abundant spirituality, hospitality and dynamic terrain? Bali’s rice terraces, jungle interiors and teeming corals might be your answer.

Temperate waters, a balmy dry season from April to October and inviting forecasts of 30C mean sinking your toes into the sands on the Indonesian archipelago’s most popular island is a staple of most backpacker itineraries.

The coastline of the “Island of Gods” is built for year-round surfing, sunning yourself with an arak cocktail and catching sunsets over the Indian Ocean from the comfort of a beach beanbag.

There’s something for everyone on the island, where lively beach clubs meet crashing swells and off-grid stretches of white sand.

Whether strolling the serene swathes of Pemuteran and Sanur or watching the dolphins dive off Lovina, here are the best Balinese shorelines to lay your towel.



1. Melasti Beach

open image in gallery Melasti Beach is located on the southern tip of Bali's Bukit Peninsula ( Getty Images )

A drop-down from the limestone cliffs on Bali’s southern coast, Melasti Beach has white sands, calm waters and some serious sunsets for a full day at the beach. The beach is also the site of the Balinese Melasti purification ceremony held a few days before Nyepi (the Day of Silence), a period of self-reflection.

2. Jimbaran Bay

open image in gallery Jimbaran is a white crescent of sand in the south ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Renowned for its skyscapes as the sun sinks below the horizon, Jimbaran Bay, a sweeping crescent of fine sand in the south, is one of Bali’s best beaches. Seafood joints line the bay selling freshly caught lobster and prawns, and guitarists strum to tourists as they eat, drink and bathe near the many holiday properties that have made the fishing village their home.

3. Kelingking Beach

open image in gallery The Nusa Penida beach is reachable by a 400-metre trail ( Getty Images )

Bali’s Kelingking Beach is not a journey for the faint-hearted. The secluded beach, situated on Nusa Penida Island, the largest of a trio on Bali’s southeast coast, is reachable only by a 400-metre trek down a limestone cliff face to the white sand and blue waters. Although travellers cannot swim off Kelingking, take the day trip during off-peak times to experience spectacular scenes at sunrise with a smaller crowd.



4. Nusa Dua Beach

open image in gallery Exclusive resorts dot the Nusa Dua coast ( Getty Images )

On Bali’s southern tip, Nusa Dua’s glitzy gated development puts four-poster cabanas and colourful parasols on the powder sands for hours of lounging in front of the turquoise seascape. Its position on the Indian Ocean and landscaped seafront make Nusa Dua an elevated beach day for some high-class R&R.

5. Seminyak Beach

open image in gallery The stylish sands of Seminyak are ideal for sunset viewing ( Getty Images )

Seminyak on the south-west coast has surf swells and boutique shopping for tourists to enjoy watersports and tan top-ups before cocktails and DJs after dark. The beach, primed for both kicking your feet up with a holiday read and lively sunset viewing sessions, buzzes with the legendary Potato Head Beach Club for social adventures with friends old and new.

6. Lovina Beach

open image in gallery Lovina is a playground for dolphins ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The black sands of Lovina on the north Bali coast are a world away from the busy coast of Seminyak. A playground for bottlenose dolphins, with calm waves and plenty of space for sunning yourself, this is a laidback stretch of sand. Think snorkelling among corals rampant with marine life and hopping on a boat tour to watch the dolphins dance.

7. Sanur Beach

open image in gallery Five miles of golden sand stretch Sanur ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Among Bali’s best, Sanur Beach boasts five miles of golden sand, gentle Indian Ocean waters and bobbing red, yellow and blue jukung fishing boats. It has a reputation for tranquillity, and its slow pace of life proves popular with families. Fringed by a promenade of restaurants and brunch spots, and with draws of paddleboarding, kayaking and yoga, this southeast seaside haunt isn’t one you’ll want to miss.



8. Pemuteran Beach

open image in gallery Bali’s serene northwest coast is a haven for beach bathing ( Getty Images )

This underrated fishing village in the northwest of Bali may be quaint, but it has maintained a natural charm to rival the hustle and bustle of the island’s southern coast. Pemuteran is a shore not only for beach-bathing but for snorkelling among vibrant coral reefs, taking the plunge to impressive dive sites and gentle dips in the crystal shallows. Keep an eye out for green turtles – there is a local hatchery to help the endangered species repopulate.

9. Canggu Beach

open image in gallery Canggu Beach is known for its vibrant sunsets ( Getty Images )

For a more lively coastline, Canggu on Bali’s southwest coast is famous for its dark sand and rolling waves. Surf breaks here are popular with beginners and experienced riders, and there are beach clubs, cafes and restaurants offering plenty of refreshments after a day spent on the sand. After dark, the popular beach is a hotspot for tourists looking to take in Canggu’s vibrant sunsets.

Following record-breaking temperatures this summer, the UK is braced for cloudy days, colder temperatures and higher rainfall in October.

While the weather is often inconsistent at home, several destinations abroad are consistently graced with hours of sunshine.

With kids back in school and many people avoiding holidays so close to the Christmas period, this is an excellent – and often affordable – month for an autumn getaway.

Southern European cities, including Seville and Valletta, stay pleasantly warm while countries in the southern hemisphere are only just beginning to enter their own summer season.

With careful planning, you can find great value holidays to destinations across the world, while still soaking up the sun. We’ve rounded up a list of some of the best.



Best autumn sun holiday destinations

1. Seville, Spain

open image in gallery Plaza de España, part of Seville’s Maria Luisa park ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 21C

21C Hours of sunshine per day: Seven

October brings cooler temperatures to continental Europe’s warmest city, but daily highs still reach a pleasant 27C. This makes it a great month to explore the Andalusian capital, as you can avoid the sweltering summer temperatures while sightseeing.

To discover the city’s Moorish influence, start at the Casa de Pilatos palace, before moving on to the Torre del Oro, or tower of gold. Then head to the Real Alcazar palace and gardens. Nearby is the city’s cathedral – a Gothic marvel that is among the largest churches in the world – and the Giralda Tower.

For those who prefer to simply wander, the banks of the Guadalquivir river are a good place to start. The María Luisa Park – and its centrepiece, the Plaza de España – are worthy of an extended visit, as are the numerous sites built for the Ibero-American Expo of 1929 (such as the Plaza de América).



2. Valletta, Malta

open image in gallery The beautiful harbour at Valletta ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 24C

24C Hours of sunshine per day: Seven

October falls in Malta’s shoulder season, but temperatures in the capital remain high enough for an enjoyable, sun-kissed trip. With highs of around 25C, October is a great time to explore the city while avoiding the scorching heat.

The city itself is a Unesco World Heritage Site, with its grand fortifications providing pleasant sightseeing opportunities as you explore. The main tourist sights include St John’s Co-Cathedral, Fort St Elmo (and the National War Museum) and the Grandmaster’s Palace.

Nevertheless, the city cannot be reduced solely to its heritage castles and religious sites. The waterfront features a collection of 18th-century warehouse buildings that now house various restaurants, cafes and shops along the promenade, while the Upper and Lower Barrakka Gardens are the city’s main green spaces.

October also sees the city’s annual Notte Bianca festival, an arts celebration that takes place in various venues across the city, for example, at the City Gates (this year, it will be held on 3 October).



3. Oahu, Hawaii, USA

open image in gallery Waikiki Beach is one of the most famous on the island ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 27C

27C Hours of sunshine per day: Eight

While all of the Hawaiian islands are undeniably idyllic, Oahu is the top pick due to its amazing natural beauty and high temperatures reaching 29C.

Honolulu, the state capital, has all the classic character of any major city, with the addition of a beachside location and a rainforest backdrop.

Despite this unique metropolis being the “centre point” of the island, it is far from its biggest draw. Hundreds of incredible beaches line the coasts, with stunning white sands found at Waikiki and Lanikai.

Other areas worth exploring include various tours of the (privately-owned) Kualoa Ranch – the filming location for the original Jurassic Park films.



4. Sardinia, Italy

open image in gallery An aerial view of the beautiful village of Bosa in Sardinia ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 18C

18C Hours of sunshine per day: Six

This Mediterranean island has long been a top tourist destination, including among Italians in the know. While average temperatures only hover around 18C, average highs still climb to 22C, making the island a top choice for that last bit of autumn sun.

The waters will also be warm, meaning you can relax on the beach (or take part in any number of water sports) in areas like the Costa Smeralda or Cala Goloritzé.

While spending all your time kicking back at various beaches may be tempting, part of the lure of Sardinia is the opportunity for exploration. The island contains some of the most picturesque towns in Italy, with Alghero, Bosa, San Teodoro, and several others home to medieval buildings, castles and colourful riverside houses.

If you’d rather stay in nature, there are also three national parks and ten regional parks, with Asinara and Gennargentu among the most beautiful.



5. Cyprus

open image in gallery A rock arch near Cavo Greco, Ayia Napa ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 23C

23C Hours of sunshine per day: Eight

One of the warmest places in Europe during October, Cyprus offers temperatures in the mid-20s. The island was granted independence in 1960, but has an extensive history involving ancient Greeks, Romans and many other historic civilisations.

If you want to delve deeper into this history, some of its most famous landmarks include the Tombs of the Kings, Kolossi Castle and the ancient city of Kourion.

While many of its towns and cities are steeped in history, today the island enjoys a reputation as a tourist hotspot. Think pristine, sun-soaked beaches, a healthy Mediterranean lifestyle and dozens of villages (including Omodos and Lefkara) where visitors can experience well-preserved Cypriot traditions, cuisine and culture.



6. Algarve, Portugal

open image in gallery A beach in Carvoeiro, Algarve ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 23C

23C Hours of sunshine per day: Seven

Tucked away in the southernmost region of Portugal’s mainland, the Algarve has similar annual sunshine hours to California, and October does not skimp on rays.

The area is famous for its long stretches of silky-soft sand, but it is also ideal for hiking. One of the best known is the Via Algarviana, which is an old pilgrims’ route that connects Alcoutim (on the eastern Spanish border) to Cabo de São Vicente.

If taking a hike is not your bag, Faro’s charming old town offers historical sites, such as the macabre Chapel of Bones.



7. Mauritius

open image in gallery A beach on Le Morne, a peninsula in the southwest of Mauritius ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 22C

22C Hours of sunshine per day: Eight

Situated in the Indian Ocean, Mauritius is always going to have to compete with the Maldives and the Seychelles.

This African country (found 700 miles east of Madagascar) still contains many of the attractions that make its rivals so popular. The weather is still perfect in October – with average highs reaching around 27C.

Water-based activities are popular, with opportunities for diving, swimming and snorkelling in the numerous coral reefs, as well as kayaking and canoeing.

If too much beach begins to bore you, fear not: the island also contains several other natural areas, including Black River Gorges National Park (covered in tropical rainforest) and the Casela Nature Park.

When you’re ready to return to civilisation, towns such as Flic-en-Flac and Grand Baie possess a pleasant mix of daytime relaxation and lively evenings.



8. Rhodes, Greece

open image in gallery Lindos, a village on the island of Rhodes ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 22C

22C Hours of sunshine per day: Eight

Another one of Greece’s seemingly endless list of important historical locations, Rhodes was once home to the Colossus, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Nowadays, it is home to a Unesco-listed Old Town, where visitors can explore well-preserved fortifications, narrow limestone streets and archaeological sites.

Like almost every Greek island, Rhodes also possesses beautiful beaches and towns. Lindos and Faliraki offer gorgeous beaches, perfect for a dip in the Aegean. They are also a great place to visit a taverna or sample mezze at the end of a long, relaxing day.



9. Cape Town, South Africa

open image in gallery October marks the start of spring in Cape Town ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 20C

20C Hours of sunshine per day: Nine

October marks the start of spring in Cape Town, when average highs stay at a manageable 22C. South Africa’s legislative capital, Cape Town, is a popular destination for Brits looking to travel further afield.

Its neighbourhoods are an eclectic blend of calm beach areas and lively artistic hubs, with the V&A Waterfront, Camps Bay and Bo-Kaap among them.

Many people head to the city for its mix of urban living and abundant countryside. The Cape Floristic Region and West Coast National Park are nearby, while the Kirstenbosch Botanical Garden is one of the most popular sites in the city.

Lion’s Head and Table Mountain offer hiking opportunities with amazing views of the city below, but the plethora of sandy beaches and hidden coves might be too tempting.



10. Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

open image in gallery Brazil’s temperatures tend to start to climb in October ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in October: 26C

26C Hours of sunshine per day: Five

Brazil’s temperatures tend to climb in October, making it a perfect time to travel a little further to visit the country’s second-largest city.

While December to February are Rio de Janeiro’s peak summer months, October may be the better option for budget travellers who want to avoid high prices.

A typical itinerary will include a trip to the remarkable Christ the Redeemer statue, a night out in the Lapa neighbourhood, and a visit to the chilled-out Santa Teresa neighbourhood.

However, the city is also home to some iconic stretches of sand. Visiting the two-and-a-half-mile-long Copacabana beach might be on your bucket list, but a trip to the slightly less well-known but just as beautiful Ipanema is also a great choice.

A 77-year-old couple gunned down their son-in-law in a California city park over the weekend, authorities said, and court documents showed the victim had been in a bitter custody dispute with their daughter.

Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was shot to death Saturday afternoon in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release.

Authorities arrested Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77 and from Dublin, on suspicion of murder and other charges. They were due to appear in court Wednesday morning. It was not immediately clear if either had obtained a lawyer, and phone numbers listed for their daughter, Candice Jang, were disconnected.

The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang's divorce case. The couple had been married since about 2012 and had three young children, court records show.

Court records show that Jang reported McKinsey to police in 2023, accusing him of shoving one of their children and using rough physical discipline with them generally.

Last October, she obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey after he was arrested and charged with misdemeanor child abuse in another case. Police said he acknowledged having slapped one child and also charged him with endangering another. At the time of his killing, he was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program, the San Jose Mercury News reported.

McKinsey responded to his wife's court filing by requesting a domestic violence protection order against her and filing for divorce. He since had sought more time with the three children, noting that he had been limited to two hours of supervised visits per week since last fall, Alameda County court documents show.

In his petition for a protection order, McKinsey, who was transgender, alleged that Chen had directed anti-LGBTQ+ slurs at him and at one of their children, the Mercury News reported. He also accused Jang of being abusive during medical procedures related to his transition.

McKinsey joined The New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

___

Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Olga R. Rodríguez in San Francisco contributed.

A new law against religious conversion has prompted churches in India to ask worshippers to sign “declarations” saying they are attending prayer meetings of their own free will.

The legislation comes into force in the western state of Maharashtra on 28 August.

It allows authorities to act against conversions that are alleged to involve coercion, fraud, inducement, or marriage. It also requires anyone planning to convert to another religion to notify their district magistrate at least two months in advance, with procedural violations carrying a prison term of up to seven years.

The “self-declaration” forms prepared by churches in the state capital Mumbai and neighbouring districts ask all worshippers to affirm that they are attending voluntarily and under “no pressure, inducement, temptation, lure, or threat of any kind”.

The churches now also require each congregant to submit a photograph and a government-issued identity number.

Pastor Sam Mathai of Vasai in Palghar district told the PTI newswire that the completed forms, which he said were being collected for “self-safety”, would be kept at church offices and produced before authorities if requested.

The collection of the “self declaration” forms, he said, had been going for two to three months.

It appears to be a precautionary measure amid growing sectarian tensions around Christian prayer meetings in the region. The move also comes in the backdrop of the case against Pankaj Devnoor, a British church leader who is barred from leaving India while he faces charges under the same law.

“Right-wing groups enter churches without intimation and beat up people,” Mr Mathai explained. “So pastors and community leaders came together to find a solution. We don’t force anyone to come and pray. The Indian constitution allows everyone to pray of their own will.”

In the past five months, Christian prayer meetings and church services have been disrupted in several places across the Mumbai metropolitan region. In most cases, the attackers have identified themselves as members of Hindu groups such as the Bajrang Dal and the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and claimed that they were preventing illegal religious conversions.

The Bajrang Dal is the youth wing of the Vishwa Hindu Parishad, which is known for running campaigns, sometimes violent, against cow slaughter, religious conversions, and what it denounces as the influence of Western culture. These groups operate within the Hindu nationalist ecosystem called the Sangh Parivar, led by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

The VHP website claims that the Bajrang Dal has campaigned against the “religious conversion of Hindus by the Christian church”.

On 12 April, a Sunday prayer meeting of 100-150 people at the Dhiraj Shopping Centre in Vasai East was disrupted after a group of men, including members of the Bajrang Dal, barged into the venue.

The incident led to five police complaints being filed over the following 24 hours, four against the person conducting the meetings and one against his accusers.

In this backdrop, churches say the “self-declaration” forms are intended to protect both pastors and worshippers from accusations under the new law.

At the New Hope Church in Virar, Pastor Steven Rozario, 49, recently told his congregation: “This is a self-declaration form. I want all of you to fill it out, attach a passport-size photograph and bring it with you next Sunday when we meet for prayer.”

According to the Indian Express, he continued: “Considering the continuous disruptions and attacks during prayer meetings, we’re keeping these forms with us so that if someone questions us in the future and claims that we forced or compelled you to attend the prayer meeting, we can show this as proof.”

He alleged that in most cases, “police do not even register FIRs against those who cause the violence”.

“The new law has given a free pass to those who break the law.”

Christians make up only about 2.3 per cent of India’s population, yet attacks and disruptions by Hindu groups targeting their religious gatherings are on the rise.

OpenAI said Monday it was delaying the release of a new artificial intelligence model out of security concerns voiced by its researchers, the latest in the company's effort to decelerate the pace of the technology's advance.

OpenAI’s decision to hold back the model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up. The announcement comes a day before AI executives are set to huddle with President Donald Trump in Washington as technology companies face new pressure to be accountable for how their models can be abused.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report the delay of OpenAI’s model release.

In a statement from OpenAI's head of safety systems Saachi Jain, the version “didn't quite meet the bar.” It had become more persistent in completing tasks, but OpenAI needed to balance that capability against unauthorized behavior.

Jain insisted the company was committed to ensuring the model was safe whether in the company's testing or is in the hands of users. "We have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” she said.

OpenAI paused training of its most advanced models last week, saying training would resume “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards.”

That was after it disclosed instances in which AI agents exceeded their instructions, including by accessing government websites without authorization.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has joined other industry leaders in calling for a slowdown, warning that companies do not yet have adequate safeguards to control the most capable systems. Altman was scheduled to deliver the keynote address for OpenAI's annual conference for software developers on Tuesday in San Francisco. OpenAI President Greg Brockman is expected to attend the White House's event Tuesday.

News.content:

CNN host Jake Tapper ripped into a district attorney from upstate New York over his handling of a case involving a former Cornell University student who was allegedly raped by seven men at a frat house.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten and his office have faced fierce public backlash after the former student, who goes by Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit earlier this month alleging that she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell in October 2024.

At one point in the night of the alleged assaults, one of the men sent a message in the fraternity’s Snapchat group saying there was “free p****” and inviting other members to join, according to the suit.

Tapper grilled Van Houten over the fact that no criminal charges were brought against the men for two years, despite the woman, who was a 20-year-old sorority member at the time, reporting the incident to the Cornell University Police Department three weeks after it happened.

“I have a daughter. I can't imagine how mad I would be if a district attorney handled this case that way for my daughter,” Tapper said on his show The Lead Monday. “Do you not acknowledge that your office dropped the ball by not looking more into what happened?”

open image in gallery CNN host Jake Tapper has ripped into Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten over his handling of a case involving a former Cornell University student who was allegedly raped by seven men at a frat house ( CNN )

Van Houten pushed back, telling Tapper, “My job under the New York State Constitution is to apply the penal law of New York State. We are constrained by that law. Whether you agree with it, whether you think someone's conduct is morally repugnant or vulgar or disgusting. I'm still constrained by the law.”

The DA has argued that the accusations provided in Jane Doe’s six-page statement to university police provide no evidence of a lack of consent as defined by New York State law.

Tapper said that he concluded from the summary of the police statement that the DA publicly released “is that she consented to a threesome with two other guys, but she did not consent to the five other guys that came into the room, and that she hid under the covers, and she pushed one away, and nothing that happened with those five other guys sounds consensual at all to me. Am I reading this wrong?”

“Frankly, you are,” Van Houten retorted. “But consent or lack of consent is very much very specific under New York State law.

“You either have to be physically compelled...or you have to be physically helpless, which is unconscious, or you have to be mentally incapacitated, which is having been given drugs without your knowledge that rendered you incapable of consenting — none of those things were articulated in her initial statement.”

open image in gallery The former student filed a lawsuit earlier this month alleging that she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell in October 2024 ( Getty Images )

According to the DA’s summary of the police statement, the woman said she came to the frat house as a “5 out of 10” on a scale of drunkenness and that she became an “8 out of 10” throughout the night. She also said she took Ketamine multiple times during the night.

Tapper repeatedly mentioned the “free p****” message to Van Houten, asking, “None of that made you think I should interview this woman? I should interview people at the fraternity that night. I should interview her sorority sisters, not because you were trying to find somebody guilty of a crime, but just to get to the bottom of what happened.”

“Well, it is absolutely horrific. You're 100 percent right. We do not independently investigate crimes in the district attorney's office. We rely on the police to investigate those crimes,” Van Houten said, adding that the woman “told the police candidly what she remembered, and maybe she remembers more now. And if she does, then we want to put that in front of the grand jury.”

It was another member of the fraternity who showed the woman the Snapchat message, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra, told the New York Post, calling that student’s actions “honorable.”

Amid the public outrage, Cornell released a statement Monday saying it supports the DA’s decision for the case to be heard by a criminal grand jury.

open image in gallery Tapper grilled Van Houten over the fact that no criminal charges were brought against the men for two years, despite the woman reporting the incident to the Cornell University Police Department three weeks after it happened ( Getty Images )

“Cornell also conducted a thorough Title IX investigation, which is separate from a criminal proceeding, over the course of several months,” the statement read.

“At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell,” the school said, adding that the fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains banned from campus.

But Cornell refused to refund the woman’s tuition after the alleged gang rape so she could transfer to another school, Giuffra told the Post.

“Her dreams were destroyed by a group of men who sought to abuse and humiliate her,” Giuffra said in a statement to The Independent. “She was subjected to unspeakable horrors that I have not seen in my 30 years of handling abuse cases.”

For those affected by rape and sexual abuse, if you are in the United States, you can call Rainn on 800-656-HOPE (4673).

Rape Crisis also offers support. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk.

An airstrike carried out by Myanmar’s military near a market in territory controlled by a powerful rebel group killed at least 49 people and wounded 58 others on Monday, the group and a rescue official said.

The attack in western Rakhine state was the latest in a series of deadly airstrikes against pro-democracy resistance forces and ethnic armed groups across the country.

Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on Feb. 1, 2021, triggering widespread opposition. After security forces suppressed peaceful protests with lethal force, many opponents of military rule took up arms, plunging large parts of the country into conflict.

Monday’s attack occurred in Kyauktaw township, about 340 kilometers (210 miles) west of Mandalay, the country’s second-largest city, according to the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group based in Rakhine which controls Kyauktaw.

It was impossible to independently confirm details of the attack.

The Arakan Army said in a statement released early Tuesday that a fighter jet dropped two bombs near a local market around noon, killing vendors, shoppers and pedestrians.

The group said 58 other people were injured, 22 of them critically .

The statement said the group "will take effective retaliatory measures soon against the individuals and organizations directly responsible for the attacks involving deliberate airstrikes that have caused mass casualties.”

Wai Hun Aung, a senior rescue official in Rakhine, confirmed the casualties to The Associated Press, citing rescue workers at the scene. He said the market was the region’s main wholesale center, drawing traders and shoppers from across the state.

“This is one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine,” he said.

Photos and videos posted on social media showed buildings on fire, damaged vehicles and parts of a nearby bridge destroyed.

The military did not immediately comment on the attack. It has previously said it strikes only legitimate military targets and has accused resistance groups of terrorism.

The Arakan Army is the well-trained and well-armed military wing of a movement seeking autonomy for Rakhine’s ethnic minority from Myanmar’s central government. It launched an offensive in Rakhine in November 2023 and has since captured a strategically important regional military headquarters and 14 of the state’s 17 townships.

The military has imposed severe restrictions on trade routes since fighting intensified in Rakhine, worsening food shortages.

In December, a military airstrike on a hospital in Rakhine’s Mrauk-U township killed at least 34 people and wounded 80 others.
