Sports.title: Leicestershire's points deduction for poor pitch reduced
Sports.content:
Leicestershire’s 27-point deduction for breaching pitch regulations in August's win over Glamorgan has been reduced to 19.

The Foxes were relegated from Division One of the County Championship last week following an innings defeat by champions Warwickshire.

Leicestershire's groundsman Callum Lewin had argued filming of an unscheduled Bollywood film - believed to be for a biopic of former India captain Sourav Ganguly - had taken place at the ground four days before the Glamorgan fixture between August 20-23, preventing the pitch from being covered for eight hours in bright sunshine and heatwave temperatures.

The Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) upheld the charge against Leicestershire for a breach of the ECB's Pitch Regulations.

It imposed an immediate eight-point deduction from the County Championship plus the 19 points Leicestershire earned from winning the match by 42 runs.

A further eight-point deduction was also suspended until the end of the 2027 season and a £5,000 fine.

Leicestershire confirmed last Thursday that they would appeal against the original sanction.

Following the CDP holding a further hearing last Wednesday, the sanction has been amended with Leicestershire having eight points reinstated.

Leicestershire chief executive Emma White said in a statement: "The (CDP) Panel made clear that the latest hearing and Amended Decision, which relates to the sanction alone, were not appeal proceedings.

"Our position on the charge is therefore unchanged. We continue to believe it should not have been upheld, and that we ought not to have suffered the points deduction we have. We therefore still intend to appeal, focusing upon the process and resultant evidential position upon which the Panel was caused to decide the case.

"Our recently instructed counsel, Craig Harris, and Oliver Laurence of Periculum Sport shall continue to act for the Club throughout the appeal process.

"As we are now engaged in that process, it would not be appropriate for the club to comment further at this stage. I would again ask all supporters to do the same, and to treat everyone involved, including players and staff from other counties, and those administering this process, with courtesy and respect, both at the ground and online."

The amended decision adjusts Leicestershire's points tally in Division One to 119, 17 behind third-from-bottom Essex.

A wholly successful appeal would lift Leicestershire out of the relegation zone and above Essex.

Sports.title: Man City charges: The big questions answered
Sports.content:
Sky Sports News chief reporter Kaveh Solhekol is back to answer the big questions surrounding the Premier League's long-running dispute in their 115 charges against Manchester City.

Reports last Friday said an independent tribunal has reached decisions in the case between the league and the club, and Sky Sports News understands the process is moving to the appeal stage.

Here's the latest on developments since, which have included Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak penning an open letter to the club's fans and chief executive Ferran Soriano saying the case could take years to conclude.

Why has the Premier League not commented?

Because it's a private and confidential process.

I've heard people criticise the Premier League for not issuing a statement, but their hands are tied behind their back.

They have to respect the process, which says that everything has to be private and confidential.

That's the reason why Premier League CEO Richard Masters has given nothing away when he has been asked about this subject. He's always said there isn't much he can say, he just has to let the process play out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri says nobody can take away Manchester City players' success

When can we expect to hear an official judgement?

What we got on Friday was a leak. It's been widely reported that Man City have lost the majority of the 115 charges they faced, but there has been no official confirmation that this is the case.

The two parties involved, the Premier League and Man City, both have to agree for any judgement to be released.

There is no definitive answer about when the judgment will be released - we just have to be patient.

How serious is Friday's leak to the process?

I think the issue of the leak could be serious if City felt they were forced to take this all the way, for instance, to the High Court. They could argue that this process has not been fair and impartial because of what happened on Friday.

Man City have argued something like this before, in their case against UEFA they brought up the fact there had been leaks to the media.

Many well-respected sports lawyers are refusing to comment on this case at the moment because they have not seen the judgement.

The judgement will probably be hundreds of pages long, it will take a while to digest, and only then will we all be in a position where we can comment on it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player According to reports, an independent tribunal has reached decisions in Manchester City's 115 charges case

Could other clubs sue if the Premier League's charges are proven?

We're into the realm of hypotheticals but if the charges are proven, I'm sure clubs will be contacted by lawyers who want to represent them and help them seek compensation.

We've seen in the past clubs sue other clubs for compensation so it is something that could happen but you have to remember that the Premier League is made up of 20 clubs.

Going forward, those 20 members have to think about the Premier League as a whole as well, so we have to wait and see how much appetite there is to take legal action against Manchester City if that possibility arises in the future.

Man City previously took UEFA to the Court of Arbitration for Sport to appeal. Why couldn't that happen here?

The Premier League regulations don't include the possibility of being able to go to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The rules are very clear. There is an independent tribunal. After the judgement of the independent tribunal, both sides can go to an appeal board.

The appeal would be heard by a new three-person panel. After that you effectively reach the end of the road because you can't go to CAS.

Having said that, if you have some serious issues with the way the process was conducted, then you do have the option, for instance, of going to the High Court and arguing it was unfair.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Why has Italy head coach and former Manchester City manager Roberto Mancini distanced himself from the club's charges from the Premier League?

What did former City boss Roberto Mancini talk about on Sunday?

This is all to do with an allegation published by German outlet Der Spiegel in 2018. They said they had documents which they claimed showed that when Roberto Mancini was the Man City manager, he had two contracts.

These emails apparently alleged that Mancini was being paid £1.45m net to be the manager of Man City, while at the same time he also had a contract which was worth £1.75m a year to coach four days a year in Abu Dhabi at a club called Al Jazira.

Man City have always said these emails have been taken out of context and are part of a wider effort to discredit the club.

Sports.title: Manchester City chief maintains club’s innocence as rivals push for verdict to be published
Sports.content:
A number of Premier League clubs are pushing for the Manchester City verdict to be published as soon as possible, with the club digging in for a long battle to clear their name.

City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, told a meeting of the European Football Clubs board on Monday that they will fight to prove their innocence after being found guilty by an independent commission of the vast majority of the Premier League’s 115 charges of breaching financial rules.

Soriano’s willingness to address the guilty verdict against City, which first emerged on Friday but has yet to be confirmed publicly by the club or the Premier League, was a surprise to other members of the EFC board, which includes two domestic rivals in Jean-Claude Blanc, the head of Ineos Sport and chief of international football relations at Manchester United, and the Everton owner, Dan Friedkin.

Soriano is understood to have addressed the board at the start of the meeting by requesting permission to make a brief statement. The Spaniard said that he wanted to make it clear that he disagreed with the ruling of the commission, and that he and City were confident of eventually winning their battle. He also added that while it had been eight years since the allegations of financial misconduct were first made against City, it could take considerably more time for a definitive conclusion to the saga.

The ongoing delay is a growing source of frustration to other clubs, who remain in the dark over the details of the case and the likely timeframe of any resolution. While club executives received a broad outline of the independent commission’s findings against City last Thursday there has been no update since, and the verdict has yet to be published. One club source said on Monday: “All we have is a void, and it would be better for everyone if it was filled as soon as possible.”

Soriano declined to comment when approached by reporters after the EFC board meeting.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino ready to accept demands for larger payouts from $6bn reserves
Sports.content:
The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, is poised to bow to demands from Uefa and Concacaf to distribute more money from its $6bn cash reserves to member associations.

In a letter sent on Monday to all six confederation presidents and copied to members of the Fifa council, Infantino indicated his willingness to “support the greatest level of additional funding”, without committing to the $10m-per-member that has been proposed.

Infantino was responding to a joint letter sent by the Uefa and Concacaf presidents, Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani, earlier this month, who called for an additional payout for all of Fifa’s 211 members of at least $10m during the 2027-2030 commercial cycle, a demand which was subsequently endorsed in a separate letter from the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa.

Infantino said the presidents’ proposals will be considered by the Fifa council during its next meeting on 15 October, after the secretary general, Mattias Grafström, has consolidated the suggestions. Under the proposed terms of Infantino’s abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, the member associations would have received an additional $20m during the next four-year cycle, plus a further payment of $20m had they signed up before a 53-day deadline that would have expired last week.

“I will not prejudge the amount,” Infantino wrote in the letter. “I will support the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered through Fifa’s proper governance process, applied fairly and supported by transparent and auditable arrangements. The ambition is welcome. The financial evidence, governance and implementation must now support it.

“A single figure can begin the discussion, but it cannot complete a global policy. I have therefore instructed the Secretary General to consolidate all submissions into one integrated assessment for consideration by the Fifa council on 15 October 2026.”

Infantino also used the letter to mount another defence of his role in FFE, which he claimed was an attempt to increase Fifa’s investment in football. “The recent commercial proposal, now withdrawn, was intended to enable Fifa to invest more in football – not to replace support that could responsibly be provided from existing resources,” he wrote.

“I welcome the constructive intent reflected in each of your letters. We may differ on the best route forward, but I have no doubt that each of us wants what is best for Fifa, its member associations and football.”

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel resists change against Czechia despite England defensive errors
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel will resist making drastic changes to his defence despite England going six games without a clean sheet before facing Czechia in the Nations League on Tuesday.

Although Tuchel acknowledged that his side were a “danger to ourselves” when they lost 3-2 against Spain last Saturday, the head coach stood by Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly after their errors against the world champions.

The message was one of continuity as England arrived in Prague for their second game in Nations League Group A3. Tuchel has injury concerns over O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa but is likely to keep the changes to a minimum at the back. James Trafford will continue in goal and Tuchel believes the defeat against Spain was down to individual mistakes rather than structural issues with England’s defending.

“I didn’t see a pattern,” the German said. “It was individual mistakes. I didn’t see a pattern in defending. I think we defended very well in a block when we were organised, but we had just big individual mistakes. But I could not see any defensive pattern that would concern me.

“From a purely defensive approach I felt that we defended much more disciplined, cohesive and organised than in some matches in the World Cup. That was a step in the right direction. We constantly pushed out from our middle block, we tried to go into the opponent’s half and pushed out of the deep block. We didn’t suffer too for long periods of time in defending. We never lost our structure.

“I will not change now because someone made an individual mistake, and they’ve been good for us through all the other matches.”

Two of Spain’s goals came from Guéhi and O’Reilly losing the ball in dangerous positions. “We need to improve these things but when we had the ball we were the biggest danger to ourselves around the box because we just had too many individual mistakes,” Tuchel said. “Purely in defending, I have no concerns.”

Lewis Hall is in line to replace O’Reilly at left-back against Czechia and Trevoh Chalobah will hope to get the nod over Jarrad Branthwaite as Guéhi’s partner in the middle if Konsa is out. England want to reach next year’s finals and losing to Spain means they cannot experiment too much against Czechia, who were beaten by Croatia in their opening game.

The big question is whether Trent Alexander-Arnold replaces Jarell Quansah at right-back and wins his first cap since June 2025. Alexander-Arnold, who did not go to the World Cup, was an unused substitute against Spain.

“He had a very good training week and an excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” Tuchel said. “Today was a good training session. Everything is fine. He’s ready to go.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tuchel has explained that starting Trafford in England’s first two Nations League games is to see whether the Leeds goalkeeper can compete at this level. Jordan Pickford, who has been the No 1 since 2018, will return for the trip to Croatia on Saturday and the home game against Czechia next Tuesday.

“We use the Nations League to see where we are with the other goalkeepers,” Tuchel said. “There was no reason from performances to open up this position for competition.

“I think it’s necessary with every other player that we are aware of ‘what if’. If a player that starts a season well, like Traff at Leeds, [he] has the chance to prove it and to play in our style. We just need to see it at some point. We use this competition to actually give him the chance to push on.”

Sports.title: Israel captain stokes feud by saying ‘our country is 10 times better than Ireland’
Sports.content:
Manor Solomon claimed Israel was “10 times better” than Ireland as fallout intensified from their Nations League match and stated bluntly: “They hate us and we don’t like them.”

Players in the Republic of Ireland side stared at the ground during Israel’s anthem and their staff faced away from the pitch. Ireland’s players also chose not to shake hands or exchange pennants with their opponents in protest at Israeli military actions in Gaza which have killed tens of thousands of people.

Solomon, who plays for West Ham, told Israel’s Sport 5 channel: “If I say what I think about them I’ll probably be banned for a few games, so I don’t want to say what I think about them. Obviously they hate us and we don’t like them.”

View image in fullscreen Republic of Ireland captain Dara O’Shea (left) turns away from Israel captain Manor Solomon before kick-off. Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty Images

Ireland won the game 3-0 in Debrecen, Hungary, on Sunday and the return next Sunday will also be played on neutral territory, in Serbia. “I’m already looking forward to the next game against them,” Solomon, Israel’s captain, said.

Pressed on Ireland’s behaviour during Israel’s anthem, he said: “They don’t interest me. We have a country 10 times better than theirs, stronger than theirs. We have an amazing country with amazing people.

“We’re proud to wear the national team’s uniform and to be Israelis; proud of our country and our soldiers. And they can pull all the stunts they want and do whatever they want. We are Israelis, we love our country – and that’s how it will always be.”

Sports.title: Nations League: Olise’s late stunner leads France past Belgium, Italy rout Turkey
Sports.content:
Michael Olise’s magnificent late strike gave France a 1-0 Nations League victory over Belgium in Brussels, as Zinedine Zidane made it two wins out of two since being named as the new head coach.

Olise came off the bench late on with the game goalless, and set off from inside his own half to score the winner in the 88th minute. Olise advanced all the way to the edge of the Belgium area before curling a shot beyond the reach of Senne Lammens.

France were missing Kylian Mbappé, who has returned to Real Madrid after injuring his left knee while scoring the winner against Turkey on Friday. The visitors still had the better of the chances with Désiré Doué cracking a shot off the bar in the first half and debutant Lucas Da Cunha striking a post early in the second half.

The contest was heading to an unremarkable goalless conclusion until Olise intervened, having been sent on in the 77th minute in place of Bradley Barcola. France sit top of Group A1 with six points and will host Italy at the Stade de France on Friday, while Belgium entertain Turkey in Liège.

Italy bounced back from an opening 2-0 defeat to Belgium in Rome, as they thrashed Turkey 4-1 on a rainy night in Bursa.

Roberto Mancini’s team dazzled in the downpour, scoring three goals inside the first half-hour as the hosts were punished for defensive errors in their muddy goalmouth. Italy went ahead when Bursa-born fullback Zeki Celik swung wildly at a low near-post corner, deflecting the ball to Alessandro Bastoni who fired into the roof of the net.

View image in fullscreen Michael Kayode celebrates after scoring Italy’s third goal inside the first 30 minutes against Turkey. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

After 23 minutes, Altay Bayindir flapped at a cross-shot from Michael Kayode and sent the ball into the path of Lazio’s Davide Frattesi, who tucked it home. Four minutes later, Kayode found himself free on the right side of the penalty area, and his near-post shot eluded the Turkish goalkeeper.

Turkey gave the restless home crowd hope in the 47th minute when Gianluigi Donnarumma was drawn to Oguz Aydin beyond the far post. Aydin found Baris Yilmaz who drilled into an empty net, but the comeback lasted five minutes. Pio Esposito headed Italy’s fourth after Sandro Tonali had struck a post.

Yilmaz looked to have cut the gap again with a curling effort but Aydin, bouncing up and down in front of Donnarumma, was offside. Esposito and his older sibling, Sebastiano, also made history in Bursa, becoming the first brothers to start an Italy game together since Aldo and Luigi Cevenini in 1915.

In League B, Northern Ireland were left frustrated after a 0-0 draw at home to Hungary where the hosts passed up chances to take all three points. Patrick Kelly twice went close in the first half, hitting the crossbar with a looping effort, and Isaac Price was denied by Balázs Tóth late on.

View image in fullscreen Northern Ireland’s Patrick Kelly tries to lob the Hungary goalkeeper – but his effort came back off the crossbar. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

Michael O’Neill’s side could not make the breakthrough, though, and there were nervous moments late on as Ruairi McConville blocked Willi Orban’s shot and Pierce Charles saved from Alex Tóth. Northern Ireland sit joint-top of their group alongside Ukraine, who drew 0-0 with Georgia in Tbilisi.

In Group B4, Sweden saw off Poland 3-1 in Solna to earn their second win in two games. Celtic’s Benjamin Nygren pounced at the far post after eight minutes to give the hosts the lead, but Sebastian Szymanski levelled with a shot that hit both posts before going in.

Yasin Ayari restored the home lead when he finished neatly even as he was losing his footing, before Arsenal forward Victor Gyökeres added the coup de grace. Bosnia and Herzegovina are second in the group after winning 4-2 against Romania in Bucharest.

In League C, Aleksa Latkovic’s 89th minute effort clinched a 3-2 win for Montenegro against Armenia to take charge of their group, while Latvia and Cyprus drew 0-0.

Sports.title: ‘Football with a smile’: Pocognoli wants happy Gilmour to tee up Scotland success
Sports.content:
Sébastien Pocognoli hopes a “smiling” Billy Gilmour will be central to Scotland’s hopes of improvement following a bruising World Cup.

Gilmour excelled in the second half on Saturday, as Pocognoli’s debut as manager ended in a goalless away draw against Slovenia in the Nations League. The Napoli midfielder missed the World Cup, where the Scots exited at the group stage, through injury. “If you have a player who plays one touch without even looking where he puts the ball it means that he understands the game plan,” Pocognoli said of Gilmour before his Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday evening.

“We don’t have a lot of players like this. Even Switzerland don’t. I need to make sure that he finds his smile on the pitch and he was smiling after the game. I saw the Billy from Brighton in Slovenia. At Napoli it is a little bit different, it is more thinking about off the ball. But when he can play he is smiling. He will make mistakes, he played bad passes against Slovenia. But he has to take the risks to play like that to see his qualities.

“I just want Billy to enjoy his football with a smile. If he can do that, the rest will come. I remember him well when he was in Brighton. I thought he was fantastic for them.”

Scotland trained on Monday at Hampden instead of their standard base next door, with Pocognoli keen to familiarise new members of his squad with the venue. “It does not look old but you can feel the history,” he said.

Quick Guide Yakin misses press conference with 'hearing issues' from plane Show The Switzerland head coach, Murat Yakin, missed his team’s Hampden Park press conference with hearing issues as the visitors suffered travel problems on the way to Glasgow. Yakin took training at Scotland’s national stadium and will hope to recover before Tuesday’s Nations League match. A Swiss FA spokesperson said: 'Murat Yakin isn’t at the press conference because he has hearing problems. He struggled with the pressure from the flight so can’t participate in this press conference. He will be at the training session and we hope these complaints will be solved, as has been the case in the past, and he can be in good health for the game.' The Switzerland press conference started late after a two-hour delay to the team's flight. 'There were some problems with the weight as we entered the flight,' the spokesperson added. 'It means we had to land again in Zurich and they had to put more fuel in the engine.' Yakin’s assistant, Davide Calla, took over media duties and said: 'We’ve spent a lot of time looking at Scotland. With the change of coach it will be a different proposition to the Euros [when the teams drew 1-1 in 2024] but we know what to expect. They will be robust, play with a lot of passion and they have a lot of quality players especially in midfield with the ball at their feet. 'In the second half against Slovenia they showed the quality they have,' added Calla. 'It was clear Scotland were better in the second half. It’s an absolute highlight playing at this brilliant stadium. We’ll have lots of motivation to play in this big match.' Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Pocognoli has also warned players not featuring regularly for their clubs that it will become increasingly difficult to win a place in his Scotland squads. Ben Gannon-Doak, Ryan Christie and Aaron Hickey are among key members of Pocognoli’s group who have had restricted domestic minutes this season. While the Belgian is comfortable with that scenario for now, that is likely to change by the time Euro 2028 qualifying begins next year.

“I think Ben will get the games because Bournemouth have the Europa League,” Pocognoli said. “He will play, he will get time. Billy has played in recent weeks since the Champions League has started. So the teams will start to rotate. What concerns me is when March comes. If the players aren’t playing a lot then we will struggle with the physical aspects of the game.

“The demands on the effort are massive. Right now it is OK because it is after pre-season. In November we will see. But we need to have players who have played.”

Sports.title: Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Nothing is over, nothing is done. Or at least not judging by the bravura, balls-out confidence of Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, who remains convinced the past three days of whiplash are simply the drumroll before the big reveal, prelude to some clinching piece of evidence that will swish away the initial finding of guilt on the Premier League’s 100-plus charges.

This appears to be the official City position right now. Rope‑a‑dope litigation. Scooby‑Doo justice. A verdict that is simply exposition, buildup to that moment where we finally get to rip off the zombie mask and reveal the cranky old amusement park owner underneath, with his bulging ring‑binder full of irrefutable evidence of City’s innocence.

This is certainly one way of going about things. Lord Pannick KC, Mystery Machine Chambers. Come for the legal expertise. Stay for the unfathomable brinkmanship.

That great escape may still present itself in more nuanced ways, most obviously in the question of what the actual punishment is here. But even in the current in-between days this feels like the end of an era. The greatest decade in the history of nation-state football projects is over. They’re selling Pep wigs in Woolworths. And we have failed, barring that promised deus ex machina, to paint it sky blue.

So what next? It is understandable there should be a great deal of confusion. This has never happened before. It is without precedent. The common assumption is that events will unfold like this: sanctions first, perhaps as early as midweek. Then an appeal. Then whatever comes next. But someone is suing someone. And it won’t be cheap or quick.

For now, the scale of City’s punishment is the only story in town. A verdict means nothing without the hammer of actual consequences. The triumphalism of those who seem personally invested in seeing City fail could still turn out to be premature.

There are many suggestions of how this may play out. Among the more lenient is a combination of a major fine, a one-season points deduction and a transfer ban. In other words, punishment that looks like punishment but isn’t really. Everyone feels vaguely vindicated. We carry on.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester City chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, issued a statement on Saturday that has only added to the sense of confusion. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

There is the suggestion of political pressure applied by City’s owners, as reported most recently by Bloomberg, with the idea floated that the United Arab Emirates government wishes to see its investment protected as a quid pro quo for its trading partnership with the UK. This is not actually a conspiracy theory. It’s how the world works. Politics is real. Football is not.

At the other end of the scale is a suggestion the Premier League will press for major sanctions as a means of heading off a disastrous round of internecine litigation, club-on-club action that would risk torpedoing the thing we’ve all been watching for the past 15 years. Yes: truth, fair play, stolen glory. But won’t someone think of the brand?

Here is one small suggestion. If the verdict does hold up, the punishment handed down should include a lengthy ban on City having any kind of sponsorship. This would at least speak to the core of the charges, the allegation that state-owned companies were used to funnel in direct investment. It would force City to grow their revenue by more standard means. It may even have a beneficial effect.

Not that anyone is talking about compromise yet. One of the most notable aspects is how utterly entrenched aspects of City’s fanbase seem to be on this. Facts are malleable, principles relative. Everything must be bent to your interests.

There is a very important distinction here. It is entirely legitimate to question the existing rules. Maybe outside investment should be allowed. Spending your own money on your own property, pumping funds into the system, adding not taking: this seems not just reasonable but commendable. How can it be a crime?

This is to wilfully misunderstand the equation. If everyone else is obeying the rules, if the entire culture is based around competitiveness, then this becomes not just deceit and deliberate cheating, but a trashing of the basic idea of sport.

And, in the end, this affects people’s lives in tangible ways. Not just hopes and dreams, but employment, wellbeing, the goals you work for all your life. How many families have been uprooted, incomes affected, moments of happiness scrubbed by outcomes that might have gone the other way?

This is the state of cognitive dissonance described in al-Mubarak’s statement, which is also the only official comment by any party so far. It is not surprising there should be zero acknowledgement of any culpability, or even legitimacy to the charges. Hang on to a rising balloon and you face a difficult decision. Let go before it’s too late or just keep getting higher. Al-Mubarak is in a difficult position here, frontman for a propaganda project that has spectacularly crashed. Faced with this he has trebled and quadrupled down, and in the most tribalist way.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans at the Etihad Stadium in 2012, when they had just won their first Premier League title. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/Getty Images

“This club matters to me,” al-Mubarak begins, a club executive who is, as things stand, guilty of destroying that club’s future prospects. There is dark talk of “media reporting”, with its implication of lies and fake news, as though this is all just another structural obstacle in the way of the true victims here, inherited dictatorial billionaires.

“Here’s what I said to my family,” al-Mubarak goes on, weirdly dragging his own relatives into the picture, before offering once again the most intriguing element, the suggestion there is some key detail here, some game-changing element City are desperate to get out, but which has so far been prevented from entering a properly constituted legal tribunal. “There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident.” This is not a standard line after being found almost unanimously guilty.

So what is he getting at? Part of the problem is the rush to demonise only one side, to see simply bad guys and good guys. In reality, it seems likely the written judgment will heavily criticise the Premier League’s governance.

Rightly so. These charges have been doggedly pursued, but what about, well, everything else? How did an organisation that maintains its serial champions have been cheating for a decade and a half allow this entity into its competition in the first place? How did it fail so completely to regulate it?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How about, to choose one example, Roman Abramovich, the Kremlin-connected oligarch on whom the British government overnight imposed sanctions as an unfit person, whose own irregularities are well documented? The Premier League has always basically been a TV rights agency masquerading as a regulator. As long as the show rolls on, well, the show rolls on.

This is the only real conclusion to be drawn from any of this. Some kind of governance is being effected here. But this remains a leaking, lurching pirate ship of an organisation. In any sane version of the current timeline there would be pressure for a complete reconsideration of how and why the Premier League exists.

One thing was obvious years before the current state of emergency: countries should not own football clubs. Sovereign wealth funds should not own football clubs. There is an irreconcilable conflict of objectives here. All is fair in foreign policy. Countries will spy, steal and misdirect to gain influence. It is pretty much a patriotic duty to do these things.

But you really don’t need to invite that level of supra-judicial chicanery into your delicate cultural treasure of a sport. What did anyone think was going to happen here? What would the people of the Netherlands think if the UK government bought AZ Alkmaar and began pumping in funds via sponsorship deals with National Rail and the Highways Agency, all the while promising to play fair? This is what the Premier League has permitted. You don’t really get to act surprised when it goes a bit wonky.

View image in fullscreen The sun sets over the Etihad Stadium. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

It is also important to remember that English football hovers like a locust cloud over every other league. The reeling-in of talent and expertise is hugely destabilising. How are you supposed to feel in Germany or Belgium about the fact City and Chelsea have between them spent more than £3bn on transfer fees, all of which is now tainted, apparently put into circulation by something other than a legitimate sporting project?

There is a fair case for Uefa to seek recompense, even to withdraw its patronage until this bandit league gets its own house in order. This won’t happen, because of eyeballs and income flows. But this is down to the balance of power, not any sensible idea of procedure or morality.

What next, then? It is hard to see how a combined 89 charges of failure to provide accurate information or to cooperate with an investigation can be overturned on appeal. But it is also far from impossible. City’s bullishness is presumably based on information from their legal team. The next stage after appeal would be the high court, where different rules on evidence and the law may apply. Perhaps the long game is to get to that stage. It may even work, as it did at the court of arbitration for sport with the Uefa case. Or maybe they’re just planning to spin it out until everyone goes broke, dies or gets into esports.

But in the end, why would you do this? What do you actually want from football? Is proving to the last decimal point that this is all technically admissible really a desirable outcome? The level of sustained, destructive aggression is telling in itself. As are the potential macro-implications.

Most obviously, this case speaks more widely to the way money and power flow in and out of Britain. One version of the endgame is that City’s owners could be forced by the football regulator to sell up. Manchester City are a vast going concern. Imagine the wider shockwaves if this were to happen.

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola with the Manchester City chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

To take one example, a significant amount of the UK property market’s enduring rock‑solid value is built on the idea of inviolable property rights, safety in ownership. Where better to park your funds than a place where the rule of law seems to work for and not against you? London alone is said to have more than £4bn worth of value bound up in dark money. Imagine the ripple effects if a decision on a set of sporting regulations ends with a sovereign state being ordered to forfeit property. Never mind the abrupt lurch into negative equity. It’s enough to make you feel a little pride once more in the power of the wig and the rulebook.

More directly, this remains an existential threat to the league. Not least in the depth of ill-feeling. City’s owners clearly have a deep hostility towards their fellow Premier League members, who are being portrayed as partial and culturally biased. Why would you want to remain part of this organisation? Why would you make any effort to protect it?

Nothing is over, nothing is done. All that seems certain is that this would probably be a good time to hoist the death’s‑head flag and get that old Super League ship rolling again. There might just be a few more takers this time.

Sports.title: Europe’s top-flight clubs to get share of £185m from Club World Cup
Sports.content:
Europe’s top-flight clubs will share half of the $250m (£185m) solidarity pot from the Club World Cup last year, ending a saga that had caused widespread frustration among those who did not participate in the tournament.

Fifa and European Football Clubs (EFC) are close to an agreement that would bring a 50-50 split between sides in Europe and the rest of the world. The fund, set aside to ensure the competition contributes to football’s wider ecosystem, will be distributed once the deal has been ratified.

EFC had sought a share of just over 60% , but compromised after Fifa insisted on a more equal global distribution. A portion of the $125m will be given to all top-division European clubs not involved in the Club World Cup, with amounts varying depending on the number of seasons a side competed at that level between 2021 and 2024.

An amount will also go to clubs with the best performance in Uefa club competitions during that period, again provided they did not play in the tournament in the US in 2025. It raises the likelihood of clubs receiving wildly varying payments. Liverpool, the Champions League runners-up in 2022, would be among those to benefit at the higher end of the scale.

EFC will stage its general assembly in Copenhagen on Tuesday and the agreement is likely to be confirmed after approval by the Fifa council, which is scheduled to meet in Zurich on 15 October.

Clubs from smaller leagues had grown particularly exasperated at the drawn-out timeline for receiving funds that, in many cases, can present a welcome lifeline. The Club World Cup winners, Chelsea, have long since benefited from their £84m payout out of the £740m set aside as prize money.

EFC threatened Fifa it would not cooperate with future Club World Cups if Gianni Infantino did not withdraw his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme. In the same letter, EFC said the lack of a solution on Club World Cup solidarity payments was “of serious disappointment to EFC and our member clubs”.

A joint venture between EFC and Fifa, intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions, remains on the table, but is unlikely to be signed in the near future given the turbulence surrounding world football’s leadership.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Infantino addressed the EFC general assembly in Rome last year, but a repeat performance is not likely this time given the prospect of a direct encounter with adversaries such as the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino spent Monday attempting to boost his standing in Europe by travelling to Riga for the opening of new offices at the Latvian Football Association. The Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, is expected to be among the delegates in Copenhagen.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel tells his England stars to stop being 'the biggest danger to ourselves' as they hunt for first clean sheet in seven following Spain errors
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has accused his England defence of being a danger to themselves.

They have not kept a clean sheet in six games since beating Panama at the World Cup, a run during which they have conceded 13 goals and leaked seven against Spain and France on their last two outings.

It might have been worse had Spain capitalised on a sequence of good early chances, mostly brought about by England's errors in possession, but Tuchel claimed to have no great concerns about the broader elements of defending.

Only that his team must kick the habit of self-destruction.

'We suffered from individual mistakes when we had the ball, especially in deep build-up,' said Tuchel, ahead of Tuesday's Nations League tie against the Czech Republic in Prague.

'It's something that we cannot repeat, especially not at this kind of level.

Thomas Tuchel has urged England to start taking more care in possession as they hunt a first clean sheet in seven games

The Three Lions shipped three against Spain on Sunday and will face Czechia on Tuesday

'To take care of this, we have to be technically absolutely clinical, under pressure. We need to improve these things. Strangely enough, when we had the ball, we were the biggest danger to ourselves around our box.

'But purely defending, no concerns. I trust we can do it. Some players of course are not here, who would also help organising our defensive block, I don't have any reason to be concerned.'

James Trafford will continue in goal in Prague, winning his fourth cap with Jordan Pickford set to return for games against Croatia on Saturday and the Czech return next week at Wembley.

Tuchel added: 'The last two matches, 6-4 against France and 2-3 v Spain, in itself seven goals in two matches is very unusual. I understand the question. I'm not concerned yet.

'I didn't see a pattern. We defended very well in a block when we were organized, but we had just big individual mistakes. But I could not see any defensive pattern that would concern me.

'I felt that we defended much more disciplined, cohesive and organised than in some matches in the World Cup. That was a step in the right direction. We constantly pushed out from our middle block, we tried to go into the opponent's half and pushed out of the deep block.

'We didn't suffer too for long periods of time in defending. We never lost our structure. So from all these things I'm not concerned. The result was heavily influenced by some individual mistakes that can happen, but the result was influenced but not the performance.'

Sports.title: Zinedine Zidane becomes an instant meme with wild touchline celebration after Michael Olise's last-gasp winner for France in Belgium
Sports.content:
Zinedine Zidane becomes an instant meme with wild touchline celebration after Michael Olise's last-gasp winner for France in Belgium

New France manager Zinedine Zidane may have given up playing years ago, but rolled back the years on Monday as he celebrated his side's last-gasp winner over Belgium.

Zidane took over from Didier Deschamps after the World Cup, and has now won both of his matches in charge so far.

After overseeing a 1-0 win over Turkey in the Nations League on Friday, he guided his team to a victory in Belgium by the same score line on Monday.

It was Bayern Munich winger Michael Olise who netted the winning goal, with his strike coming in the 88th minute of the tense clash.

And Zidane wasn't hiding his emotion with his celebration as he sprinted down the touchline as soon as the ball hit the net.

The former midfielder then took it upon himself to boot a ball away in joy as one of the spare balls placed on a cone around the outside of the pitch went flying.

Allez, en haute définition, et avec la prise d'élan au complet! pic.twitter.com/7kgYOXw0jN — Saoirse Mulrane (@SaoirseMulrane) September 28, 2026

Zinedine Zidane caught the eye with his energetic celebration following France's win over Belgium on Monday

The France bench leapt up behind him, but there seemed to be no one happier than the 54-year-old.

Zidane, who won three Champions Leagues as Madrid manager, has signed a four-year deal with Les Bleus as he succeeds his former Juventus and France team-mate Deschamps.

Deschamps left his 14-year tenure as France manager at the end of the World Cup, with his side losing 2-0 to eventual champions Spain in the semi-finals. They finished fourth after a 6-4 defeat by England in the third-place play-off.

It is Zidane's first foray back into management since leaving Real Madrid in 2021, revealing he has rejected offers in the meantime as he waited for his 'dream' to become France boss.

'The French team was the only thing I wanted to do,' Zidane told reporters at his unveiling.

'I've always looked at this team through the eyes of a future manager. I didn't take a club job for that reason. The only thing I wanted to do after Madrid was manage the French national team.

The former midfielder has won both of his matches in charge since taking over this year

'I could have taken on a three-year role because Deschamps was there. He made that decision in January 2025, and the very next day I knew I wanted to be the next one. We met with the president and the deal was sealed.'

Deschamps oversaw 185 matches and 120 victories, guiding France to the 2018 World Cup title, the 2020-21 Nations League trophy, and the Euro 2016 and 2022 World Cup finals.

He and Zidane share a long association, having also been team-mates in France's 1998 World Cup-winning side on home soil.

Zidane, who retired from playing in 2006, played a pivotal role in that triumph and won the Ballon d'Or that year. He made 108 appearances for the national side, scoring 31 goals and contributing 29 assists.

France have two matches remaining in the current international break. They will take on Italy on Friday, before the return match against Belgium next Monday.

Sports.title: Piers Morgan insists Man City '100 per cent have to be relegated' after guilty verdict - as Simon Jordan claims the Abu Dhabi project is DOOMED
Sports.content:
Piers Morgan insists Man City '100 per cent have to be relegated' after guilty verdict - as Simon Jordan claims the Abu Dhabi project is DOOMED

Piers Morgan has called for Manchester City to be relegated after the club were found guilty of the 'vast majority' of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.

City, who are certain to appeal the verdict, are nervously awaiting punishment after being found guilty of 114 of their 115 rule-break charges, according to sources, with the club accused of widespread financial cheating over a period of sustained success between 2009 and 2018.

The punishment eventually imposed on Manchester City could range from a fine or points deduction to relegation or even the stripping of trophies.

Morgan, a fervent Arsenal fan, called for City to face Premier League relegation at the very least, along with a series of points deduction over the next few seasons, after being found guilty of 'cheating the system'.

Speaking to Simon Jordan and Daily Mail Sport's Oliver Holt on Football Uncensored, he said: 'They (Man City) 100 per cent have to be relegated. 100 per cent. This idea they get away with a fine and a transfer ban - no, no, no, no.

'I think they should be relegated, I think there should be a points deduction for the next four seasons. There's got to be a proper punishment. The fine is irrelevant, Abu Dhabi have gazillions pumping out of their oil barrels every day. It's got to hurt them.'

Piers Morgan has called for Man City to be relegated after being found guilty of rule breaking

City were found to have broken 114 of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League, having profited from an era of sustained success between 2009 and 2018

Holt, who urged in his Daily Mail column that City should be stripped of their titles as a deterrent, agreed with Morgan's suggested sanction - while Jordan insisted that the punishment cannot 'scorch' the Premier League.

The former Crystal Palace chairman also claimed that the guilty verdict should spell the end of the Abu Dhabi United Group's 'doomed' project at Manchester City.

He said: 'This project is doomed now for Abu Dhabi. The whole idea behind utilising football was to change the perspective on these entities, these regimes.

'What I do want to see is the ownership separated, because I do believe the ownership is entirely culpable. Abu Dhabi cannot in my mind recover from this in terms of an ownership with a sports franchise.

'Even if they do find irrefutable evidence, there will still be the argument it was a technicality. Their project of delivering sport and a prism of the way that their society was looked at, is toast. And so the consequence is there for them.'

City have publicly maintained their innocence throughout the process, with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak saying last week: 'Our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began.'

Man City were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League with a hearing concluding in December 2024.

Their statement that February insisted that they were 'surprised' by the charges.

The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period, with the most serious across an eight-year spell.

A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years.

Simon Jordan claimed that the guilty verdict should spell the end of Abu Dhabi's City project

The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history.

City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era.

The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023.

Between the years mentioned, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League, four FA Cups and seven EFL Cups.

Sports.title: Man City chief warns it will take 'a lot more time' before 115 charges saga is settled - with broadcasters unlikely to seek refunds from Premier League despite paying BILLIONS to screen club's glory years
Sports.content:
Man City chief warns it will take 'a lot more time' before 115 charges saga is settled - with broadcasters unlikely to seek refunds from Premier League despite paying BILLIONS to screen club's glory years

Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano has warned their fight against the Premier League will take ‘a lot more time’ to conclude.

Soriano was at a private meeting with the executive board of European Football Clubs’ body along with other bosses of top clubs and, according to sources, was quick to address the elephant in the room.

‘It’s taken eight years to get here,’ Soriano told the assembled club chiefs, ‘and it’s going to take a lot more time’.

Soriano is understood to have asked to address the room and said all the noise so far had come from a media leak and that there had not been any official communication.

City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a statement on Saturday: ‘The process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.’

City have been found guilty of all substantive charges brought by the Premier League regarding breaches of their financial rules, over a time period in which they lifted three titles as part of an eight-trophy haul.

Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano (left) has warned their fight against the Premier League will take ‘a lot more time’ to conclude

Broadcasters will not demand compensation from the Premier League despite paying billions to screen Man City's glittering era of dominance (Pictured: Man City lifting the 2012 title)

The situation has raised the prospect that broadcasters who paid billions to screen that glittering era in the club’s history could seek effective refunds, given there would be clear question marks over the integrity of what they paid vast sums to screen. However, it is understood broadcasters will not demand compensation from the Premier League — even if they throw the book at Manchester City.

Daily Mail Sport has been told by those close to the situation that such a move would be ‘highly unlikely’. At one stage, there had been discussions among broadcasters over a form of ‘discount’ tied to future rights deals, with negotiations domestically due to take place in the middle of next season. Again, such a situation is thought unlikely, with the market dictating the price.

The news may well come as a relief to top-flight clubs celebrating what appears to be a clear victory for the competition while worrying about the financial implications. It is thought that the only way that rights would drop dramatically would be if City’s punishment results in the loss of large numbers of subscribers between now and the next deal, which is also seen as unlikely.

Meanwhile, worried City staff were emailed a statement from chairman Khaldoon Al-Mubarak on Saturday which was also posted on the club’s website.

It is understood that few where in the club’s central offices on Friday, when the news broke. Al-Mubarak reiterated that he was confident that City would prevail.

The findings of the tribunal, which concluded in December 2024, are still to be made public.

An appeal from City’s expensively assembled legal team is viewed as an inevitability. They have 14 days to lodge such a request which would be heard by a separate panel.

A wide range of punishments, including expulsion, are available under Premier League rules. The original panel would take arguments from both sides before deciding on a penalty it feels befits the crime.

Sports.title: Michael Wynn Jones dead at 85: Delia Smith's husband passes away as Norwich lead tributes to their former chairman
Sports.content:
Michael Wynn Jones dead at 85: Delia Smith's husband passes away as Norwich lead tributes to their former chairman

Michael Wynn Jones, the husband of TV cook Delia Smith, has died at the age of 85.

Wynn Jones's death was announced by Norwich City, where he and Smith had been majority shareholders for 28 years.

Smith and Wynn Jones stepped back from the board last year, after agreeing a deal to reduce their holding in the club to 10 per cent.

The couple became honorary life presidents after stepping away.

'Everyone at Norwich City is deeply saddened by the passing of our honorary life president, Michael Wynn Jones,' a Norwich statement read.

'Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85.

Michael Wynn Jones, left, has died at the age of 85, Norwich City have announced

'He will be greatly missed.

'His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth Hospice.

'Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom, and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones.

'At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.'

Outside of football, Wynn Jones had worked as an editor on several magazines, including Mirror Magazine and The Spectator.

Wynn Jones founded and served as chairman of New Crane Publishing Ltd, as well as being the author of several books of biography and social history.

Wynn Jones and Smith, who married in 1971, became majority shareholders in Norwich back in 1998.

The Canaries were promoted to the Premier League on five occasions under their ownership, going up as Championship winners on three occasions.

Norwich enjoyed a three-year spell in the top flight between 2011-12 and 2013-14, but also suffered five relegations from the Premier League during Wynn Jones and Smith's time at the club.

Sports.title: James Trafford's big chance: Leeds keeper set to start for England in Prague knowing that whatever happens, Jordan Pickford will return for the next two games. So can he now make his case to be No1 for good?
Sports.content:
James Trafford's big chance: Leeds keeper set to start for England in Prague knowing that whatever happens, Jordan Pickford will return for the next two games. So can he now make his case to be No1 for good?

When it comes to grabbing anything with both hands you would expect goalkeepers to be at an advantage, what with the big gloves and all that practice.

Opportunities to challenge Jordan Pickford as England's number one however tend to slip through.

Maybe modern keepers spend too much time learning to punch things clear or passing it about at the back to claim anything cleanly nowadays.

Dean Henderson has seemed close at times. Nick Pope and Aaron Ramsdale had their moments. Sam Johnstone's and Alex McCarthy's were more fleeting.

In Prague against Czechia, the chance belongs to James Trafford for the second time in four days and it can only be positive for England if he can deliver a performance to create at least some semblance of competition for the No1 shirt.

Pickford's dominance is stressed by this nugget of trivia doing the rounds after Saturday's 3-2 defeat by Spain: On each of the last five occasions England have conceded three or more, Pickford has been absent.

James Trafford will start in goal for England against Czechia with a chance to stake his claim

Henderson was in goal for two of them, Pope and Ramsdale for one each and now Trafford, although he did at least emerge with some credit from the Spain game.

There were smart early saves when Thomas Tuchel's team were in a mess and confidence to demand the ball at his feet, although England's young keeper must take his share of the collective blame for the fraught opening phase at Wembley.

Even if he was under instruction to play with risk and invite the Spanish press by delaying the release of his passes, the decisions he made under pressure did nothing at all to suggest his presence in goal would offer a more soothing experience than Pickford's trademark hyperactivity.

In Prague on Tuesday it will likely be a very different type of contest.

The Czechs have a new Spanish coach. Santi Denia spent 14 years in charge of various age levels of Spain youth teams including the U21s beaten by an England side including Trafford in the 2023 Euros final but are entering a new reset phase and are not expected to possess the slick cohesion and authority of the world champions.

Perhaps that was the appeal of this two-game strategy as Tuchel studies Trafford in two very different international environments. Once at home against the best around, the other away in a place where England will represent a prized scalp.

Tuchel has confirmed that unless something goes awry, Pickford will return against Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday and for the return against Czechia at Wembley, which will take his haul to 93 caps.

At 32, there is time on his side to cruise past Peter Shilton's 125-cap record if he can keep swatting aside the young challengers.

He is trying to break past Jordan Pickford (right) to become England's permanent No1

Pickford has proved a very capable England goalkeeper, matured into the role and is without doubt better for all the experience but his place has rarely been under serious threat.

Trafford must come with other ideas. He must dislodge his mate. His stars have belatedly aligned, playing regular Premier League football in a strong team with a commitment to defend properly.

This is more than half the battle because all jokes about missed opportunities aside they are truly scarce for homegrown goalkeepers in elite competition.

He rode out a difficult season in the Premier League with Burnley to excel as they bounced back from relegation by winning the Championship only to be set back again when Pep Guardiola lured him back to Manchester City then swerved to sign Gianluigi Donnarumma and relegate Trafford to his domestic cup keeper and cover.

'I won two trophies,' replied Trafford in a flash when reminded of this. 'It obviously wasn't ideal how it panned out but looking back I got two trophies to my name, so you take the positives and you play the cards you're dealt.'

Even so, this time last year he was playing for City in Carabao Cup ties at Huddersfield and Swansea, which was hardly ever going to convince Tuchel to wave him in past Pickford and Henderson of Crystal Palace, who is missing from this squad through injury.

At 23, Trafford is the same age Pickford was when he first broke in and made a debut against Germany in November 2017 four days before Joe Hart won his final cap, then won the spring auditions with Jack Butland and Pope to start in the 2018 World Cup.

Pickford seized his moment. Can Trafford do the same?

Sports.title: From 'repulsive' to indispensable: How Jude Bellingham has become central to Thomas Tuchel's plans... as under-pressure manager looks to England's 'real' deal to climb him out of a hole
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has been here before with England. In need of a step forward. Looking for a launchpad.

This time last year it came in Serbia as England travelled to Belgrade on the back of a mundane series of results and won 5-0 in World Cup qualifying.

Tuchel believes the few days spent training between a dull 2-0 home win over Andorra and their game in the Stadion Rajko Mitic were among the most crucial of his two years in office.

‘I felt something change and it was for the better,’ Tuchel has said.

All of that happened in the absence of Jude Bellingham. Back then – with Bellingham injured and Tuchel wrestling with issues of hierarchy within his squad – the England manager began to consider a future without the Real Madrid star as a regular starter.

As England landed in Prague on Monday looking to move on from Saturday’s defeat to Spain at Wembley, things have changed to a degree that it is now impossible to imagine a Tuchel team without Bellingham in it.

‘Jude looks like a real member of the squad on and off the pitch,’ said Tuchel last night.

Jude Bellingham has become central to Thomas Tuchel's England plans after a rocky start

The Real Madrid midfielder was immense during England's World Cup campaign last summer

‘The key in itself is that players want to come and want to really play and don't only say it but then prove the point when they are here.’

Such has been Bellingham’s transformation from enduring problem to the next England captain in waiting that even Tuchel’s language around him has changed.

It was as recently as early summer 2025 that Tuchel was describing some of the 23-year-old’s behaviour as ‘repulsive’ after a fractious defeat to Senegal at the City Ground in Nottingham.

Yet as he spoke in the Wembley interview area on Saturday night, he was comfortable enough to suggest Bellingham is at his best when playing with ‘rage’.

That reflects a softening of the relationship between player and coach. Bellingham still chooses to keep the majority of his thoughts on the matter to himself and that’s his prerogative.

Tuchel, though, has seen what he wanted to see from his most talented player around St George's Park and on England away trips. On the field, meanwhile, he has seen an improvement in the tactical and positional indiscipline that used to leave Tuchel forever concerned about just what Bellingham may do next.

‘I liked his performance a lot the other day because it was very consistent throughout the 90 minutes,’ he said.

‘It was a very mature, very good performance. He was always involved.

‘Jude can play in these high intensive patterns and then needs time to recharge the batteries.

‘But against Spain he had played economically and was always a difference maker, always available.’

England’s defeat by Spain at the weekend has left Tuchel under a little pressure. As such, he needs to look to players who can bring his team the consistency it now undeniably needs.

Missing the likes of Declan Rice in the centre of midfield and with his defence looking as unsure as any England back line has done for a long time, Tuchel’s England will need its big players to stand up in games against Czechia (home and away) and Croatia over the next eight days.

Having been England’s best player at the World Cup in America, Bellingham would appear to at last be feeding off the responsibility that comes with his status.

For a while it wasn’t the case. Too often his messages on the field of play were the wrong ones but it was noticeable on Saturday after captain Harry Kane slipped in missing a penalty that would have given his team a 3-1 lead, Bellingham was the first one on the scene to acknowledge exactly what had happened.

This is what Tuchel means when he talks about Bellingham looking like a ‘real member of the squad’. The 53-year-old knows that Bellingham will always present with rough edges. The task is to make sure it’s the opposition that takes the impact of them.

Tuchel has a big decision to make over whether to give Trent Alexander-Arnold his chance

The Three Lions are gearing up to face Czechia in the Nations League on Tuesday night

Asked if Bellingham himself had grown to love playing for his country, Tuchel said: ‘Yes and we also have to provide an environment and atmosphere where players can actually feel free and express themselves and be the best vision of themselves.

‘It is a give and go. We need to provide that and the player needs to have the hunger and the excitement to show up.’

England face a Czechia team short on form and results tonight but lost 2-1 here in 2019 and have some cleaning up to do after the nature of their defeat to Spain.

Tuchel knows what he saw when England had the ball at Wembley. England played with a purpose and belief that we didn’t often see during the summer’s World Cup and Bellingham – along with Barcelona’s Anthony Gordon - was at the heart of it.

Equally, England were a calamity waiting to happen in their own half and at the centre of the defence Tuchel only has inexperience in the shape of Jarrad Branthwaite and Trevoh Chalobah to call on as he looks to fix it.

Tuchel craves continuity with this England team. He has a spine of seven or eight players that he would pick every game if he could. Yet the fact he is missing a few and the nature of this September/October schedule means that he will have to mix and match a little in the days to come.

He was reluctant to yet again enter the Trent Alexander-Arnold debate, offering only two or three sentences when asked to explain his qualities. It feels as though that is one kind of background noise he could do without. The truth is, however, that Tuchel cannot rely on eleven players to take him where he wants to go ahead of the home Euros in 2028. He needs a core of sixteen or seventeen and maybe he is not quite there yet.

With his own country Germany losing to Greece this weekend under their new coach Jurgen Klopp, it was put to Tuchel that international management is maybe rather harder than people think.

‘Everyone told me that it is tough to form a team,’ nodded Tuchel.

Thomas Tuchel is under pressure after the World Cup and Saturday's defeat against Spain

‘There are so many ideas in football and everyone comes with different ones and the focus was, you know, to bring them together, play properly as a team and implement patterns of play. ‘And we are a step further. We had a tournament together, we had this experience together. We digested it.

‘We had a result that some think was not enough. Some think it was a good result. But we continue and this helps us.

‘It is a process. We are lacking a lot of players who have been with us from the World Cup, otherwise we would have been one more step ahead but I think you could see it was clear against Spain what we were trying to do.’

Expected England XI to face Czechia: (4-2-3-1) Trafford; Quansah, Guehi, Branthwaite, Hall; Anderson, Lewis Skelly; Rogers, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane

Sports.title: Bankrupt England rugby legend Lawrence Dallaglio forced to sell his World Cup winner's medal amid 'excessive spending' and bitter divorce
Sports.content:
England rugby legend Lawrence Dallaglio is selling his World Cup winner's medal as he confronts his ongoing financial troubles following his 'excessive spending' and bitter divorce from his wife.

The 54-year-old was declared insolvent last year after he and his wife of almost 20 years, Alice, divorced.

It ended with Dallaglio, who was a key member of England's 2003 World Cup-winning side, being forced into selling their family home in Richmond, south-west London, for £2.4million last May, after it had been put on the market for £3.3million months earlier.

The day after the sale, the former rugby star was declared bankrupt and was ordered to hand over his share of the proceeds to pay off an overdrawn directors loan of more than £366,500.

Typically, restrictions imposed by bankruptcy end after 12 months in England and Wales but they can be extended by a judge.

Dallaglio received a three-month exemption in May until August 7.

However, the restrictions were extended last month, with reports suggesting he had continued spending – leaving 'nothing' to pay his debts.

Now, the former England captain has put his winners' medal up for auction with an estimate of £50,000 to £80,000.

He was part of the side which beat Australia on their own turf in 2003 to lift the William Webb Ellis trophy following Jonny Wilkinson's dramatic extra-time drop goal.

Dallaglio, who played 85 times for England, is also parting with his 2007 World Cup runner's up medal which could go for £10,000.

Lawrence Dallaglio is selling his World Cup winners' medal after being made bankrupt

The England rugby legend's lavish spending and divorce from his wife Alice has led to his financial ruin

His 2003 Six Nations winner's medal from England's Grand Slam campaign is valued at £5,000.

Dallaglio, 54, is also selling his medals from his illustrious club career with London Wasps.

He won two European cups and three league titles while captaining the club, which are all being sold with individual estimates of £8,000.

His British and Irish Lions cap is priced at £5,500 and his England cap could achieve £5,000.

The overall collection, which also includes his player of the year awards, is set to raise £180,000 at Budds in Wellingborough, Northamptonshire.

The auctioneer said of the World Cup winner's medal: 'It was presented to Dallaglio on November 22, 2003 in Sydney, following victory in the Rugby World Cup Final against host nation Australia,

'England defeated Australia 20-17 after extra time. It was the pinnacle of world rugby and the singular greatest achievement in English rugby history.'

Dallaglio made his England debut in 1995 and retired from international rugby after the 2007 World Cup.

The powerful back row forward played one more season of club rugby, leading Wasps to the 2007-2008 Premiership title, before hanging up his boots. He has since worked in punditry. The sale takes place on October 13.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."
