Meanwhile, in a strange twist, CNN is getting new owners with close ties to Trump. NPR's David Folkenflik reports on the unease inside the network as Paramount moves to take over Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN's parent company.

Sponsor Message

Mass shootings across South Africa have killed nearly 40 people in recent days. The attacks in Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban struck a restaurant, tavern and house party, and police have not announced motives in the latest cases.

Picture show

toggle caption Afif Amireh for NPR

Born in 1947, the year before Israel's creation, Sliman Mansour said he didn't always think of himself as Palestinian. "In the early 1970s, I started to discover I'm a Palestinian," he told NPR. "So my art took a 90-degree turn."

Living under Israeli occupation, he said, made politics impossible to escape. But he also believed beauty was part of how art reached people: "If you don't speak to the hearts of the people, if you don't speak to the feelings of the people, then you don't reach people."

Beauty, he said, was "an important way to reach these hearts."

Mansour died on Aug. 24 at 79 and was buried in Bir Zeit, in the occupied West Bank, near the olive groves of his ancestors. Listen to an in-person interview with him, and see some of the art here.

Life advice

Andee Tagle/NPR

Being a parent can be overstimulating. Therapist and mom of three Cassidy Freitas says finding small moments to reset can help regulate your emotions. In her new book, Mom Needs a Moment, she offers a few techniques:

😤 In moments of high stress, pause and take a few intentional breaths before considering what is really driving your emotions.

😤 When parental guilt sets in, think about what you would say to a friend in the same situation - and offer yourself the same grace.

😤 Every parent loses their cool sometimes. Acknowledge what happened, own the mistake and take time to reconnect with your child.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption Cormac Toler-Scott/The University of British Columbia

Scientists in Canada discovered two new sea spider species in the Salish Sea — the first found there in more than a century.

Stanford professor Bryant Lin spent years studying lung cancer before becoming a Stage IV patient himself — just as new treatments are changing the disease's outlook.

D.C.'s Rat Rangers lead nighttime safaris through trash-strewn alleys to teach residents a simple lesson: If you want fewer rats, start with human behavior.

World.title: Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way
World.content:
Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way

AFP via Getty Images/Collage by Emily Bogle/NPR

President Trump has spent much of his second term trying to make his physical mark on Washington, D.C., earning — or perhaps awarding himself — the moniker of "builder-in-chief."

"The best thing I do in life is build," he told reporters in May.

Trump tore down the East Wing of the White House to build an even bigger ballroom (and military complex underneath). He built a helipad on the South Lawn after separately paving over the Rose Garden. He had the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool repaved in "American flag blue," a project that was supposed to take two weeks but is still unfinished many months later, after a botched installation and several unfounded arrests.

Sponsor Message

He's had new statues installed and existing ones restored, including two equestrian statues glaringly gilded over the summer. He wants to build a sculpture garden of "national heroes" in West Potomac Park and overhaul the locally beloved East Potomac Golf Links, changing it from a municipal resource into a championship-level venue.

The list goes on. Trump seeks to add his name to the Kennedy Center building, or else have it demolished altogether. He's trying to fast-track a controversial 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery, most recently rebranding it as a military complex — despite originally telling reporters it was intended to honor "me."

"I have heard the president say: 'I am president because I am rich. I am rich because I am a developer. I am a developer because I have exquisite taste,'" said Greg Werkheiser, whose law firm, Cultural Heritage Partners, is involved in several lawsuits against Trump's projects. "It would appear that much of his self-worth is tied to this mythology of Trump as a builder."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement that "President Trump can walk and chew gum at the same time," saying he is delivering on campaign policy promises while also "ensuring the People's House and our Nation's Capital will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come."

Sponsor Message

"Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump," he added.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Trump's second-term projects have prompted lawsuits, protests and tens of thousands of public comments overwhelmingly in opposition. While some of these undertakings are pegged to the country's 250th anniversary, critics have long accused the president of rushing to memorialize himself out of fear that no one else will. And Trump confirmed as much in a New York Magazine piece published earlier this month.

"Nobody will do it once I'm gone," said the 80-year-old, second-term president. "When I leave here, nobody will."

Trump and those in his orbit maintain he is uniquely qualified to put his stamp on D.C. because of his decades-long career as a New York City real estate developer. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told Fox News last year that "in large part, he was reelected ... because he is good at building things."

But people who worked with him at the time point out that his early-career building projects and strategies were fraught too, boosted by financial workarounds and plagued by lawsuits. And, more broadly, historians and legal experts worry that Trump is setting a dangerous precedent by treating D.C. as his personal construction playground.

"The worse his approval ratings, the economy and the war get, the more time he spends in the sandbox playing with America's historic sites as if they were his personal toys," Werkheiser said.

Barbara Res, who served as head of construction for the Trump Organization in the 1980s, says Trump's efforts to cut corners with ambitious projects are not new, but take on a painful significance in a moment when he is "ripping through" the nation's capital.

"There was no regard for the law back then. But he wasn't the king of the world; he wasn't the president," Res said. "Now he has no regard for law … and he gets away with it."

Sponsor Message

A history of disregard for historic preservation

toggle caption Marty Lederhandler/AP

Res, who left the Trump Organization in 1998, stressed that there is a big difference between a builder and a developer.

Trump was the latter, overseeing big-picture decisions like hiring architects, engineers and contractors. Even so, she said he often made demands about details that usually made the job harder, such as telling crews to reuse old HVAC equipment in new ductwork as a cost-cutting measure.

"His father was a builder in Brooklyn … and Donald seems to think that gives him credibility as a builder, 'cause he walked around with his father," she said. "Maybe he does now, but when we were doing the work, he didn't really know much about construction."

Res is an outspoken Trump critic: in 2020, she published the book Tower of Lies: What My 18 Years of Working with Donald Trump Reveals About Him. She concedes that "he did do good things" for real estate, but that was before he was president.

"The White House and the capital are not to his credit, so I don't think that would be part of his legacy," she said. "Probably his most important building is Trump Tower."

Trump Tower was Trump's second major independent project, and his first built-from-scratch skyscraper. And it was marred by a historic preservation scandal before it even opened.

In 1979, Trump — then a budding developer in his early 30s — bought the flagship building of the Bonwit Teller luxury department on Manhattan's Fifth Avenue, with plans to tear it down and build Trump Tower in its place.

Penelope Hunter-Stiebel was a curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art at the time. When she heard of Trump's plan to demolish the 1929 building, she jumped into action to save the historic artwork on its facade: two classical-style 15-feet-high limestone sculptures of nudes dancing with scarves, and a massive art deco decorative metal grille.

toggle caption AP/AP

Hunter-Stiebel believed the sharp contrast of two different architectural styles — added to the same building in the span of a single year — would make for a great addition to the Met's collection. And she thought Trump could benefit, too.

Sponsor Message

"We had been chasing wrecking balls as buildings of architectural ornament that were significant were destroyed around New York," she said. "I thought in this case, looking up Trump, it was a chance of changing the direction."

Hunter-Stiebel approached the Trump Organization with an offer: "Young Donald," as he was called, could not only get some positive PR for salvaging the artwork, but he could likely also get a tax deduction.

She said Robert Miller, who owned the gallery across the street, had agreed to appraise the works and valued them at around $200,000. He told The New York Times in 1980: "The reliefs are as important as the sculptures on the Rockefeller building. They'll never be made again."

Hunter-Stiebel says she reached an agreement with the Trump Organization. But shortly after scaffolding and demolition crews arrived in the spring of 1980, she noticed the metal grille had vanished (its whereabouts remain a mystery). Then came a panicked call from Miller, who spotted jackhammers across the street.

"[I] got in a taxi, and got in a classic New York City traffic jam, nothing moving down Fifth Avenue," she recalled. "So I got out and I ran 10 blocks, which I remember because I was nine months pregnant."

They decided that Miller — a less recognizable player in the drama — would approach the foreman, with cash he frantically collected from his employees, to try to save the sculptures.

Hunter-Stiebel says the foreman told Miller, who died in 2011: "The young Donald has said specifically that there's this crazy woman at a museum up the avenue who wants them, and I have to be sure they're absolutely destroyed."

They watched in horror as the jackhammers went to work. As of 2016, at least one piece of the sculptures lived on the Miami balcony of former Trump Organization executive Louise Sunshine, who did not respond to NPR's interview request.

Sponsor Message

There was immediate fallout from the incident. The New York Times ran a front-page story in which Trump Organization executive "John Baron" (now a well-known Trump alias) said removing them carefully would have cost more than three times their appraisers' estimated value and delayed demolition by over a week. (Almost two decades later, in 1998, Trump paid $1.375 million to settle a class-action lawsuit involving the use of undocumented Polish laborers during that demolition.)

Res said Trump told her a different version of the story: He offered the sculptures to the Met, but was turned down. Because they were not "landmarked," she said, "I don't see anything wrong with that except lying about it."

But to Hunter-Stiebel, the incident represents "Trump's first experience of the negative delights of power."

"I'm afraid we have seen the same behavioral pattern in large scale, and a strange delight in doing things that can only be destructive … including [to] the person making those decisions," she added.

Acting not as a builder, but as an owner

toggle caption Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

There's a world in which Trump's career experience as a developer could benefit D.C., said historian Tim Naftali, a professor at Columbia University's School of International Public Affairs.

"But the president hasn't acted just as a builder," he said. "He's acted as an owner, and that's the difference. The president of the United States does not own the United States. The president of the United States doesn't even own the White House."

Naftali said previous presidents have all approached their White House role as custodians. That doesn't mean they didn't make changes: There's a long history of presidents renovating the White House. But other than Truman, who paid for the second-story balcony with his government-funded "household account," they all went to Congress for authorization and funding.

Trump has not done that for his building projects, even though his party controls both houses of Congress. Experts say that creates a dangerous precedent for future occupants of the White House.

"The building projects are simply a symptom of President Trump's theory of government, which is that he alone is the federal government of the United States," Naftali said.

Beyond the White House, Naftali said D.C.'s most iconic monuments — honoring George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Jefferson and more — were built through "presidential inspiration mixed with congressional action." Presidents angled for monuments honoring their predecessors, not themselves.

Sponsor Message

Naftali thinks of four-term president Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who made clear in his lifetime that the only memorial he wanted for himself was a small block of granite with his name on it.

"Yes, he pushed for a memorial, but it was the Jefferson Memorial," Naftali added. "Not the 'Jefferson Memorial brought to you by Franklin Delano Roosevelt.' It was the Jefferson Memorial, built [and] financed by Congress."

Charles Birnbaum, the CEO and founding president of The Cultural Landscape Foundation — which sued the administration over the reflecting pool — says Trump has made clear that "the sort of social norms and decorum that existed historically is no longer being applied."

He noted, for example, that Trump has appointed non-expert allies to the federal arts panels tasked with reviewing D.C. construction. At the same time, the administration is also moving to roll back legal protections for historic places across the country.

"All of these proposals that we're seeing, what they have in common is they're not preserving and protecting. They are destroying, diminishing, altering," said Birnbaum. "And that is where Washington is a case study right now of what this administration wants to export to the rest of the nation."

When most recent presidents think about their legacy, Naftali said, they think about the work itself and, to some degree, the one building they expect will eventually bear their name: their presidential library, usually built outside of D.C. in a location of personal significance. Trump has said his — a planned skyscraper in Miami — will most likely be a hotel.

When it comes to shaping his own legacy, Trump has bucked presidential norms in many ways. Beyond his controversial construction projects, he's the first sitting president to have an airport named after him, and the first in a century to have his face on currency.

Sponsor Message

And while these acts may seem relatively trivial at a time of broader economic and international turmoil, Naftali said, they should ring alarm bells to anyone who cares about the separation of powers. He suspects Trump may be eager to jam his projects through before the midterms, when the makeup of Congress may shift.

Trump told New York Magazine that the embattled White House ballroom will be made of "nuclear concrete," saying it would physically be hard for Democrats to one day tear it down. The reporter of that story, Ben Terris, told NPR that Trump is "trying to cement his legacy, literally, and … make something that nobody can take away from him."

But to Naftali and others, the greater risk is in what might be lost along the way.

"We Americans will pressure Congress in one way or another to do something with whatever is left of the building program once the president leaves office," Naftali said. "The bigger issue is, do we want our separation of powers of doctrine to survive through our 300th birthday?"

World.title: U.K. examines if Iran or Russia are involved in foiled attack near base used by U.S.
World.content:
U.K. examines if Iran or Russia are involved in foiled attack near base used by U.S.

toggle caption Alastair Grant/AP

FAIRFORD, England — Five young British men arrested on explosives and terror charges near a U.S.-operated air force base in England were released on bail Monday, and counterterror detectives said they were investigating "multiple lines of inquiry," including whether there is a link to Iran.

The men were detained early Sunday after three vans were spotted in the countryside near RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran.

Investigators haven't concluded whether the incident was state-backed. They are investigating a possible link to Iran, Russia or non-state militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners.

The five suspects, who haven't been named, were initially held over suspected explosives offenses, and later also arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Police said the men are all British nationals from London and in their 20s.

toggle caption Alastair Grant/AP

Britain's national news agency, PA, reported without citing sources that police had not found viable explosives. Announcing that the suspects had been bailed, the head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said that the suspects face stringent conditions and "absolutely remain under investigation."

Sponsor Message

Taylor said lines of inquiry include that the suspected offenses were committed by "proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."

Iran denied involvement. The Iranian Embassy in London said that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" about the incident.

Residents were evacuated from 85 homes in the village of Whelford near the base on Sunday, and army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine three white vans.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Monday afternoon that "thanks to the excellent work of the army's explosive ordnance disposal team," the scene was now safe and residents could go home.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would chair a meeting of the government's COBRA emergency committee later Monday "to make sure we have the full picture."

The arrests came after reports of suspicious vehicles

U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been detained following cooperation between the U.S. and Britain, and had been "under view" for some time. Police, however, said the arrests were triggered by a late-night call about "suspicious vehicles" near the base.

A local farmer said she called police after seeing three oddly parked vans as she drove home late Saturday night, and that nearby she came across "a large group of men," some with their faces covered. She said they scattered when they saw her vehicle.

Sponsor Message

She declined to be identified to protect her identity because she was describing what she saw as potential security lapses.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the farmer "did exactly the right thing" by calling police but only had "a partial view" of the operation.

The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British intelligence services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025.

Iran has been linked to a series of attacks in Europe

Britain didn't join the U.S. and Israel in the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28, and initially denied Trump's request to use bases in the U.K. to strike Iran. But then Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the U.S. use bases in Britain for what he called "defensive" operations against Iran's missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain's allies in the Gulf.

American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict.

Iran has said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

Several people also have been charged with plotting to commit arson in the U.K. on behalf of Russia-linked groups.

Sponsor Message

U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the incident is a "reminder of the threats our country faces."

Miliband met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations in New York last week and told him that "Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on U.K. soil," according to a U.K. readout of the conversation.

U.S. Air Force says personnel remain vigilant

The U.S. Air Force said that its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant," but "for operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures."

The U.S. Embassy in London has warned Americans in Britain to be cautious and mindful of their personal security.

Trump said that authorities had the suspects "under view for a long time and we got them."

"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday.

World.title: B.C. politicians, leaders condemn white nationalist gathering on First Nation reserve
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. politicians and leaders are denouncing a gathering of white nationalists on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve, just east of Kamloops.

Kúkpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir told CBC News on Sunday the nation had received reports that morning of a gathering of about 20 to 30 men, wearing white face masks and black caps, standing together around the reserve while hoisting flags over their shoulders.

In a news release, Casimir said "individuals associated with Second Sons Canada, a group linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology, have been seen and documented within our community.

"White supremacy will not instill fear in generations of survivors and intergenerational survivors who have already carried fear for far too long."

CBC News has verified that video circulating on social media of the gathering is authentic and depicts members of the group Second Sons Canada near the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve.

Casimir said the group was seen on reserve land, and RCMP said they were called to an area on the reserve.

Casimir said the reserve's security told the men they were not permitted to gather and asked them to leave. However, they did not leave until RCMP were called and arrived at the scene.

'Clearly intended to intimidate': RCMP

Kamloops RCMP's officer in charge, Supt. Jeff Pelley, said in a news release Monday that front-line officers from the Tk'emlúps RCMP detachment received a report of the group near Chief Eli Larue Way around 7:25 a.m. PT.

Pelley said officers immediately engaged with the group, which then left the location and "continued throughout various parts of the city."

"The posting of a banner bearing the words 'got bones,' combined with the use of masks to conceal their identities while making such public statements is a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division," Pelley said in the release.

WATCH | CBC investigative unit looks into views of Second Sons: Leaders of growing ‘nationalist’ club praise Nazis, say ‘race war is here’ | Duration closed caption 7:22



He said the RCMP takes the matter seriously and will "continue to engage the group" as part of its investigation.

He asked anyone with information, photos or video, or anyone with knowledge of future gatherings, to contact the RCMP.

Politicians condemn event

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke out against the gathering in a social media post on Monday afternoon.

"The cowardly act that took place at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc yesterday, is abhorrent," he wrote on Facebook.

"It has no place in this country. My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate."

Carney said the gathering is a reminder of the shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system.

"Courageous Survivors shared the truth, so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation."

Speaking at the Vancouver International Airport Sunday afternoon, NDP Leader David Eby said there has been a rise "in this kind of white nationalist behaviour" in B.C., adding that more needs to be done "to fight it."

"This is just disgraceful, disgusting behaviour. It's very clear that these people were trying to intimidate, make people feel fearful," he said, adding that the masked men would face severe retribution if their identities were known.

Lorne Doerkson, interim leader of the B.C. Conservative Party, condemned the gathering in a post to social media.

"The white nationalist gathering on Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc land this morning was hateful and meant to intimidate. It has no place in British Columbia," he said.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, in a post on social media, called the gathering "abhorrent."

"Hate and discrimination of any kind are unwelcome in British Columbia and on behalf of all members of Centre BC, I condemn this behaviour and stand in solidarity with the Tkʼemlúps First Nation," she said.

'Not going to deter us': chief

Casimir said the nation's planned events for Truth and Reconciliation Day on Sept. 30 will go ahead.

"We will not be intimidated," she said.

"This is not going to deter us from gathering, reflecting or honouring our survivors and the children who returned home."

Rosanne Casimir, chief of the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc, says the incident won't deter the community from 'gathering, reflecting, or honouring our survivors and the children who returned home.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

But the incident, Casimir said, is an example of a broader problem.

"Everyone should always be concerned because there's so much racism and discrimination out there."

On Monday morning, Casimir told CBC News's Daybreak Kamloops that community safety is the nation's top priority.

She recommended members stay alert and connected, and report any suspicious incidents.

"We're going to continue moving forward and continuing the work of Truth and Reconciliation. And ... if anything, it just reminds us why this work remains so important."

CBC News reached out to Second Sons Canada but did not hear back before publication.

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., currently igniting the internet.

The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7." She alleges they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024.

The lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court and viewed by CBC News, alleges the assault happened on campus at the Chi Phi fraternity house, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them for "free pussy."

It further says that the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university — an allegation Cornell denies.

None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. But the case has unleashed online fury, drawing comparisons to last year's Hockey Canada sexual assault trial in London, Ont., which saw all five players acquitted.

The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Sept. 28. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

On Monday, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available — by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury," district attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBC News in a written statement.

Cornell, in its own statement Monday, said it supported the DA's decision for a criminal grand jury to hear the woman's allegations, but disputed the lawsuit's characterization of how the university punished the accused.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Kyle Kimball, vice-president for university relations, said in a statement posted online.

The statement also said the on-campus Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

Here's what to know about the case and why it's caused so much fury online.

What's in the lawsuit?

According to the lawsuit, the assault began the night of Oct. 19, 2024. Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time, had been drinking with her sorority, and again at a nightclub and then "stumbled" alone at 11 p.m. to the Chi Phi fraternity house on campus to visit a friend — one of the accused.

"Plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours," the lawsuit says. It also says the nightclub served the woman "at least one" alcoholic beverage even though it had marked an X on her hand showing she was underage.

At the frat house, she was given a beer, and her friend allegedly proposed a threesome with another member, to which she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit states.

The accused allegedly took her upstairs and led her to a room with another of the accused. She was pressured to snort ketamine, the lawsuit alleges, adding that she had never used that substance before. They also "plied her" with cannabis and rum, it says, after which the two men "began engaging in sexual acts with plaintiff, all without her consent."

As they engaged in oral and vaginal sex, one of the accused also repeatedly slapped her buttocks, resulting in bruising, the lawsuit says. One of the men left to have a nap, and another entered the room. The two remaining men then began another alleged assault on the woman.

At 1:42 a.m., one of them sent a Snapchat message to the rest of the fraternity, claiming there was "free pussy." The suit includes an image of the alleged message, and some of the purported responses from the accused, including, "like you can walk in and whip it out."

WATCH | Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada trial: Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada sex assault trial | Duration 3:24 Closing arguments in the sexual assault trial of five former world junior hockey players are being presented in court on Monday. All five players have pleaded not guilty. Part of the evidence includes text messages between the accused as a group and also to the complainant. CBC News spoke to several lawyers who aren’t involved in the trial to see how the messages may or may not factor into the judge’s decision.

According to the suit, "multiple" other fraternity members then entered the room. One of them allegedly put ketamine on his erect penis and told the woman to snort it, which she did. The men then began snorting the substance off her naked body, the suit states. Two men took her to another room, where they allegedly assaulted her again.

The alleged incident ended at 5:45 a.m., and Jane Doe passed out. She returned to her sorority house "in a state of shock," the documents state, and soon realized the events were becoming "public knowledge" on campus.

She reported it a few weeks later to the Cornell University Police Department around Nov. 8, 2024. She alleges the seven accused were issued temporary suspensions and allowed "to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays."

The university released a statement and investigated, but ultimately closed it at a later date, according to the lawsuit.

Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the alleged assault and the university's purported handling of it, the lawsuit says. She is suing the seven men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, Moonies Bar and Nightclub and others, seeking undisclosed damages.

The seven Chi Phi members named in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.

"Ms. Doe has had her dreams destroyed as a result of what has happened to her," her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CBC News in a written statement.

"The fact that her trauma has been made public has been very difficult. However, she has been gratified by the outpouring of support that she has received from the public."

Online backlash to 'the culture of rape'

As the lawsuit made headlines, the backlash was swift. Online, Cornell alumni called on each other to stop donating to the school. Some people publicly turned down their acceptances, and others launched campaigns targeting the university, the local police and the various workplaces of the so-called "Cornell 7."

The seven accused were identified by Cornell's student newspaper editorial board on Sept. 21 in an editorial titled, "Cornell won't, we will."

A screenshot of a Threads post by Dr. Amani Jambhekar posted Sept. 25, 2026. (@ajvictorymd/Threads)

A former South Park writer launched a website to expose the accused. Actors Josh Gad and Florence Pugh posted online condemning the alleged assault and what the lawsuit described as the university's handling of it.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned what she called a "culture of rape" at elite institutions while speaking about the alleged incident, at a town hall in Ithaca over the weekend.

"This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices," said Ocasio-Cortez, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. “What we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore.”

On Monday night, Ithaca Mayor Robert G. Cantelmo called for an immediate moratorium on all student and special event permits, including "Greek life and other student group gatherings," given what he called the "appalling response" by Cornell's administration.

"This is a miscarriage of justice and continues to pose a significant threat to students and residents who may be victimized at unsafe and under-monitored on- or off-campus student events," he wrote in an online statement.

Cornell's response

The university said in a statement Monday that it conducted its own investigation at the time and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.

In response to the allegations, Cornell said "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

The school said it conducted an internal disciplinary investigation in 2024. It said a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, and both the woman and the accused testified and presented evidence.

In a statement last week responding to the lawsuit, Cornell said federal privacy law barred it from disclosing specific information on individual students.

People walk through the Cornell University campus on Nov. 3, 2023 in Ithaca, New York. (Matt Burkhartt/Getty Images)

Reopening the case

Van Houten, the district attorney, said Monday that in light of the attention the case has received, he wanted to clarify why the original investigation did not result in criminal charges. He said that Jane Doe went to campus police at the time, but did not, in her initial sworn statement, make any allegations of being gang-raped or drugged.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual," he said.

The prosecutor also said the woman's attorney did not contact him about her statement or about reconsidering the decision not to prosecute.

The Ithaca Police Department said in a statement Monday it was "disturbed" to hear of the accusations, adding that the alleged incident had never been reported to them.

"The Ithaca Police Department learned of these allegations recently through the media,” it wrote.

A woman walks by a Cornell University sign on the Ivy League school's campus in January 2022. (Ted Shaffrey/The Associated Press)

'She was traumatized'

Giuffra, Jane Doe's lawyer, defended his client while blaming the university police investigation.

"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode," Giuffra told CBC News.

He questioned why she wasn't contacted by the DA's office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors.

"It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she ... never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Giuffra added.

Multiple media now report that the seven accused men have sought legal representation. CBC News has reached out to Jeremy Saland, one of the lawyers identified, and has not yet heard back. But Saland told BBC his client denies the allegations.

His client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat," but "did nothing else," the outlet reported. Saland said his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine."

In a post on Threads Sunday, AI training company Data Annotation Tech wrote it had terminated its contract with one of the accused.

"We are deeply sorry for what happened at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 and extend our concern to everyone affected by the incident," the company posted.

"Any future reinstatement of Matthew Ingalls' contract will be considered only after the civil proceedings are concluded and the court’s findings have been reviewed."

World.title: This Ontario city had its 'worst' problems with homecoming parties, even filling a hospital ER
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The homecoming parties in Guelph, Ont., over the weekend may have been the "worst" yet, Mayor Cam Guthrie says. As CBC's Aastha Shetty explains, police had to shut down traffic near Stone Road Mall late Saturday afternoon after the crowd ballooned in size, spilling into nearby parking lots.

The homecoming parties in Guelph, Ont., on Saturday may have been the "worst" yet, Mayor Cam Guthrie says.

Videos shared on social media show thousands of young people dressed in red, yellow, white and black partying on off-campus properties near Stone Road Mall.

Thousands of young people gathered in the area in the afternoon, and the crowd ballooned. Some videos show items being thrown into the crowd and young people climbing up the exterior walls of a building before falling into a bush.

Police closed Chancellors Way between South Ring Road West and Stone Road West on Saturday just after 5 p.m. and said in a post on X that the move was "necessary to protect people's safety."

Guthrie said people in the area "are ticked" by the party and the disruption to their neighbourhood.

"I don't blame them," he told CBC Kitchener-Waterloo's The Morning Edition host Craig Norris in an interview on Monday morning.

"It was probably the worst amount of issues that we've ever experienced in the history of homecoming parties.

"Not only has there been a huge amount of resources required from our own staff for the front-line staff, if you can think about waste and transit and bylaw issues, but then our emergency services as well: police, fire and paramedics."

Guthrie said there was a ripple effect from homecoming that "impacted the entire community, including neighbourhoods and businesses ... that experienced a lot of property [damage]."

'Significantly larger' crowd this year: police

The Guelph Police Service said the number of people at the homecoming party "was significantly larger than in recent years and generated several public-safety concerns."

"Officers responded to incidents involving objects being thrown, people climbing buildings and other structures, as well as reports of shoplifting and vandalism affecting nearby businesses," police said in a release Monday afternoon.

"Although no known serious injuries have been reported at the time of this release, emergency responders treated multiple people for injuries, including cuts and lacerations, and responded to a number of intoxication-related medical calls."

Most people enjoyed the day responsibly, but behaviour that puts others at risk cannot be accepted. - Gord Cobey, Guelph police chief

Additional police resources were brought in, including officers with the tactics and rescue unit.

"Their efforts helped restore order, prevent further injuries and allow emergency personnel to safely access those requiring assistance," police said.

They said "several criminal and provincial offence charges," but did not provide an exact numbers.

"Investigators continue to review reported incidents, video and other evidence, and additional charges may be forthcoming."

Guelph police Chief Gord Cobey said homecoming is a chance for the community to celebrate.

"Most people enjoyed the day responsibly, but behaviour that puts others at risk cannot be accepted,” Cobey said.

People treated for head injuries from thrown bottles

Guthrie said he was also told the emergency department at Guelph General Hospital was filled with people from the homecoming parties who needed medical care.

Dr. Alex Folkl, chief of emergency medicine at Guelph General Hospital, said in a statement to CBC News that the emergency department treated approximately 60 people in relation to the homecoming festivities.

People were treated for "head injuries caused by thrown bottles, lacerations and intoxication."

"Homecoming-related visits place significant pressure on critical hospital resources. This weekend, our emergency department was stretched beyond capacity," Folkl said.

"Had we also experienced an influx of seriously ill patients or even a small multi-patient trauma event, there was a real risk that we would not have been able to provide every patient with the timely level of care they required."

He also urged college and university students "to make safe, responsible choices around alcohol and substance use."

"Doing so can reduce the risk of injury and help prevent avoidable visits to the hospital."

University 'deeply disappointed' by street party

On Friday, the day before homecoming, the University of Guelph issued a statement on social media reminding students to be "mindful that your actions reflect those around you."

"Remember your Gryphon values and be respectful of your neighbours and the community you became a part of when you became a UofG student. Be safe and look out for yourself and each other," the post said.

Rene Van Acker, president and vice-chancellor of the University of Guelph, said on Monday that school officials are "deeply disappointed" by the unsanctioned gathering and "we are clear that this cannot happen again."

An image taken from a video shared on Instagram show Guelph police responding to the homecoming party Saturday evening. (iamasevvy/Instagram)

"While most students celebrated responsibly this weekend, there were incidents requiring intervention by emergency services and law enforcement," Van Acker said.

Both Guthrie and Van Acker said that in the past, they knew students from Guelph weren't just at the homecoming events. Guthrie said people who have been charged in previous years have come from other cities.

Van Acker said some Guelph students did take part, and "engaged in behaviour that was unacceptable and fell well below our community’s expectations."

"Where individuals are found to have violated university policies or applicable laws, the university will take action."

Van Acker also thanked first responders, hospital workers and city staff for their support on the weekend.

Hard to stop the parties, mayor says

Homecoming parties in Guelph in recent years have also made headlines for similar large gatherings.

But Guelph isn't alone in dealing with unsanctioned student parties.

Waterloo has become known for an unsanctioned St. Patrick's Day party that happens near Wilfrid Laurier University each year, while other cities, including London and Kingston, have grappled with homecoming celebrations that have gotten out of control.

Guthrie said it's not clear how to put a stop to the parties because once they happen on private property, there's "really nothing the government can do to try to step in."

"Especially in the world of social media right now, you say you can't do that here — and even that can be challenge to even suggest that — and then in literally 10 minutes, everybody's going to know that it's just going to happen somewhere else," he said.

These stills are taken from videos on Instagram that were posted on Saturday by people who said they were at the Guelph homecoming parties. The photos, from left to right, show a young person falling off a building while climbing it, police responding to the party and the crowd of people in the afternoon. (Instagram/Guelph Motives/Raytomusic1/djtwanyy_)

He said he and others appreciated the students who gathered on Sunday to pick up trash and recycling, but that doesn't mean it's OK "for things to get out of control" the day before.

"These these students and or their guests that come here, they are guests in our city and the respect has to be there for us."

Over the next few days, Guthrie said, he will be in talks with officials from the university and emergency services. While Guthrie is not seeking re-election and a new mayor will be chosen on Oct. 26 during Ontario's municipal elections, he said the conversations "can't wait a month."

World.title: OpenAI scraps release of new AI model over safety concerns
World.content:

OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation artificial intelligence model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's ‌safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday.

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and rival Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month joined industry leaders in calling for a slower pace ​of AI development and stronger safety measures.

OpenAI has ​warned that Astra, its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as ​Anthropic have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached ⁠safeguards, including an ⁠OpenAI model that accessed Australia's health system ‌database.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch the model, which was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle ⁠more complex tasks without human assistance.

WATCH | When OpenAI has gone rogue: OpenAI’s AI went rogue at least 4 times. This researcher caught 3 of them | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 6:01 An independent research lab says it uncovered at least four additional incidents of OpenAI’s AI agents attacking websites without authorization. Conrad Stosz, head of governance at Transluce, explains how his team detected the rogue activity and intervened in three cases.

The Journal reported that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in ‌which it did not always accurately disclose what actions it had taken.

"While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and ​authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," ⁠said Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

"Of course we want ⁠to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's ⁠in ⁠the company, or when ​we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have ​an extremely high bar ⁠in terms of safety and alignment," Jain said.

The decision comes just ahead of OpenAI's developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.

World.title: Hamilton steel plant to lay off hundreds of workers as U.S. tariffs prompt 'survival' move
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stelco Holdings Inc. said on Monday that it plans to idle part of its Hamilton plant in order to "ensure the survival" of the company, as U.S. tariffs squeeze its sales.

Stelco said the decision will impact up to 500 employees.

In a memo obtained by CBC News on Monday, the company said it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant, with operations set to begin winding down on Oct. 9.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, estimates 350 steelworkers will be laid off. He says he was briefed on the situation in a meeting with the company on Monday morning.

"Obviously, we got to meet with the company, and find out who's getting laid off, [and] make sure it's done by seniority," Wells told CBC News on Monday. "Christmas ain't that far away, and we have no idea the duration of these layoffs … People are concerned. I don't blame them."

The company said this will not impact its ability to supply hot-rolled steel products.

"This is an unfortunate but necessary action to help ensure the survival of Stelco in what has become a challenging and unsustainable market for cold-rolled and coated products caused by the ongoing and sustained trade disruptions impacting the Canadian steel industry," Stelco vice-president of sales Frederic Fafard stated in the memo.

An aerial photo of the Stelco Hamilton steel production facility. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in June applying up to 50 per cent tariffs to certain steel and aluminum imports from Canada.

"Stelco’s market for cold-rolled and galvanized products has contracted significantly, while import penetration for these products remains at heightened levels," Fafard said in the memo.

"While the measures taken by the federal government in Canada have served to reduce imports into Canada overall, import volumes remain at levels that prevent Stelco from being able to bridge the gap in the market created by the trade crisis."

Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Hamilton-based Stelco in a $3.4-billion Cdn cash-and-stock deal that closed in November 2024. In a news release announcing the deal, Stelco's then-CEO Alan Kestenbaum stated the transaction "keeps national interests at the forefront and recognizes the importance of the workforce."

"We're very disappointed," Wells said. "In particular, when Cliffs bought us in the fall of 2024, they made commitments. One of those commitments was to maintain the same number of unionized employees."

In an email to CBC News on Monday, a Cleveland-Cliffs spokesperson confirmed Joly has been in touch with chairman and CEO Lourenco Goncalves.

"Both Cliffs and the Canadian government have the interests of the Stelco workers in mind, and will continue to work together to minimize the impact of the current market situation on Canadian workers," wrote Pat Persico, the company's senior director of corporate communications.

She said that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.

"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in a previous email.

"We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."

Industry Minister 'extremely disappointed'

In a statement on Monday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly slammed the decision to lay off workers, while noting Ottawa had offered to help Stelco weather the impact of U.S. tariffs.

"Our government has made clear to the company that we are ready and willing to provide financial support to sustain operations and protect jobs. Its decision to reject these practical proposals and continue with layoffs is extremely disappointing," she said.

"Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs have made significant commitments to Canadian steelworkers. We will use every lever possible to defend Canadian industry, protect jobs, and secure our supply chain."

Trump announces new steel plant in Iowa

On Monday, U.S. President Trump touted a new $15-billion US investment plan by Minnesota-based steelmaker Mesabi Metallics as evidence that American tariffs on imported steel are working as his administration intended.

The company announced plans to build a massive plant in Iowa, with production set to begin in 2030.

"I imposed powerful 50 per cent tariffs on all foreign steel, and now our steel industry is roaring back to life." Trump said at a news announcement in the Oval Office. "Everyone is building their plant here because they don't want to pay tariffs. It's really not that complicated."

The move is raising concerns north of the border, where Kevon Stewart, director of United Steelworkers District 6, said his phone has been lighting up with calls from distressed Canadian workers.

"Everything is timing right now," he told CBC News on Monday.

"This is not only a wake-up call, because the call for action has been there before. But we've got to come up with a game plan that ensures workers are protected if and when these measures are implemented."

He said such protections could include increased benefits, or removing the waiting time for benefits.

Colin Mang, an economist at McMaster University in Hamilton, said the layoffs announced Monday are "a consequence of our trade war with the United States." For Stelco, he said the situation is worsened by a steady flow of foreign products coming into Canada.

"The lack of access to the American market has meant that we have a surplus of steel production capacity here in Canada, and there just isn't enough domestic Canadian demand in order to absorb all of the output from the steelmakers here," Mang told CBC News.

"The Canadian government has worked to restrict the amount of steel coming into Canada, but when you look at a variety of steel products, particularly the kinds of flat products that Stelco manufactures, Canada has imported about 1.2 million tons from other trading partners around the world. That's because we continue to have free trade agreements with a variety of countries. So, it's very difficult to restrict imports from our other trading partners."

Blair Dickerson, president of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, said his thoughts are with the workers impacted by Monday's announcement. He also called upon Canada's federal government and the Trump to resolve their ongoing trade tension.

"Days like today demonstrate how challenging the tariff situation is, and provide a stark reminder as to the urgency of finding a solution," Dickerson said in an email.

"Recognizing the Government's support to date, Canada must continue and deepen the work of keeping unfairly traded steel out of our market, enforcing our measures at the border, and ensuring our producers can be competitive here at home."

'The fight is not over': Hamilton mayor

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said she plans to fight to ensure Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs live up to the commitments their executives made to workers in her city.

"The fight is not over," she told the CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.

LISTEN | Hamilton's mayor reacts to layoffs: As It Happens 6:54 Hamilton steelworker layoffs 'painful for our community,' says mayor As of next Friday, about 350 Hamilton, Ont., steelworkers will be out of work, according to their union. Stelco, the U.S.-owned company that operates the Hamilton plant, blames the layoffs on trade disputes between the U.S. and Canada. But Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath says the fight isn't over. She spoke to As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"This particular company has been very clear ... that they support Donald Trump and his tariffs, and desire to pull all steelmaking back into the United States.

Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said it's ironic for a company's whose leadership supports Trump to criticize U.S. tariffs for eroding its business.

"The CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, he's the biggest supporter of Trump and his tariffs. So, it's tough to have any sympathy when you know they're the basically the master of this disaster."

World.title: Obby Khan stepping down as Manitoba PC leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Obby Khan is stepping down from his position as leader of Manitoba's Opposition Progressive Conservatives, saying divisions within his caucus have left him "no choice" but to resign.

Khan made the announcement just after 5 p.m. CT Monday, after he survived what appears to be a symbolic confidence vote on Friday.

It's not clear which member of the PC caucus triggered that vote, or for what reason.

Speaking to reporters at the legislature Monday evening, Khan said the votes in that confidence motion were two to one in his favour, but "a small group of MLAs have decided that those results are still not enough."

"It has become clear to me that after Friday's majority vote in my favour would not resolve the divisions within our caucus, it has left me no choice," Khan said.

Under the PC Party's constitution, a new leadership race can only be triggered at this point in the election cycle if the position becomes vacant, the leader ends up mentally or physically incapacitated, the leader requests a leadership race or a simple majority of PC members vote in favour of a race at a general meeting.

However, Khan said over the course of the weekend, he learned some members of the PC caucus planned to meet Monday evening in what he described as an effort to "subvert the democratic will" of the caucus.

WATCH | Obby Khan's full resignation speech on Monday: Obby Khan's full statement on resignation as Manitoba PC leader | Duration closed caption 19:02 Obby Khan announced late Monday afternoon that he is stepping down as leader of the Manitoba Progressive Conservative Party, the province's Official Opposition. He said he will also leave the party caucus to sit as an Independent MLA. Watch his full remarks here.

The decision to resign is "not [about] whether I could fight.… You all know me, I like to fight," said Khan.

But "I will not spend the next chapter fighting with my own party, my own caucus, when I came here to fight the NDP … and to hold this government accountable," he said.

Khan said he will resign from the PC caucus, effective Tuesday, but will continue on as the MLA for the Winnipeg constituency of Fort Whyte, sitting as an Independent.

"I cannot be a part of a caucus with a small minority membership that lacks moral integrity, that will not abide by our rules, our principles, our code," he said.

Khan thanked some members of the 20-person PC caucus by name during his resignation speech, including former interim party leader Kelvin Goertzen, as well as MLAs Ron Schuler, Greg Nesbitt, Rick Wowchuk, Derek Johnson, Trevor King and Colleen Robbins.

'Far bigger than me'

Khan became the party leader last year , after former Manitoba Premier Heather Stefanson stepped down in early 2024.

He won the leadership in a tightly contested leadership race against Wally Daudrich, a Churchill hotel and ecotourism company owner who quit the party in June.

Khan, who was an entrepreneur and a former football player with the CFL's Winnipeg Blue Bombers before entering politics, was first elected to the Manitoba Legislature in 2022 , winning the Fort Whyte seat in Winnipeg in a byelection.

He became leader in a contest sparked by the resignation of Stefanson, who stepped down as party leader months after her PCs lost the fall 2023 provincial election to Wab Kinew's NDP.

Khan celebrates his win in the Fort Whyte byelection with then Manitoba premier Heather Stefanson on March 22, 2022. (Ian Froese/CBC)

When elected to the role last year, Khan became the first Muslim, as well as the first Canadian from a South Asian ethnic background, to lead the party.

"For the first time in the party's history, someone who looked like me, prayed like me, carried a family story like mine stood here as the party leader," Khan said Monday, having to pause to collect himself as his voice cracked with emotion.

"That is far bigger than me.… Whatever happens after today remains history."

Khan did not take questions from reporters after his nearly 20-minute speech at the legislature on Monday.

Manitoba's legislature is slated to resume on Tuesday.

As of Monday, the Tories held 20 of the province's 57 seats, including Khan's. The governing NDP have 34, the Liberals hold one. There are two Independents as of Monday — Khan will become the third.

The next provincial election is not slated until October 2027.

Not a surprise: prof

Under Khan, the PCs have struggled to whittle away at the popularity of Wab Kinew's NDP government. In a byelection last year, the Tories narrowly held on to the rural Manitoba Spruce Woods seat — a normally safe riding the party has held since 2011.

Christopher Adams, a political studies professor at the University of Manitoba, says he's not surprised Khan stepped down, given the premier's popularity and the NDP's hold in the province.

"Political parties, when their caucus feels that they aren't going to go anywhere, they are very quick to get rid of their leaders," he said.

"I think MLAs are looking around saying, 'Look, is our party going to survive? Am I going to survive in the seat that I hold if we continue on the trajectory that we have?'"

The announcement did come as a surprise to PC party president Peter Smith, who said Khan told him he'd learned a lot from the vote and discussion the caucus had Friday.

"It's a tough position to be in, and I suppose at some point, he had discussions with the caucus and just determined that it wasn't going to be productive moving forward," Smith said.

"It's a bump in the road for sure, but the message of the party is bigger than the leader, and we feel we have a good message."

Khan's time as Tory leader has also seen him butt heads with the NDP in the legislature, in particular with Kinew, in what Adams has previously described as "outright hostility" between the party leaders.

Last October, Khan apologized after making a gesture in question period that mimicked shooting himself in the head while Education Minister Tracy Schmidt was answering a question.

And earlier this year, the Speaker of the legislature ruled Khan had made "hateful" remarks when he called Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara, who is non-binary, "a terrible person, whatever you are."

The PC Party said as of Monday evening, it did not yet know who will be serving as interim Opposition leader.

In a two-line statement Monday evening, Tory deputy caucus chair Josh Guenter, the MLA for Borderlands, acknowledged that Khan had stepped down and will sit as an Independent.

The PC caucus will meet Tuesday morning and will "have more to share tomorrow," Guenter's statement said.

Daudrich said it's a "good day" for the party.

"I think the party's future has never been brighter since Duff Roblin took out a membership," he said in an interview with CBC News on Monday evening, suggesting the party hasn't had as great a vision for Manitoba since Roblin led the party in the 1960s.

In a post on social media Monday evening, former interim leader Goertzen thanked Khan for his work as leader.

"Leadership in politics is always challenging and comes with sacrifice," including time away from family, wrote Goertzen, who has said he will not run for re-election in his Steinbach constituency.

He wished Khan "well in the time ahead," and said he hopes "he has more time to make special memories with his son."

World.title: London says Argentina “lacks the ability” to take the Falklands
World.content:
London says Argentina “lacks the ability” to take the Falklands

28th Monday, September 2026 - 09:33 UTC Full article

Streeting also said “this issue was settled in 1982” and that the will of the archipelago's residents, “the overwhelming majority of whom choose to be British”, remains unchanged

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Argentina “lacks the ability” to take the Falkland Islands and that the United Kingdom “has the ability to defend” them, in an interview with the Sunday paper The Sun on Sunday published on Saturday. Asked whether London could protect the archipelago militarily if Buenos Aires sent warships, he answered yes.

“This isn't 1982,” the minister said, dismissing the position of Argentine President Javier Milei as “the same old bogus propaganda”. In referring to Argentine claims he used a colloquial pejorative term for the country's citizens, which Spanish-language versions rendered simply as “the Argentines”.

Streeting also said “this issue was settled in 1982” and that the will of the archipelago's residents, “the overwhelming majority of whom choose to be British”, remains unchanged. That is the British government's position and it is contested by Argentina, which maintains the dispute remains open; the archipelago is still on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose, on a 92% turnout, to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The remarks were published three days after Milei's address to the UN General Assembly, in which he called on the organisation to act over what he described as unilateral British actions and argued that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the archipelago. Some British coverage framed Streeting's words as a response to the televised address Milei delivered on September 3, so it is not established which specific intervention he was answering.

The week in New York produced opposing positions from the same podium. On Tuesday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham included the archipelago among challenges to the rule of law; that same night, Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno exercised the right of reply, saying the British occupation “dates back to 1833, when United Kingdom forces occupied the Malvinas Islands, breaching the country's territorial integrity and expelling the legitimately established Argentine authorities and population”, while reiterating Argentina's “full willingness” to resume negotiations. Milei spoke on Wednesday, and that same Wednesday the United Kingdom entered a written statement of rejection into the assembly's record.

Argentina's government has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors over hydrocarbon exploration in waters near the archipelago. None of the allegations has been proven. No official Argentine response to Streeting's remarks has been recorded so far.

The 1982 war lasted 74 days and left 649 Argentine service personnel, 255 British and three residents of the archipelago dead.

World.title: Chile reinforcing its military presence in Magallanes Region and Antarctica
World.content:
Chile reinforcing its military presence in Magallanes Region and Antarctica

28th Monday, September 2026 - 08:09 UTC Full article

Minister Barros said defense requires planning and Chile must have the necessary capacities to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of its people.

Chile announced the reinforcement of its military capacities in the Magallanes Region, extreme south of the country with a plan that includes renewal of aircraft, modernization of armored vehicles, increased vigilance and presence in the austral territory and Antarctica, updating of military strategy based on experiences from the current war scenarios in Europe and Middle East.

The announcement was made by Defense minister Fernando Barros, at the base of Chabunco, next to Punta Arenas, together with the commanders of all services. Chabunco is headquarters and seat of the Fourth Chilean Air Force Brigade, FACH, with jurisdiction over southern Patagonia and protection of bases in Chilean Antarctica.

The announcement was done at a very sensitive moment for relations between Chile and Argentina, following repeated statements from Argentine nationalist groups during August and September, regarding alleged ‘shared sovereignty’ over the Magellan Strait, straining bilateral relations.

Minister Barros insisted that defense requires planning and Chile must have the necessary capacities to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of its people.

Chilean Defense said that strategic planning means replacing in Punta Arenas the current F-5 fighter jets by fourth or fifth generation aircraft, the renewal of the helicopter fleet plus strategic air transport, essential for Antarctica missions, and for the Navy long range maritime patrolling with air coverage. The Army will see the refurbish of its Leopard 1 tanks and remote control modern warfare.

Some land bases will be reformed to have a permanent presence and the strategic bases in Chilean Antarctica are to have increased air and maritime connections, confirming a greater presence form the country.

Apparently Chilean Defense has been working on these plans for some time and with a 2043 horizon, but not only with a military objective, but rather with “a standing Chilean logistics responsibility regarding the Magellan Strait and Antarctica”.

All of this erupted when Argentine head of Air Force Chief of Staff Gustavo Javier Valverde made some comments regarding the Magellan Strait that generated an immediate reaction from Chile, Taking advantage of the calendar, an anniversary of the possession of the Strait by Chile in September 1843, the Chilean vice-president, members of the Senate’s blocks plus Magallanes joined in a tour de force reaffirming sole and complete Chilean sovereignty of the Magellan Strait.

Likewise in a visit to Argentina, and again in Chile, president Juan Antonio Kast said that Argentina “does not have and will never have”, sovereignty over the Magellan Strait because it has been clearly judged, and agreed, by treaties with Argentina.

And if this was not enough five F-16 from the northern FACH base of Los Condores in Iquique, next to Peru flew non-stop with an early warning aircraft AEW, and a Stratotanker KC-135 to refuel fighter jets in flight to Magallanes Region, for an air display over Punta Arenas. Apparently the F-16 will remain a couple of weeks in the extreme south of Chile.

Chile’s FACH has proven experience with the Stratotanker KC-135 since last April when the Air and Space Show in Santiago, FIDAE, it successfully refueled two F-35A Lightning from US Air Force in their journey from Florida to Chile for the show.

Summing up, according to Chilean sources the challenge for the administration of president Kast is to advance with the military modernization while keeping open, friendly cooperation channels with Argentina.

The Kast message is clear: Magallanes Region, the Strait and its projection to Antarctica are a Defense strategic planning priority for Chile, and with the funds needed or expected to be invested, allegedly having the necessary congressional support.
