A party that ran the country for 20 years

The Dominican Republic, where the PLD opposition party is fighting over its 2028 candidate. Photo: Oleg Yunakov, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Juan Bosch, a former president, founded the PLD in 1973. Under Leonel Fernández and then Danilo Medina it won five presidential elections between 1996 and 2016.

The break came in October 2019. Fernández narrowly lost a primary to Gonzalo Castillo, Medina’s favourite. He alleged fraud and founded a new party, Fuerza del Pueblo (People’s Force).

The count, supervised by the Central Electoral Board (JCE), which runs Dominican elections, gave Castillo 48.3 percent to 47.3 percent.

The PLD lost power in 2020 to Luis Abinader of the Modern Revolutionary Party (PRM), with Castillo taking about 37 percent. In 2024 its candidate, Abel Martínez, finished third with 10.4 percent, behind Abinader and Fernández.

Medina still chairs the party, but the constitution bars him from another term. The country’s politics and economy are set out in this Dominican Republic explainer.

The fight over 523,000 names

The PLD calls its 18 October exercise a consultation. Any registered voter who does not belong to another party may take part, not only members.

On 23 September Francisco Javier García, a former tourism minister and hopeful, said about 523,000 people had been removed from that list. He told a radio programme the move was meant to help Castillo.

“They have turned this internal process into a Persian bazaar,” he said. He claimed party central committee members were being offered 1 million pesos (about US$16,900) each, 10 percent up front.

No evidence of the offers has been made public, the newspaper Diario Libre noted. The dollar figure uses the central bank’s reference rate of about 59.3 pesos per US dollar.

The disputed names are roughly a quarter of the 2.16 million members the party has on file with the electoral board.

The organising commission, known as Conap, replied on 25 September that nobody had been struck off. It said the 523,781 people also appear on the membership lists of at least one other party.

They have until noon on 8 October to confirm, online and then in person, that they belong only to the PLD. “Nobody has been excluded from the party’s register,” the commission said.

Why the electoral board said no

The PLD asked the JCE to lend it 1,800 electronic devices for the vote. The board refused in a letter made public on 25 September.

It said such an event is “not among the acts permitted by law at the current stage of the electoral calendar”. It had lent 500 devices for training.

Dominican law sets fixed windows for parties to choose candidates. The commission itself says the formal nomination must take place between July and October 2027, under the 2018 law on political parties.

So it calls 18 October a non-binding measure of support, not a primary.

Four hopefuls, one absentee

The central committee approved eight hopefuls in February. Four have since withdrawn, one of them to back Castillo.

Those left are García, Castillo, Francisco Domínguez Brito, a former attorney general, and Manfred Mata. A CID Latinoamérica poll reported on 23 September put Castillo ahead of Martínez and García among PLD sympathisers.

Castillo carries a legal cloud. In May a judge ruled he should not stand trial in a large corruption case. State lawyers appealed in June; he calls it political persecution.

Martínez, a former mayor of Santiago, the country’s second city, refuses to join the consultation.

What comes next

The commission was due to hand out the final voter list, rules and timetable on Monday. Disputed members have until 8 October to re-register.

The last such consultation, in 2022, drew a little over 500,000 people by the party’s count. Turnout will show how much pull the PLD still has.

The result will not make anyone the official candidate. That choice comes in the second half of 2027, and the winner on 18 October could still face rivals then.

Nor does the row mean a formal split. No hopeful has left the party, and García was still campaigning for the vote on 27 September.

The stakes lie in 2028. Abinader, re-elected in 2024, cannot run again, and a divided PLD would leave Fuerza del Pueblo as the ruling party’s clearer challenger.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the PLD?

The Dominican Liberation Party was founded by former president Juan Bosch in 1973. It governed from 1996 to 2000 and from 2004 to 2020, and is now in opposition.

Is the 18 October vote the party’s official primary?

No. The organisers call it a non-binding measure of support. Under Dominican law the formal nomination must happen between July and October 2027. The electoral board refused to lend equipment for this vote.

Who is likely to be the PLD’s candidate in 2028?

Nothing is decided. Four hopefuls are in the race, and one September poll put Gonzalo Castillo, the 2020 candidate, in front. The 2024 candidate, Abel Martínez, is staying out of the consultation.

When is the next Dominican presidential election?

In May 2028. President Luis Abinader is in his second term and cannot run again, so the main parties are all choosing new candidates.

World.title: Dominican Republic Business Chief Warns Early Campaigns Invite Crime Money
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic, a Caribbean nation of about 11 million people, is a stable democracy and the region’s most visited destination. Washington also lists it as a major transit country for drugs.

— The background The law says campaigning for party nominations may start only on 4 July 2027, before elections in February and May 2028. Hopefuls from all three main parties are already holding rallies.

— Why now The race to succeed President Luis Abinader, who cannot run again, has filled weekends with mass events. The electoral authority has not sanctioned anyone for campaigning early.

— What happened In a television interview reported on 27 September, the head of the main business federation warned that a long, unpoliced campaign creates an “enormous risk” of organised crime money entering politics.

— Who is who Celso Juan Marranzini chairs CONEP, the umbrella body of Dominican business. The Central Electoral Board (JCE) runs elections and is meant to police campaign timing and spending.

— What it means for you No rule has changed. For investors it is a signal that business leaders see weak campaign-finance control as a governance risk before the 2028 vote.

— Still open Whether the parties accept the political pact Marranzini proposes, and whether the electoral board ever uses its power to disqualify early campaigners.

The Dominican Republic’s leading business federation has warned that early campaigning is opening the door to organised crime money. The next general election is not until May 2028.

Celso Juan Marranzini, president of CONEP, said the long, costly unofficial campaign makes it ever harder to know who pays for it. He called for a pact among the parties to stop it.

What the business federation said

Santo Domingo’s Zona Colonial, the historic centre of the Dominican Republic’s capital. Photo: Максим Улитин, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons

CONEP, the National Council of Private Enterprise, groups the country’s main business associations and speaks for the private sector. Marranzini spoke on D’Agenda, a Sunday interview programme on the television channel Telesistema.

“It must be made very clear who is going to supervise, and how,” he said, according to the newspaper El Nacional. What is spent on a campaign, he argued, is simply not audited.

Defying the legal calendar, he said, creates “an enormous risk that more and more organised crime money seeps in”. Listín Diario carried the same warning on 28 September.

He did not accuse any party or politician. His point was about cost: rallies that move thousands of people are far dearer than posters.

“I think we are still in time, but it is an issue that requires a lot of attention,” he said. He also noted “a growing disenchantment” with the parties, despite all the activity.

A campaign that never stops

Marranzini said the habit is old. In 2016, he recalled, posters of hopefuls for 2020 were on electricity poles the day after that year’s election.

This cycle is no different. On 20 September Carolina Mejía, mayor of Santo Domingo’s National District, named the Senate president her campaign chief at a mass event.

Mejía wants the nomination of the ruling Modern Revolutionary Party (PRM). So does David Collado, the tourism minister, whose team held simultaneous meetings in Santiago, Mao, Higüey and Bahoruco that weekend.

The same day Gonzalo Castillo, a hopeful of the opposition Dominican Liberation Party (PLD), told supporters he would be president. His party holds its own internal vote on 18 October.

Leonel Fernández, a three-time former president, uses events of his Fuerza del Pueblo (People’s Force) party to pitch a government from 2028.

What the law says

Dominican law sets a strict calendar. The pre-campaign, when hopefuls may seek a party nomination, opens on 4 July 2027.

Candidates may be formally chosen only between July and October 2027, ahead of municipal elections in February 2028 and the presidential vote in May. Rallies held before July 2027 fall outside the legal window.

The penalties on paper are heavy. Under the 2018 law on political parties, early campaigners “will be sanctioned with the inadmissibility of their candidacy”.

The 2023 electoral law adds fines of one to 200 minimum wages. They apply to parties, hopefuls and campaign chiefs who hold rallies too early.

None of this has been applied. The JCE created a unit in 2022 to pursue electoral offences, yet has sanctioned no one for early campaigning, Listín Diario reported.

Marranzini offered one reason. The board, he said, is busy running elections and a new identity card, leaving little capacity to track party money.

Why crime money is the worry

The concern is not abstract. The US government lists the Dominican Republic among the major transit countries for illegal drugs bound for the United States.

In 2021 a sitting congressman from Abinader’s own party, Miguel Gutiérrez Díaz, was arrested in Miami on US drug-trafficking charges. Abinader said at the time that everyone must pay for their deeds.

Marranzini pointed abroad as well. He cited Guatemala, which he said is heading to elections with around 20 candidates while “nobody knows what could happen”.

Similar fears are heard elsewhere. In Panama, a bill that raises campaign donation caps has drawn warnings about organised crime money.

What comes next

Marranzini wants the parties to agree a pact that limits the permanent campaign and says clearly who audits the money.

His warning is a call for tighter oversight, not an allegation. He named no party that has taken crime money, and none of the reports cited any case.

Nor does it change the calendar: the pre-campaign still opens in July 2027. The electoral board keeps the power to disqualify early campaigners, if it chooses to use it.

For now, the rallies continue every weekend. The country’s politics and economy are set out in this Dominican Republic explainer.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is CONEP?

CONEP, the National Council of Private Enterprise, is the Dominican Republic’s main business federation. It groups the country’s business associations and speaks for the private sector on policy.

Is campaigning already allowed in the Dominican Republic?

No. The pre-campaign for party nominations opens on 4 July 2027. The law allows the electoral board to disqualify hopefuls who campaign earlier, but it has not done so.

Did CONEP accuse any party of taking crime money?

No. Its president warned that unaudited, early campaigning raises the risk of organised crime money entering politics. He named no party or politician.

When is the next Dominican election?

Municipal elections are due in February 2028 and the presidential and congressional vote in May 2028. President Luis Abinader cannot run again.

World.title: Colombia Strips Ex-Senate President Iván Name of Seat in Pension Bribery Ruling
World.content:
Colombia · Justice

Key Facts —The ruling. Colombia’s Council of State has stripped former Senate president Iván Name of his seat — the loss of investiture known locally as political death — after finding proven influence peddling in the handling of the government’s pension reform. Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. —The money. The court found Name received 3,000 million Colombian pesos, delivered in two instalments of 1,500 million on 12 and 13 October 2023, through intermediaries Sneyder Pinilla and Sandra Ortiz. —The empty chair. Of 16 pension-reform plenary sessions examined between February and April 2024, Name failed to chair 14 — 87.5 per cent — without legal justification; first vice-president María José Pizarro presided in his place. —Pizarro named, not accused. Pizarro appears at least 85 times in the 129-page ruling, but the court does not say she received money or knew of the payment. She says she acted under her legal mandate. —What is next. Name can appeal to the Council of State’s full administrative chamber, and a separate criminal case against him continues at the Supreme Court of Justice.

The Council of State’s ruling against Iván Name reconstructs a chain that begins with 3,000 million pesos in cash, passes through a Bogotá hotel and a geolocated phone trail, and ends, in the court’s conclusion, with a Senate presidency deliberately vacated so that the pension reform could pass. In the middle of that operation stands María José Pizarro — mentioned at least 85 times, yet formally accused of nothing.

Colombia’s Senate in session in Bogotá: the pension-reform plenaries of early 2024 are at the heart of the Council of State’s ruling.

A 129-Page Ruling That Ends a Political Career

The decision, notified on 25 September and reported in detail on Monday by La FM and Infobae, declares the loss of investiture of Iván Name, the Green Alliance senator who presided over the Senate while President Gustavo Petro’s reform of the pension system moved through Congress. The chamber found the causal of influence peddling — tráfico de influencias — duly proven. An appeal lies to the full administrative chamber of the Council of State.

The 129-page judgment is not only about money. It is a reconstruction of how the Senate’s most important sessions of early 2024 were conducted — and of who was actually in the chair when the pension reform was debated and approved. The case file reviewed by the court includes parts of the criminal process that continues against Name before the Supreme Court of Justice.

Two Deliveries and a Geolocation Trail

According to the ruling, the money moved in two parts. On 12 October 2023, Sneyder Pinilla handed 1,500 million pesos to Sandra Ortiz at the Hotel Tequendama Suites in Bogotá; the second 1,500 million followed the next day. One of the most striking pieces of technical evidence: the geolocation of telephones placed Ortiz and Pinilla on a route that ended at the Bassel I building, where Name kept an apartment. Chats, call records, photographs and witness testimony complete the file, La FM reported.

The court’s account of the purpose is the heart of the sentence: the money was tied to a parliamentary consideration — that Name, from the Senate presidency, would favour the passage of the pension reform. The government needed the reforms unblocked, and Name’s institutional position had the power to influence how the plenaries ran. The ruling also records that Carlos Ramón González, then director of the Administrative Department of the Presidency, allegedly ordered the delivery of the money to the then Senate president to unblock the government’s reforms.

The Chair Name Kept Leaving

The chamber analysed 16 Senate plenary sessions between 28 February and 23 April 2024. Name stepped away from chairing 14 of them — 87.5 per cent — and the court found no constitutional or legal explanation: no leaves of absence, no vacancies, no material impossibility were recorded. These were not minor sessions either, the ruling notes: in them, reports were voted, the articles were debated and the reform was approved.

Nor was it an isolated pattern. On 6 March, for example, Name opened a session presiding and then handed the chair to Pizarro; other sessions show alternation with Senator Didier Lobo. The court documented each plenary through tables of dates, times and audiovisual and documentary records that identify who presided and how the debates unfolded.

The testimony that ties the operation together came from Olmedo López, the former head of the UNGRD disaster agency, in a declaration of 26 August 2024. López said Name’s collaboration included leaving the president’s seat to María José Pizarro to ease the handling of the plenaries — an assertion the chamber says was corroborated by the Senate’s official gazettes and the session recordings. The presidency of the Senate, the ruling underlines, is not a merely ceremonial post: it carries effective powers to direct sessions and enforce the rules, so ceding it repeatedly had real consequences for the legislative process.

Pizarro’s Defence: ‘A Legal Mandate, Not a Favour’

Pizarro, the former senator and first vice-president of the Senate, answered on Monday after her name surfaced 85 times in the judgment. “There is no way to claim there are ‘accusations’. That is what you say, not the courts,” she told El Tiempo, stressing that the ruling formulates no charges against her. “The role of the first vice-presidency is to replace the president when he is not present. That is a legal mandate, and one I was elected for.”

She added that Name’s absences made quorum difficult — several sessions came within one or two votes of collapsing — and that she repeatedly pressed him to attend. The then opposition, she said, “used every kind of manoeuvre for months to prevent or delay the debate on the pension reform”, while those opposition members who did attend enjoyed full guarantees to speak and vote their proposals.

What Happens Now

Name can appeal to the Council of State’s full administrative chamber; the criminal track against him runs separately at the Supreme Court. The ruling lands in the middle of the UNGRD affair, the disaster-agency scandal that has become one of the defining corruption cases of the Petro administration. For Pizarro — daughter of assassinated presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro and a prominent figure of the governing coalition — the decision brings no accusation, but 85 mentions in a bribery ruling guarantee political exposure in the weeks ahead.

What We Could Not Confirm

We have not independently reviewed the 129-page ruling; the figures, dates and findings above rely on detailed reporting of the text by La FM and Infobae. Whether Carlos Ramón González ordered the delivery is described in the ruling’s account as an allegation, not a proven conclusion. Beyond her remarks to El Tiempo, Pizarro has issued no fuller statement, and whether prosecutors are examining her conduct in any separate file is not publicly known. The timetable of the Supreme Court’s criminal case against Name is also not public.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Colombia’s Council of State strip Iván Name of his Senate seat?

The court found proven influence peddling: Name received 3,000 million pesos in October 2023 to favour the passage of the pension reform, and systematically ceded the chair of the decisive plenary sessions — 14 of 16 examined — without legal justification.

Is María José Pizarro accused in the UNGRD bribery case?

No. Pizarro is mentioned at least 85 times in the ruling as the first vice-president who presided over sessions in Name’s place, but the court does not conclude that she received money, knew of the payment or was party to the agreement. She says she acted under her legal mandate.

Can Iván Name appeal against the loss of his seat?

Yes. The ruling admits an appeal before the full administrative chamber of the Council of State. Separately, a criminal process against Name over the same facts continues at the Supreme Court of Justice.

How much money was involved in the pension bribery scheme?

The court found Name received 3,000 million Colombian pesos, delivered in two instalments of 1,500 million on 12 and 13 October 2023, through intermediaries Sneyder Pinilla and Sandra Ortiz.

World.title: Haiti’s First Vote in a Decade Draws Nine Presidential Hopefuls
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

HAITI · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — The country Haiti, which shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic. It has had no elected president since Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in July 2021.

— Why it matters The vote is meant to be Haiti’s first national election in a decade and to end years of transitional rule by unelected leaders.

— What happened Nine men had registered online to run for president by the morning of 23 September, Le Nouvelliste reported. The electoral council’s own count two days earlier was seven.

— Who is involved Candidates include former interim prime minister Claude Joseph, former interim president Jocelerme Privert and Wilner Joseph, who launched his campaign on Sunday 27 September.

— What it means for you A 13 December first round is still the official date. Any slip would extend transitional rule, which business groups say must end to restore confidence and economic activity.

— Still open The final electoral rules, the length of the next presidential term, and which candidates the electoral council will approve.

The field for the Haiti presidential election is taking shape, with nine men registered by the morning of 23 September. The Port-au-Prince daily Le Nouvelliste obtained the list from the online platform of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP), which runs Haitian elections.

Who has signed up

Le Nouvelliste named them as Claude Joseph, Ricardo Jean-Pierre, Gary Beaudo, Wilson Jeudy and Wilner Joseph. The others are Jocelerme Privert, Maxo Joseph, Munir Joseph Moura and Gandy Dorfeuille.

Claude Joseph founded the Engagés pour le Développement party and served as interim prime minister, the news site Juno7 reported. Privert was interim president before Moïse took office in February 2017.

On Sunday 27 September, the Viktwa platform launched Wilner Joseph’s campaign at a rally in Pétion-Ville, Juno7 reported. Viktwa says it groups 52 parties and political structures.

What the electoral council says

The CEP’s own statement of 21 September counted seven presidential candidacies, 162 for the Senate and 419 for the lower house. Both Juno7 and The Haitian Times reported those figures.

The council has extended online candidate registration to 9 October. It also reported 628,755 registered voters, just over 10 percent of the potential electorate.

The Haitian Times reported that nearly 20 municipalities could not receive candidate filings at their usual offices because armed gangs are present. On Thursday 24 September, Peterson Pierre-Louis took over as CEP president from Jacques Desrosiers, Juno7 reported.

Pressure for a credible vote

Four business associations said on 22 September that Haiti needs “a realistic and definitive timetable”. They said the private sector refuses to let elections become “a mere formality”, Le Nouvelliste reported.

Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé spoke at a United Nations meeting on 24 September. “The next Government of Haiti must go through the ballot box,” he said.

What Is Not Yet Known

Le Nouvelliste, in an editorial, said candidates are still waiting for a third version of the electoral decree. It argued they cannot know if the next term lasts four, five or six years, as a new constitution is drafted.

The CEP has not yet ruled on which candidacies are valid, and Le Nouvelliste called its list provisional. Candidates must still file documents in person before a final list is published.

It is also unclear how diaspora voting will work. Nor is it known whether registration will reach enough voters before the Haiti presidential election on 13 December.

For background, see Haiti Explained 2026 and Haiti December Election Set as First Vote in a Decade.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many candidates registered for Haiti’s presidential election?

Nine men had registered online by the morning of 23 September, Le Nouvelliste reported; the electoral council’s own count two days earlier was seven.

When is Haiti’s election?

The first round is officially set for 13 December — the country’s first national election in a decade.

Who is running?

Candidates include former interim prime minister Claude Joseph, former interim president Jocelerme Privert and Wilner Joseph, who launched his campaign on 27 September.

What is still unsettled?

The final electoral rules, the length of the next presidential term, and which candidates the electoral council approves.
