World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019063/Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.title: Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019063/Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.content:
Chinese scientists have identified a pathway connecting the spleen to the brain that may in part explain why women are more susceptible than men to cognitive decline as they age.

The study, published Sept. 18 in the peer-reviewed journal Neuron, was led by Ma Huan, vice dean of the School of Brain Science and Brain Medicine at Zhejiang University, in eastern China.

Existing literature shows that although women live on average longer than men, they are more susceptible to cognitive impairment from midlife onwards. Scientists have lacked a clear biological explanation for this phenomenon, attributing it until now primarily to estrogen.

The new research, however, has found that the spleen may influence brain aging through a pathway involving a gene on the X chromosome, which becomes more active in women as they age.

Using gene-expression data from 11 major organs in a preexisting database, the team found that beginning around age 40, signs of cellular senescence — when cells stop dividing and begin to malfunction — rose sharply in women’s brains and spleens, exceeding levels observed in men of the same age. A similar pattern was confirmed in naturally aging mice and in donor human brain tissue.

The researchers’ findings raise a key question: Is cognitive decline in part the result of the body sending a signal to the brain telling it to age?

In searching for that signal, the researchers identified miR-10a-5p, a microRNA — a type of gene expression regulator — whose levels rose in the spleens and brains of middle-aged female mice but not in their male counterparts.

The team then looked for proteins that regulate miR-10a-5p and discovered that RBMX, a protein encoded by a gene on the X chromosome, binds to, stabilizes, and allows the microRNA to accumulate. This process only occurred in female mice, as females carry two X chromosomes.

Next, the researchers injected mice with a compound to block miR-10a-5p, finding this lowered its levels in their brains, as did removing their spleens — indicating that the organ is a major source of the microRNA. Because the compound used does not efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier, the results imply that muting it elsewhere in the body may be enough to alter levels in the brain.

Once inside neurons in the brain, miR-10a-5p suppresses a protein called γCaMKII linked to calcium regulation within mitochondria — structures within the cell that generate its energy. When levels of this protein fall — which occurs during middle age in females — calcium signaling weakens and energy output declines, pushing neurons toward senescence. Restoring the protein in mice with reduced γCaMKII reversed these changes.

“We’ve tended to treat cognitive aging as something confined to the brain,” Qu Jing, the first author of the study, told Sixth Tone. “This work suggests the brain isn’t an isolated organ, and age-related changes in peripheral tissue may start shaping its condition much earlier than we assumed.”

The findings also suggest that because some of the brain’s miR-10a-5p originates elsewhere in the body, testing for it in patients’ blood could help assess brain-aging risk long before cognitive symptoms appear. Second, because reducing miR-10a-5p levels in the body affects the brain, it may be possible to protect against cognitive decline without developing a drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

“One important message from this work is that midlife isn’t just a stage where you wait for aging to happen, but a possible critical window for maintaining long-term brain health,” Qu said, adding that because the study points to a connection between the immune system and the brain, sustaining a well-functioning immune system may matter for cognitive health too.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.title: In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.content:
SHANGHAI – At the Sept. 19 Shanghai premiere of her feature debut, “Shanghai Daughter,” Shen Zhongmin carried a rubber seed from the forests of the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, nearly 3,000 kilometers away in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, where her late father had worked.

“The seed fell from the canopy and struck me as I retraced his life there,” Shen, 41, tells Sixth Tone.

Her father was among the millions of urban Chinese youths “sent down” to work in rural areas under the Down to the Countryside Movement, a campaign that ran from the mid-1950s through the late 1970s. He spent a decade on a state-run rubber farm near China’s border with Myanmar but rarely spoke to his daughter about those years.

Shen, who works professionally as Agnis Shen, first traveled to Xishuangbanna in 2011, the year after her father died. A former culture editor at the Shanghai-based magazine The Bund and the author of “The Traveler’s Desire,” a collection of short fiction. She returned to the region repeatedly, retracing her father’s life and meeting people from his generation.

Nearly a decade after her first trip, those encounters and widespread coverage of a herd of wild Asian elephants wandering north from Xishuangbanna helped inspire the idea for a film. The herd’s journey drew attention to the rubber plantations that had transformed parts of the region’s rainforest habitat.

Blending fiction with documentary methods, “Shanghai Daughter” follows Ming, a fictional Shanghai woman played by Liang Cuishan, as she seeks out her father’s former acquaintances in Xishuangbanna.

She encounters workers’ dormitories facing demolition and a landscape where mining and modern agriculture are replacing former rubber plantations. She also meets rubber tappers, village doctors, ethnic Dai villagers, and ecological researchers, all of whom appear as themselves and recount their own experiences.

“The film asks how we deal with memory,” Shen says. “When you want to understand something from the past but cannot find reliable firsthand records, how do you search for the answers?”

“Shanghai Daughter” had its world premiere in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival in February and was later selected for the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the Malaysia International Film Festival.

Seven months later, the film’s Shanghai premiere drew at least a dozen former sent-down youths from the city, all now in their 70s. They traveled about an hour by subway to attend.

At the theater, they shared old photographs from their years in Xishuangbanna, including images taken with Shen’s father, Shen Wanxiong, and posed for a group photo with the director.

Among them was Shen Weilong, 73, a former rubber tapper who had worked alongside Shen Wanxiong and describes him as his best friend. Looking at one of the photographs, he jokes, “This one doesn’t show just how handsome he was. If you want to know what he looked like, just look at his daughter.”

As he speaks about his generation, tears well in his eyes. “Our generation is rarely talked about, and now our time is running out,” he says.

Sixth Tone spoke with Shen Zhongmin the following day as she continued a multi-city promotional tour. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Not a single scene in “Shanghai Daughter” was shot in Shanghai. Why did you choose the title, and what does it mean to you?

Shen: “Shanghai daughters” was originally a local term. Villagers near the farms used it for daughters left behind by sent-down youths. Over time, the label seemed to replace each woman’s real name.

Because of my father’s history, I am also, in a sense, a “Shanghai daughter,” and so I went there too. In Xishuangbanna, the phrase took on a double meaning for me. It suggested a kind of twin existence, like looking in a mirror. We seemed to have completely different yet intersecting destinies, one born in Shanghai and the other 3,000 kilometers away in Xishuangbanna.

To me, “daughter” carries something different from either “woman” or “boy.” One of the first Dai expressions my father taught me was “long yin,” meaning “girl.” The image of a girl carries a particular gentleness that can help heal or ease the deep wounds and heaviness behind this subject. The emotional connection extends beyond father and daughter to one girl and another, and one daughter and another.

I did not want to remain trapped within a particular historical wound or view that period only through criticism. I hoped to create something relevant to the present and oriented toward the future, an expression of repair, renewed empathy, and hope.

Sixth Tone: By telling the story from a daughter’s perspective, the film approaches the sent-down youth movement through one family. How does that perspective differ from other portrayals of the movement?

Shen: This is a deeply personal and highly artistic undertaking. It emphasizes experiencing and observing our surroundings and sensory world anew.

While writing the screenplay, I did extensive research. I gathered oral histories, consulted historical archives, and reconnected with researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who study rainforest restoration. But I wanted to hold back those “concrete” materials for as long as possible and put perception first. Thoughts and opinions can easily create divisions, and once expressed, they have their limits. Perception, however, can be shared and remains more open.

Later, an academically minded journalist asked whether this might be related to ecofeminism. I thought the observation was perceptive. It points toward a perspective that moves beyond anthropocentrism and rejects a structure in which “I am the center, and everyone else is the other.”

Sixth Tone: Rubber trees, dragon fruit, and other elements of the landscape recur throughout the film. How did you use them to connect personal memory with the region’s history?

Shen: During my fieldwork in Xishuangbanna, I often walked around whenever I had time. I gradually came to see the landscape itself as a theater. All the legends and stories I had heard, with their intense dramatic and emotional tension, lay silently buried in a small hill in the village.

Generations have cultivated different crops there, from rice and corn to bananas and, more recently, dragon fruit. A small patch of primary forest protected by the Dai people remains on the hillside. Beneath the present landscape lie my father’s old dormitory and the former rubber plantation.

People disappear faster than memories, but stories spanning more than half a century survive in the land’s subtle traces. When you look at the plants and the land and listen to their voices, it feels as if they are telling you stories, though not in a language humans can hear.

I brought the rubber seed to the screening because, to me, it represents a transformation of cause and effect. More than half a century ago, people had little choice but to clear primary rainforest and plant rubber trees to meet the needs of national development. We now understand that this harmed local biodiversity.

A Chinese Academy of Sciences team is rehabilitating degraded rubber groves. Its goal is not to return them to primary rainforest, which would be scientifically unsound, but to rebalance relationships among species. The researchers are restoring poor-quality groves left by haphazard planting and tapping and introducing species that can bridge rubber plantations and native tropical rainforest. By giving the rubber trees a range of “good neighbors,” they can gradually restore the ecosystem’s layers.

To me, they are taking the “effect” of an earlier decision and planting within it a new, positive “cause,” one that may bear better fruit in the future. The relationship between seed and fruit becomes a metaphor for the transformation of cause and effect. I find that deeply inspiring.

Making the film also took me to Malaysia, where I saw some of the country’s earliest rubber trees. Without that initial transplantation, rubber would not have been planted on such a large scale in Xishuangbanna, and many of these stories would not exist.

Sixth Tone: Why did you blend fiction and documentary methods rather than make a conventional documentary centered on your own search?

Shen: I have always felt that the boundary between reality and fiction is unclear, much like the line between dreams and waking life. Historical narratives also have a dreamlike quality for me, something I have explored in my fiction.

If I had relied on documentary methods alone to examine the sent-down youth movement or my relationship with my father, the film would have felt too narrow.

I drew on my own experience to present subjects I have long cared about in a more contemporary, open form. If I had appeared as myself and made a pure documentary, the film would have become too narrow, confined by the standards of historical fact and leaving viewers less room to project themselves into it and experience it openly.

Sixth Tone: How did you approach your father’s past and his former co-workers while making the film? How did they respond after the premiere?

Shen: My father rarely spoke about the decade he spent in Xishuangbanna. People of his generation generally do not talk about those experiences.

You could sense a deep wound behind the way an older audience member spoke yesterday. At times, his questions seemed to judge other people, but they ultimately revealed his own views and emotions.

I didn’t even know my father had tapped rubber. He had never told me what work he did there. Only when I first walked into the plantation did I understand that these were rubber trees and that his generation had planted and tapped them.

At first, I avoided contacting my father’s former co-workers. I knew they would be eager to help and provide a great deal of firsthand material. But the film began with the particular relationship between my father and me. He had told me very little and died before I could learn more, so I went there to search for and reconstruct that missing part of his life.

I also did not want to disturb them for what was, after all, a small personal project. Revisiting those experiences can be extremely painful, especially for some of them.

Since yesterday’s premiere, I have spent all morning replying to their messages. Today, they are gathering for a reunion lunch to discuss the film.

One of my father’s former co-workers wrote: “Thank you to the screenwriter, creative team, and director for bringing a fitting close to our 50 years as sent-down youths.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A still from “Shanghai Daughter.” Courtesy of Shen)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019062/Report Links Alibaba’s Resale App to Sex Trade Involving Minors
World.title: Report Links Alibaba’s Resale App to Sex Trade Involving Minors
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019062/Report Links Alibaba’s Resale App to Sex Trade Involving Minors
World.content:
A domestic media investigation has found vendors using Alibaba’s secondhand platform Xianyu to solicit illicit sexual services, including some allegedly involving minors.

State owned Hebei Television reported that vendors used fake listings for massages, modeling shoots, at-home personal training, and swimming lessons to direct users to private messaging platforms, where the transactions were allegedly arranged.

Xianyu said on Sept. 18, when the investigation was published, that it has been working with police since January to dismantle 15 prostitution-related groups and had frozen nearly 100,000 accounts suspected of directing users to pornographic content.

In its latest statement on Wednesday, Xianyu called for a “cross-platform alliance” to combat illicit sexual content and the exploitation of minors, stressing that the conversations cited in the investigation took place on other messaging platforms after initial contact on Xianyu.

The investigation triggered widespread debate on Chinese social media, with several related hashtags topping microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list. The most-viewed has garnered 490 million views as of Wednesday.

One listing cited in the report advertising swimming lessons directed buyers to a private chat group on Tencent’s business messaging app WeCom, where a 99-yuan ($15) deposit provided access to a price list for sexual services for additional fees. The reporter placed an order and provided an address. Shortly after, a woman arrived at the location saying she offered flirting, kissing, and bathing services.

The report also found a vendor allegedly offering girls as young as 14 for prostitution, charging 20,000 to 30,000 yuan. Another vendor sent reporters photos of a 16-year-old’s ID card as evidence of her age, offered to arrange video calls, and said the girls could fly to meet buyers if they covered the airfare.

Xianyu’s customer service told Hebei Television that automated systems are largely used to review its product listings, with human reviewers involved only in appeals.

Following the investigation, Xianyu said that it would strengthen automated detection by improving its keyword filters and image-detection algorithms, and step up manual reviews of suspicious listings and accounts.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone found that listings for “at-home modeling shoots” no longer yielded results, but “at-home shoots,” as well as “fitness” and “swimming” services, remained available.

With more than 600 million users, Xianyu is China’s largest secondhand trading app. In recent years, it has evolved into an informal services marketplace, offering everything from résumé writing to odd jobs like finding an owner’s lost pet or smuggling someone into a sold-out concert, with prices often negotiated through private chats.

The platform has repeatedly come under scrutiny for users selling illicit products and services. A 2019 report by Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper found Xianyu vendors were listing ads for 1-yuan items of clothing as a way to lure young women into chatting with them, with the eventual aim of providing sexual services. In 2021, consumer protection authorities ordered Xianyu and 11 other resale platforms to crack down on listings directing users to illicit sexual transactions.

Chang Dongyue, a partner at Shanghai Droit&Elite Law Firm, told Sixth Tone that Xianyu’s low barriers to entry and reliance on user traffic and transaction volume, combined with pressure to minimize moderation costs, create conditions for illicit listings to resurface repeatedly.

Under China’s Cybersecurity Law, platforms must remove illegal content, while the Law on the Protection of Minors requires them to delete illegal content directed at minors, retain evidence of the content, and report it to authorities.

In response to Xianyu’s comments on cross-platform collaboration, Chang noted that cooperation on illegal activity is necessary. “Banning accounts on individual platforms only removes one link in the chain,” he said. “Without genuine cross-platform cooperation, enforcement will be less effective.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019056/Runaway to Record Breaker: Zhao Jiaju on Willpower, Pain, and the Tor des Géants
World.title: Runaway to Record Breaker: Zhao Jiaju on Willpower, Pain, and the Tor des Géants
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019056/Runaway to Record Breaker: Zhao Jiaju on Willpower, Pain, and the Tor des Géants
World.content:
Editor’s note: In the early hours of Sept. 16, Zhao Jiaju crossed the finish line to win the 2026 Tor des Géants endurance trail race, covering 336.1 kilometers and cumulative elevation gain exceeding 24,000 meters through the Italian Alps in a record 65 hours, 55 minutes, and 22 seconds. Here, the 31-year-old talks with The Paper about the experience and shares how it feels to be the race’s first Asian champion.

The Paper: How’s your body holding up?

Zhao: It’s dehydrated. During the race, the sun just hammered down on us. It was so dry that my lips split open. My scalp was scorched red — in a few days the skin will start peeling off in sheets.

But still, I’m recovering, getting better day by day. My feet still hurt, but not as badly as they did. My upper body is fine, actually. It’s the legs that took the real beating.

Sometimes when I touch my body, it feels unreal. That feeling was far stronger yesterday; it’s less noticeable today. Even when I pinch myself, it doesn’t hurt as much.

The Paper: You wore the No. 1 bib, and at the start said you were going to win in record time. Were you really that confident?

Zhao: I didn’t think my physical capacity was strong enough, but I knew my willpower was. After all these years on the trail, it’s been honed to a fine degree. I knew the Tor des Géants would come down to sheer willpower, to who could hold on longest when everything inside you is screaming to stop. I knew that’s where I held an advantage.

Before the race, I truly meant that bold claim about breaking the record. I believed I could, and that’s the power of belief.

I started running 100-kilometer ultramarathons in 2017. Since then, I’ve been regularly competing in 168-kilometer events. I’ve always been able to run long distances. I didn’t train specifically for this race. I just spent about a month here (in northwestern Italy’s Aosta Valley) beforehand to adapt to the terrain, altitude, and food. After that, it was about drawing on years of accumulated endurance.

The Paper: Did you complete any 300-kilometer training runs?

Zhao: No, but I often run 168 kilometers. When I was 23, I competed in the Ultra Gobi (an ultra-endurance race through China’s northwestern Gobi Desert). I could handle 400 kilometers of hardship even then. So finishing 330 kilometers wasn’t the hard part. The challenge was setting a faster time and pushing my limits.

The Paper: When did you feel most exhausted?

Zhao: Climbing that final slope — everything hit me all at once. When I was most exhausted, my mind was still clear, but my vision began to blur. All I could make out was the hazy white glow where my torchlight hit the ground. My eyes kept trying to close.

I repeated to myself, “You’re doing something incredible right now.” When my eyes were about to shut, I’d slap myself hard across the face, bite down on my tongue, and grit my teeth. Every slap, every bite brought a moment of clarity. My vision would snap back into focus, like a camera lens adjusting from blurry to sharp.

The Paper: Footage from the race shows you running alone at night, with only a small headlamp beam cutting through the darkness. What would you think about in those moments?

Zhao: “Get to the next aid station. Get supplies.” For the first 200 kilometers, my mind would wander. But during that final 100 kilometers, I didn’t dare think about anything because the course has many dangerous sections. I focused entirely on the ground in front of me, reminding myself how many more climbs were ahead, what the next ascent would be like, and how to navigate the terrain beneath my feet. There was no mental space for anything else.

The Paper: What was it like having your wife at the aid stations, preparing food for you and helping with massages and recovery?

Zhao: She really went through it. I need to buy her some gifts to make up for it.

Many top Chinese runners now have family members provide support at aid stations. The people closest to you know you best, and they can tolerate your moods. During a race, when you’re pushed to extreme limits, your truest self comes out. Having your closest people there to help you makes it easier.

Things have gradually gotten better for athletes from China. Sponsors are now willing to support our families in traveling with us to compete, which is really helpful.

The Paper: Do you remember the moment you crossed the finish line?

Zhao: Honestly, I was thinking, “Just take me back. I need to lie down.” I was practically asleep on my feet. When I reached the summit, my vision blurred. I’d been forcing myself to hang on, pushing to the line. The moment I crossed it and all that tension was finally released — the full-body pain, that overwhelming urge to sleep — it swept over me.

My body and mind had reached breaking point. But once I recovered a bit, I was extremely excited. I looked at what I’d achieved and realized that I’d pushed past my limits. That really hit me.

The Paper: After the race, you said you felt “worse than death.” Why put yourself through this?

Zhao: Achieving the glory and fame I dreamed about as a kid — that’s part of it. But I also want to push the boundaries of my body and my will. That way, when I face even greater obstacles, I’ll be able to get through them more easily. I need these moments of suffering to become a stronger, tougher version of myself. I came out here representing China, and so many people were cheering me on. I had to show everyone how powerful human endurance and willpower can be.

When I was 15, I was inspired by that same kind of energy. Back then, I wanted to be a champion fighter. I watched Bruce Lee films, and he made me realize that human potential is limitless, that you have to learn how to command your body and unleash its full power. Now I hope I can pass that energy on to others who need it.

The Paper: Does being champion bring pressure or motivation?

Zhao: Win or lose, it’s motivation. I’ve had an optimistic attitude ever since I was a child.

My family treated me well, so I had a carefree childhood. I’ve always loved to laugh — so much so that I developed terrible forehead wrinkles very early. In elementary school, my physical education teacher said I looked like a little old man. I loved making people in my class laugh, too. That gave me the ability to transform negative energy into something positive and feed it back to myself. That’s what’s allowed me to keep going.

The Paper: Some have talked about you working as a delivery rider, but you’ve had many different jobs, right?

Zhao: I’ve been a florist, I prepared steamed dishes in a restaurant, and I worked at a hardware factory in Hangzhou (capital of the eastern Zhejiang province). Later I delivered food in Wuhan (capital of the central Hubei province), made fried chicken, and worked at a hotel front desk as well as an electronics factory in (the southwestern city of) Chongqing.

I was even a security guard at the Beijing National Stadium. I worked at karaoke bars in several cities — I think that was the most comfortable. It left me lots of time for training. I would get off work at 3 or 4 in the morning and head straight to training. I’d then wake at noon, have lunch, and train again in the afternoon.

The Paper: What first interested you in trail running?

Zhao: Before trail running, I was into marathons. In 2014, I was working at a flower shop when I saw marathon banners during a morning run around Hangzhou’s West Lake. That’s how I learned about competitive races. My dream back then was to become a champion fighter, but I had no systematic training, no club willing to take me on, and no way to compete. I was desperate for a path forward. I thought marathons suited me — they’re all about willpower, right? When I started competing, my initial results weren’t ideal. After a year or two, my performances improved, but still not enough to break into China’s top tier.

Then I discovered trail running. In 2016, I saw people taking part in 100-kilometer races. This was an even greater test of willpower. So I quit my job to compete, throwing myself wholeheartedly into trail running. The sport was still relatively new in China, and the prize money was generous. I was determined to carve out my place. I won my first championship in 2017. After that, things just kept getting better.

The Paper: You’ve repeatedly mentioned the importance of willpower.

Zhao: It goes back to when I ran away from home at 15. My parents worked in factories and were raising my younger sister. They wanted me to find a stable job, learn a trade, and live a comfortable, ordinary life. But I wanted to chase my dreams, to become like the people I saw on TV — strong, accomplished, and the best at what they did. So I left home. My parents even reported me missing to the police. More than 10 days passed before I called them to let them know I was safe. They told me that as long as I wasn’t doing anything illegal, I could do whatever I wanted, and that I should tell them if I ran into trouble. But when difficulties arose, I didn’t want them to worry. I felt I had to rely on myself. If you depend on your family, you’ll never grow strong enough to fly on your own.

Back then I lived on the streets. In Hubei province, I walked from Fang County, on the edge of Shennongjia forest area, to Shiyan City — about 100 kilometers. Those were the most painful 11 days of my life. I walked under the blazing sun. The daytime temperature rose to at least 39 degrees Celsius. I walked all day and into the next, blisters forming all over my feet. That was the first time I’d walked such a distance. I wore a tank top; my skin turned black, burned and peeling. I thought, “How can life be this painful?” But when I finally got through it, I felt incredible. I was 15 years old, and I’d endured all that suffering.

That lesson carries over into my racing. The person you have to defeat is yourself. Those hardships are what made me stronger. Racing has put me through everything — brutal weather, muscle pain, nausea, dizziness, nosebleeds. All that suffering. I’ve never felt sorry for myself or wanted others to pity me. The suffering I seek out makes me powerful. It makes me fearless for the future. That’s why I love this kind of pain.

The Paper: Is that because you’ve always had a clear direction?

Zhao: Yes. From the start, I’ve had one goal: to be one in a million, to find the path where I can shine, and keep working at it step by step. There’s no need to rush. As long as I keep at it, I’ll succeed.

The Paper: What’s your vision for the future of trail running?

Zhao: Whether it’s race organizers, participants, or local residents — everyone recognizes the balance between humans and nature. As more people venture into the mountains, the mountains should remain clean and beautiful. I’d love to see that become a reality.

The Paper: After completing the 2026 Tor des Géants, you said you wouldn’t compete in any more ultramarathons over 168 kilometers. Is that your body talking, or a shift in mindset?

Zhao: This race pushed me to my limit. I was truly exhausted. I don’t plan to race such a long distance again in the near future. To break through again would be excruciating. I don’t know what price I’d have to pay. So for now, I don’t want to try.

The Paper: So what are your plans now?

Zhao: I’ll continue racing. I love the feeling of standing on that starting line. Winning once doesn’t mean you’ll win next time. Trail running depends on your physical state. As long as I’m fit to race, I’ll be on that starting line, blood pumping, ready to give everything to my next race.

I haven’t thought about retirement. If one day I stop placing in races — perhaps when I’m in my 50s and can no longer satisfy my competitive drive — then I could work behind the scenes. Many athletes’ lives have shown us that you can win world championships in your 40s and 50s. I still have expectations for myself at that age.

Reported by Wei Jiaming.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

World.title: Baste Duterte testifies at VP Sara impeachment trial
World.content:
(2nd UPDATE) Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte complies with the impeachment court's subpoena to take the witness stand at the trial of his sister

MANILA, Philippines – Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte arrived at the Senate on Tuesday, September 29, to testify at the impeachment trial of his older sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

Baste arrived past 9 am and was brought to the holding room for witnesses while awaiting the start of the trial at 10 am.

The mayor, the prosecution’s hostile witness, was earlier subpoenaed to appear before the court from Monday, September 28, to Wednesday, September 30, 2026. He asked the court on Monday to allow him to appear at the trial on Tuesday or Wednesday, which the court granted.

Play Video

The prosecution had requested the issuance of a subpoena to the Davao mayor in connection with the contracts of the Davao City government with Gencorp, which is linked to the Vice President.

Rappler earlier published an exclusive report detailing how Gencorp cornered P15 million in food and catering contracts from the PhilHealth Davao Regional Office and Davao City Hall between 2022 and 2025.

The Vice President declared in her 2024 and 2025 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she has been a stockholder of Gencorp since 2013, but her name is not in the filings of the company with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). She was elected vice president in 2022.

The younger Duterte was not initially identified as a witness by the prosecution team in its pre-trial brief, although it is not precluded from asking him to testify as among the unnamed, reserve witnesses. This changed after it was found that the Davao City government had contracts with Gencorp.

Baste himself had confirmed that Gencorps got at least 19 contracts with Davao City Hall worth P33.26 million — more than twice the amount earlier reported — and that these were all aboveboard. He had also claimed that he did not know of any Gencorps links to his sister.

Kapunan to Baste: ‘Have a nice day’

When asked to comment on the arrival of Baste at the Senate for the trial on Tuesday, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said: “Ang masasabi ko sa kanya, have a nice day. Marami kaming itatanong są kanya at marami siyang i-e-explain.” (What I can say to him is, have a nice day. We have many questions to ask him and he has a lot of explaining to do.)

Kapunan said Baste’s compliance with the subpoena didn’t come as a surprise, considering the evidence that the prosecution had presented in connection with Davao City Hall’s contracts with Gencorp.

“As mayor, he’s head of the procurement agency. Hindi niya puwedeng sabihin na hindi niya alam kung sino ang may-ari ng Gencorps kasi part ng due diligence ‘yan (He can’t say that he doesn’t know who owns Gencorp because that is part of due diligence),” she said. – With reports from Sundy Locus, Dwight de Leon/Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] I’m 73. And I went back to school.
World.content:
I hope more older Filipinos return to classrooms. We need places where generations can meet — where experience encounters new knowledge, where assumptions can be challenged.

I enrolled in three certificate courses at the Development Academy of the Philippines. They covered geopolitics, international relations, strategic futures, oceans, the law of the sea, and maritime security.

Attending these courses virtually became one of the most stimulating things I did this year.

I did not go back to school because I needed certificates, missed homework, or had suddenly developed a fondness for deadlines.

I was curious. I wanted to understand what was happening in the world, and why.

But there was a practical reason too. I needed this knowledge for my work. I wanted to ask better questions and give better advice about policies that matter. People at work now come to me with questions about security — not because I am an expert, but because I am studying it.

Curiosity is a wonderful thing. But one has to be useful too.

Abstract until…

In our maritime security course, retired associate justice Antonio Carpio showed us historical maps. They made me appreciate something deceptively simple: geography is neither a blessing nor a curse.

We cannot push China farther north. We cannot move Taiwan farther south. We cannot wish the South China Sea away.

But geography should not determine a nation’s fate.

A short basketball player cannot suddenly become six-foot-eight. But he can learn to run faster, pass better, play stronger defense, see the court differently, and use what he has to his advantage.

Countries have to do the same thing.

Then came the law.

Attorney Fretti Ganchoon, senior state counsel at the Department of Justice, gave us a terrific lecture on the oceans, UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea), and international law.

These can sound terribly abstract — until a marine is struck in the head, somebody loses a thumb, or fishermen come home injured and their wives wonder whether, on the next trip, they might become widows.

Attorney Isabel Cañaveral, legal officer of the University of the Philippines Institute for Maritime Affairs and Law of the Sea, took us through the maritime zones, jurisdictions, rights, and obligations created by UNCLOS.

After that, an ocean no longer looked like empty blue space to me. It had boundaries, rights, responsibilities — and consequences.

Simulating a crisis

Then Florence Principe Gamboa, managing editor of FACTS, made us confront what happens when geography, law, and politics collide with an actual emergency.

She put us through a simulation involving the evacuation of Filipinos from Taiwan. Suddenly, geopolitics became very real. Who is in charge? Do we know where our people are? How do we move some 250,000 Filipinos out of Taiwan if commercial flights stop? Which Taiwanese agencies do we coordinate with? How do we communicate with our people and our counterparts on the ground? And perhaps the most important question: has the evacuation plan actually been tested?

These are not minor operational details. In a crisis, they may determine whether a plan works at all.

A plan on paper is not enough. Discovering its weak points after the crisis begins is already too late.

That raised another question: what if we could think about crises before they happened?

That was what the Strategic Futures and National Security course taught by Dr. Oliva Domingo of the UP National College of Public Administration and Governance asked us to do.

Choices that can change a future

Strategic foresight is not fortune-telling. It is a disciplined way of looking at several plausible futures, using what we know today while recognizing what we do not know.

I chose chronic kidney disease.

Not because I wanted to turn kidneys into a security threat, but because disease on a large enough scale affects a country’s choices. (READ: [OPINION] Philippines’ peculiar health policy: Waiting until kidneys fail)

Young people on dialysis will not be joining the Armed Forces or the Coast Guard. And when government spends billions treating preventable disease, those resources come from the same national budget that must also fund education, infrastructure, social protection, and security.

My paper, therefore, was not really about kidneys.

It was about choices made early enough to change a future.

I developed several scenarios. In the future I considered most desirable, government acted much earlier: preventing diabetes and hypertension, regulating unhealthy food environments, giving incentives to urban and town planners to create places where people could walk, play, and socialize, and teaching children early about eating well and staying healthy.

By the time a problem becomes a crisis, our choices have already narrowed.

And across all these subjects — maps, oceans, evacuation plans, chronic disease — one issue kept returning: governance.

Security does not exist only at sea, at a border, or inside a military installation. It depends on whether institutions work, agencies speak to one another, responsibilities are clear, and whether somebody has thought about what happens on Monday morning after the crisis erupts on Sunday night.

I came away with a conviction that sounds almost embarrassingly ordinary: grand strategies do not work unless somebody makes sure the operational details work too.

What older people bring to the classroom

Which brings me to the DAP Learning Team, led by Dean Alyn Joy Baltazar. They worked quietly in the background, making sure lecturers and students remained connected despite weak and unreliable internet; schedules ran on time; lectures were recorded, transcribed, and uploaded promptly; submissions met deadlines; and Spotify somehow managed to play the coolest music during our breaks.

In class, we talked about governance, coordination, and institutional capacity. The DAP Learning Team demonstrated all three — without announcing that they were doing so.

These courses made me question assumptions, test the logic of my own arguments, discard ideas I had become too comfortable with, and look at familiar problems differently.

I brought experience into the classroom. Not necessarily wisdom.

I have worked in policymaking and implementation, nationally and internationally. I have seen policies succeed and fail. I have watched institutions evolve. More importantly, I have known people whose lives were affected by all of them.

Experience changes the questions one asks.

I can still be impressed by an idea. But I am much more interested now in whether it works.

Who will implement it? What happens when it reaches the bureaucracy? What happens when conditions change? And ultimately: how will it make people’s lives better?

That is why I hope more older Filipinos return to classrooms.

We need places where generations can meet — where experience encounters new knowledge, where assumptions can be challenged, and where people can disagree without pretending that anyone already has all the answers.

I went back to school because I was curious. I also wanted to be useful.

I came away understanding something I had not expected.

Education does not change the map. It changes how we read it. And that can change what we decide to do next. – Rappler.com

Marilen J Danguilan is a medical doctor who studied at the University of the Philippines Diliman, the London School of Economics, and Harvard University Kennedy School of Government. She was a Takemi Fellow at the Harvard School of Public Health. She is external affairs officer of Salubris Medical Center and serves as adviser to the Peacebuilding Department of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation.

World.title: Trump, Xi ‘stalemate’ summit was a glitzy gift to China
World.content:
US-CHINA TALKS. Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks during a meeting with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of their visit to the Zhongnanhai Garden in Beijing, China, May 15, 2026.

Despite the lack of substantial agreements, the summit is viewed as a 'PR win' for China, showcasing their diplomatic leverage and allowing them to avoid making concessions on contentious issues like Taiwan and Iran

US President Donald Trump hoped his pomp-filled summit with Xi Jinping in Washington last week would showcase the strength of his personal relationship with the Chinese leader.

Instead, the limited outcomes showed just how far apart Washington and Beijing remain on key issues, and reinforced a view among analysts that Xi sees little reason to grant Trump major political victories ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“The US-China relationship has settled into a managed stalemate,” said Craig Singleton, senior director for China at US-based think tank, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

“The elaborate pageantry matters precisely because there is still relatively little substantive progress to showcase.”

Both sides said they reached consensus on lowering tariffs for a $60 billion batch of non-sensitive goods, but there was no timeline for adoption. At the same time, a deadline for a broader trade accord was pushed into next year.

The absence of a Chinese CEO delegation accompanying Xi also highlighted the challenges of overcoming US suspicion of Chinese investment, casting doubt on the viability of a two-way investment scheme the leaders unveiled at a Beijing summit in May, analysts said.

“The Trump-Xi summit created a positive political atmosphere but did nothing to narrow differences, or reduce mutual suspicions,” said Drew Thompson, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore.

‘PR win’ for China

White House officials had tempered expectations before the summit, pointing out that the leaders would also meet at international forums in Shenzhen and Miami before year end.

But while the uneventful meeting capped off a diplomatic week that exposed the limits of Trump’s powers, Joe Mazur, geopolitics analyst at Beijing-based consultancy Trivium, said it served as a “PR win” for China.

From the outset, Trump went out of his way to fete Xi – the leader of a country he has previously said is “killing America” with unfair trade practices.

He broke protocol to greet him at the airport, the first time a US president has done so for a world leader in 11 years.

Later, addressing a coterie of top government officials and tech magnates assembled for a lavish state banquet in his honour, Trump said they “had never gotten along better.”

“The extraordinary courtesy the Americans extended to Xi Jinping met and far exceeded China’s expectations,” said Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official and vice president of Beijing-based think tank Global Governance Institution.

“The Chinese do not feel that a visit necessarily has to result in a specific number of agreements, or in tariff reductions or other such outcomes … The mere fact that they meet, nod to one another, and shake hands speaks volumes.”

Xi is also in no rush to make concessions, analysts say.

China’s dominance in production of rare earths, minerals critical for sectors from tech to autos and defence, gives it a powerful source of leverage, while its trade with the world has surged despite Trump’s tariff threats.

Trump did not come away completely empty-handed, however.

China has proposed cutting tariffs on a range of US agricultural goods, from corn to dairy, a commerce ministry list showed on Monday, September 28. In return, the US will reduce levies on Chinese imports such as toys, fireworks and Christmas ornaments.

That will be welcome news for American farmers, who form one of Trump’s key voting blocs, ahead of midterm elections that look challenging for his Republican party.

But commodity analysts were also quick to add that soybeans, one of the US’ largest exports, did not feature on China’s list, leaving those purchases potentially hostage to any deterioration in ties.

Buying time on Taiwan

China also gave little indication it is willing to help Trump end the war in Iran that has dragged the US president’s approval rating to the lowest in his political career.

Shortly after Xi’s departure, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng pushed back against the US on Iran and its threats against Cuba at a UN General Assembly meeting in New York.

The Chinese leader also did not shy away from pressing Trump on thornier topics such as US support for Taiwan, the democratically ruled island claimed by Beijing.

Trump avoided the subject in his public comments, in a stark contrast with the May summit, at which he called a pending $14-billion package of arms sales to Taiwan a “negotiating chip” with Beijing.

Washington has cast the busy summit schedule with Xi as important to keeping ties on an even keel between the world’s two biggest economies.

But frequent interactions of the leaders also buy Beijing time on unwanted US actions such as the arms sales to Taiwan, said Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group.

“That’s a major strategic win for the Chinese and a major loss for Taiwan and a lot of US allies and partners in the region,” said Chan, a former US diplomat in China. – Rappler.com

World.title: US, Iran separately talk with mediators in latest bid to end war
World.content:
US President Trump indicates a willingness to continue talks despite previously rejecting Iran's proposal, while Iran awaits a definitive US response before deciding on its next steps

US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday, September 28, as part of a renewed effort to end seven months of war, according to officials of both countries.

Any further talks are expected to focus on an amended version of a seven-day proposal that Iran presented last week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters.

The war began in late February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, killing thousands of people over seven months and shocking global markets as vital waterways for oil remained choked. The US and Iran have twice previously agreed to ceasefires in mediated peace talks, in April and June. Those agreements quickly unraveled.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi, who remained in New York after attending the General Assembly, said Iran expected to receive the US response to its latest ceasefire proposals and its conditions for restoring passage of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, according to state news agency IRNA.

“If the Americans claim they are seeking an agreement or a peaceful solution, we have presented that solution,” Araqchi said.

US officials separately spoke with mediators on Monday, US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House, without giving further details.

Trump has flagged further talks this week

Iran’s seven-day plan envisages an end to all hostilities in Iran and Lebanon, the unfreezing of billions of dollars’ worth of Iranian assets, an end to sanctions on Iranian oil and the lifting of the US blockade on Iranian ports.

Iran would then allow the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for oil tankers, and the two sides would also resume talks on Iran’s nuclear program and Trump’s wish to seize or eliminate its highly enriched uranium.

Trump said on Saturday, September 26, he had rejected Iran’s proposal, saying Iran wanted a swift agreement because of the crippling economic pressure it is under. However, he also told Axios on Sunday that he expected US negotiators to engage in further talks this week.

Araqchi said on Sunday, September 27, that mediators had not formally conveyed a US rejection, and that Iran was awaiting Washington’s definitive position before deciding its next steps.

“Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” he said on Sunday, adding that only a negotiated solution could resolve the impasse. – Rappler.com

World.title: Should Sara Duterte have listed all her guns in her SALNs?
World.content:
Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.

Senator-judges couldn't care less about Vice President Sara Duterte's gun records, but prosecutors say they are just presenting a 'complete picture' of her true wealth

Senator-judges were reluctant to allow the prosecution’s offer of testimony on Vice President Sara Duterte’s gun collection, and apparently, it’s a matter that hit too close to home.

Many lawmakers are gun enthusiasts themselves – Senate Majority Leader Migz Zubiri even proudly declared himself to be pro-gun at open court on Monday, September 28. Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto said he and other senators usually put their weapons under “personal properties,” implying that he himself didn’t itemize his guns in his SALNs.

From where senators are standing, it’s a non-issue that Duterte did not declare her firearms one by one in her SALNs.

So did the prosecution just waste a vital day in the court?

What the law says

Prosecutor Bel Zamora argued that Section 32 of the the 2025 omnibus SALN rules require the individual declaration of firearms. The defense team, however, quickly brushed off that argument, arguing that such guidelines cannot be applied retroactively.

“The 2025 CSC rules… do not have application to the SALNs of the Vice President as those will be applicable only for submission beginning 2026,” defense lawyer Carlo Narvasa argued.

The 2025 CSC rules consolidate and replace five previous CSC resolutions, including a 2013 resolution that provided guidelines for filling out a SALN form.

Indeed, CSC Resolution No. 1300173 in 2013 did not explicitly state that firearms should be specifically declared in one’s SALN. It did say though: “Personal properties collectively acquired or are of minimal value may be declared generally or collectively.”

What constitutes “minimal value” is unclear, and the prosecution’s witness from the Philippine National Police Firearms and Explosives Office, Police Major Joericson Sangalang, doesn’t have the acquisition cost of Duterte’s firearms as well. PNP FEO can only estimate based on market value – Duterte and her husband Mans Carpio’s gun collection could cost around P7 million.

What’s certain though is that Duterte and her spouse have 51 registered firearms, including 22 from Duterte herself. There are no records with the PNP to indicate that these were donations.

In trouble for non-disclosure of guns

Some public officials and employees faced legal obstacles in the past for failing to disclose their guns in their SALNs.

Prosecutor Terry Ridon cited customs official Recaflor de Leon who, in 2015, was suspended without pay by the Ombudsman for failing to declare his three licensed firearms from 2003 to 2011.

A press release from the Department of Finance, the complainant in the case, said De Leon should have itemized his personal properties because as per SALN instructions in 2008, there should be a breakdown for items under the category “others” if the value exceeds P100,000.

In 2018, the Ombudsman charged former police chief Alan Purisima with perjury before the Sandiganbayan for failing to disclose his wife’s properties, as well as his firearms from 2011 to 2012.

“The disclosure and declaration is required under Section 7 of Republic Act No. 3019 (Anti-Graft Law) as amended and Section 8 of Republic Act 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees),” the charge sheets at the time said.

RA 3019 instructs public officers to file a true, detailed SALN, while RA 6713 says a SALN shall contain information on personal property and acquisition cost, and “all other assets such as investments, cash on hand or in banks, stocks, bonds, and the like.”

In the same year, the Ombudsman indicted former Marantao, Lanao del Sur mayor Mohammadali Abboh Abinal for not disclosing his firearms and vehicles from 2007 to 2012.

The prosecution’s point

Despite unfavorable remarks from senator-judges – with Raffy Tulfo even describing the offer of testimony on Duterte’s guns as a “waste of time” – the prosecution asserted that the vice president’s gun collection was an important matter.

“Even though they say it’s only P7 million, when you submit your SALN, you are certifying under oath that it’s all that you own,” private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said in a Rappler interview. “This is where we will attempt to show to the public and the impeachment court that there is a pattern on the part of the Vice President of hiding her wealth.”

Play Video

Prosecutor Ridon’s justification was along the same lines.

“We wanted to be able to present a most complete picture of the true wealth of the Vice President,” Ridon said during a press conference. “It’s part of the truth-telling of the prosecution on this matter.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Victoria Bossong shows golden potential with fastest time in Asian Games 800m heats
World.content:
SPEED. Victoria Bossong in action for the Philippines in the women's 800m heats in the 2026 Asian Games.

Victoria Bossong makes a strong case for the women's 800m gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games as she posts the fastest time in the heats

MANILA, Philippines – Winning an Asian Games gold medal looks like a very real possibility for Victoria Bossong.

The Filipina-American middle distance specialist posted the fastest time in the heats of the women’s 800m on Monday, September 28, at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium as she reinforced her status as one of the Philippines’ top medal bets.

Bossong clocked 2 minutes and 2.32 seconds to banner the eight-woman final on Tuesday, September 29.

China’s Li Chunhui turned in the second-best time of 2:02.35, followed by Uzbekistan’s Sabokhat Samijonova with 2:02.64.

Bossong can go significantly faster as she owns a personal best of 1:58.52, which she achieved just last June in the USA Track and Field Lone Star Grand Prix.

That mark eclipses the Asian Games record of 1:59.02 set by Kazakhstan’s Margarita Mukasheva in the 2014 edition.

Bossong, whose mother, Catalina Atienza, is from Mindoro, gained eligibility to represent the Philippines in July and is flying the national colors in a multi-sport event for the first time.

Aside from Bossong, EJ Obiena is expected to deliver for the Philippine athletics team as he looks to defend his crown in the men’s pole vault final, also on Tuesday.

The Philippines has won one athletics medal so far courtesy of John Cabang Tolentino, who clinched the bronze in the men’s 110m hurdles. – Rappler.com

World.title: From Deals to Delivery: What is at Stake in President Tokayev’s Germany Visit
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will visit Germany from Sept. 29-Oct. 1, with meetings in Berlin and Munich coming at a time when Kazakh-German relations have grown significantly in both political and economic terms, but are also entering a more demanding stage.

Germany is one of Kazakhstan’s key European partners for investment, technology and industrial cooperation. For Berlin, Kazakhstan has become increasingly important as a source of energy and critical raw materials and as part of efforts to diversify supply chains. The question now is whether those complementary interests can translate into deeper industrial ties, particularly in processing, manufacturing and technology.

Munich is more than a stop on Tokayev’s German visit

The Munich part of the visit deserves particular attention because Bavaria is significant in Kazakhstan’s economic engagement with Germany. Bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and Bavaria reached 3.4 billion euros in 2025, putting Bavaria first among Germany’s federal states by trade with Kazakhstan, according to Kazakhstan’s Prime Minister’s Office. The two sides have expanded cooperation in industry, agriculture, technology and raw materials, with German companies including Horsch, Linde Gas and Rhenus already operating in Kazakhstan.

The significance of Bavaria is not only the size of its trade with Kazakhstan. It also lies in the structure of its economy, with strong positions in manufacturing, engineering and technology. For Kazakhstan, closer ties with such a region fit its broader effort to attract German companies into local production rather than rely mainly on imports of finished equipment.

That makes Munich a useful lens through which to view the wider relationship. It offers a closer look at whether the strategic agenda discussed between governments in Berlin will translate into decisions by companies.

Kazakhstan seeks to change its role in the relationship

The push for a more advanced economic relationship has been building since Tokayev’s visit to Berlin in September 2023. At the time, Kazakhstan and Germany were discussing critical raw materials, green energy, transport and logistics and greater German investment in non-resource sectors. Tokayev proposed a consortium for joint raw-materials projects and invited German companies to help develop production in Kazakhstan. Bilateral trade rose 25% to $2.8 billion in 2022, while German businesses invested almost $6 billion in Kazakhstan, nearly 90% of it outside the resource sector.

A year later, when German Chancellor Olaf Scholz made his first visit to Kazakhstan in 14 years, the agenda had expanded to energy, green transformation, mining, transport and logistics, agriculture and climate cooperation. A business forum in Astana produced 36 documents worth $6.3 billion covering mechanical engineering, innovation, logistics, petrochemicals, information technology and industrial automation.

The relationship continued to grow in 2025. Bilateral trade reached $4.4 billion, up 9.5% from the previous year. German investment rose 28.5% to $700 million, bringing cumulative German investment since 2005 to about $7.8 billion. More than 1,100 companies with German capital operate in Kazakhstan.

But Kazakhstan’s ambition is increasingly about changing the structure of the relationship, not only expanding its volume. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said in June that Kazakhstan wants to transform traditional trade and investment ties into deeper industrial and technological cooperation through production localization, technology transfer and training. The government pointed to CLAAS and Horsch as examples of phased localization that could be extended to other sectors.

Valeriy Sitenko, senior expert at the Institute of Foreign Policy Studies under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, puts that shift in broader terms. He highlights that Kazakhstan’s role should evolve from transit to production.

“If previously the emphasis was mainly on transport connectivity and Kazakhstan’s transit function, today there is a transition toward deeper integration: the inclusion of Kazakhstan and Central Asia in global value chains. In the new model, Kazakhstan acts not only as a transit space, but as a production and technology hub,” Sitenko told The Astana Times.

That would change the logic of cooperation. Instead of simply connecting Kazakh resources with European markets, Kazakhstan would seek to retain more of the value created from those resources through processing and manufacturing.

Sitenko identifies machinery, chemicals, electrical engineering, critical minerals processing, IT and renewable energy as potential areas. He also points to Germany’s dual vocational education system, where companies are directly involved in training workers and aligning skills with production needs. The latter is particularly relevant to Kazakhstan’s industrial ambitions. German expertise could shape not only what is produced, but also the skills base built around new production.

Germany’s strategic interest is growing, but business is moving carefully

Germany has its own reasons to deepen the relationship. The German Federal Foreign Office describes Kazakhstan as Germany’s largest trading partner in Central Asia and an important supplier of energy and raw materials, noting that shifting global trade and energy flows have increased the region’s strategic importance.

Energy remains part of that relationship. By Scholz’s September 2024 visit, Kazakhstan was already supplying crude oil to Germany’s Schwedt refinery, and the bilateral agenda included energy, critical raw materials, mining and technological cooperation.

The economic relationship has also become more concrete this year. A Kazakhstan Investment Day in Frankfurt in February brought together around 200 representatives of German companies, financial institutions and industry associations. KfW IPEX-Bank and Solidcore Resources also signed a $100 million term sheet linked to the Ertis hydrometallurgical plant.

Yet strategic interest does not automatically mean that German companies will make large, long-term investments. Stephan Meister, a German expert on Central Asia, points to a basic commercial consideration that is less visible in government-level discussions: the size of Kazakhstan’s domestic market.

“It’s a difficult question, since Kazakhstan is in terms of population a small market, so there is a question about how much it makes sense to invest in bigger industrial production and for which markets,” he said to The Astana Times.

He also questions whether Kazakhstan’s investment environment has changed enough to encourage more German capital.

“German business is more cautious before they invest, and in terms of rule of law, transparency and business climate, not much has changed in the last years in Kazakhstan which has improved the investment conditions,” Meister said.

For Kazakhstan, that raises a practical question about the markets new production would serve. If large projects are not aimed primarily at domestic demand, they need to be competitive in wider regional and international supply chains. Market access, predictable business conditions and financing therefore matter alongside the availability of raw materials.

The constraints are not only on Kazakhstan’s side

Meister also points to a factor that complicates the usual discussion of why German investment may be slow: Germany itself is going through a difficult economic period. German companies, he argues, are becoming more cautious about where they commit capital, making the search for new markets more difficult even when the strategic case is strong.

This creates a gap between Germany’s growing political interest in Central Asia and the risk appetite of its private sector. Germany may see Kazakhstan as useful for diversifying energy and raw-material supply chains while companies continue to ask whether individual projects are commercially compelling enough to justify the risks. Meister sees another issue on the German side: political engagement.

“My impression is the main limitation on the German side is the lack of a political vision for relations with Central Asian countries, more investment on the leadership level into the countries of the region, including Kazakhstan, and a lack of understanding about the importance of the region,” he said.

According to him, German companies are slower and more risk-averse than some competitors and often lack sufficient political support when entering Central Asian markets. That leaves both sides with something to prove. Kazakhstan needs to make the country more attractive for long-term industrial investment and demonstrate that production can serve markets beyond Kazakhstan. Germany, meanwhile, faces the question of whether its growing strategic interest in Central Asia is strong enough to translate into more active support for German companies entering the region.

What the visit could clarify

The two governments already have a broad network of mechanisms for cooperation, from the Central Asia-Germany format launched in Berlin in 2023 to bilateral platforms bringing together ministries, businesses and financial institutions. Sitenko notes that the institutional tools for a strategic partnership are already in place and need to be used more effectively. Meister, however, points to Germany’s lack of a clear political vision and its companies’ cautious approach as factors that could slow new investment.

The difference between these two views is useful in understanding what will be at stake during the visit. Kazakhstan is looking to use German technology and capital to retain more value from its own resources and move further into production and processing. German companies, for their part, need projects with sufficient scale, predictable conditions and access to wider markets.

The Munich leg is therefore particularly relevant. Bavaria’s growing trade and business ties with Kazakhstan offer one of the clearest examples of where the broader relationship could go, especially in manufacturing, technology and industrial cooperation.

Sitenko also points to the less visible side of economic ties: education, skills and movement between the two countries. He notes that scaling German-style dual education and easing visa procedures could strengthen business, professional and academic links alongside larger industrial projects.

What emerges from the visit may therefore be more important than the number of new agreements announced. The stronger signal would be whether the existing framework produces projects that create more value in Kazakhstan and give German companies a stronger commercial reason to deepen their presence.

World.title: Kazakhstan Returns to Asian Games Show Jumping After 20-Year Absence
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s national equestrian team is completing final preparations in Tokyo ahead of its return to show jumping at the Asian Games after a 20-year absence, with four riders set to compete in the team and individual events at Aichi-Nagoya 2026.

The Kazakhstan team includes Oleg Sokolenko, Raisa Sokolenko, Nurila Turisbekova and Ksenia Batalova. The competitions will be held at the JRA Equestrian Park in Tokyo.

Speaking ahead of the draw, Kazakhstan national team head coach and Master of Sport Azamat Khassenov said the riders were following their training program and gradually approaching competition, Kazakhstan’s Equestrian Federation reported on Sept. 28.

“After a 20-year break, Kazakhstan is represented at this level again, so this is a significant event for us. We want to represent the country and achieve a good result,” he said.

Khassenov said the team had adapted well to local conditions, with close attention paid to the condition of both the riders and horses. The upcoming draw will influence the team’s tactics, notably the order of performances and the opponents they will face.

Kazakhstan will compete in both the team and individual show jumping events. The team competition is scheduled for Oct. 1 and will feature two rounds followed by the medal ceremony. The individual competition will take place on Oct. 3 and 4. Obstacles will range from 145 to 155 centimeters in height, depending on the round.

World.title: Kazakh President Honors Rybakina for Historic Tennis Achievements
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Elena Rybakina on Sept. 28 to congratulate her on winning the US Open and becoming the first Kazakh tennis player to reach the top of the WTA rankings.

He also awarded her the Barys Order, third degree, for outstanding sporting achievements and her contribution to the development and promotion of tennis in Kazakhstan.

During the meeting, Tokayev highlighted the historic significance of Rybakina’s achievements and her influence on the younger generation.

“After your victories, our children are taking an interest in tennis, enrolling in sections in large numbers and wanting to become champions themselves. You set a positive example for our children, and this is very important. Our children should engage in sports, as it is crucial for their future,” he said.

He noted that Rybakina’s three Grand Slam victories would become part of tennis history and said he was confident she would continue to achieve major results.

Tokayev also praised Rybakina’s conduct on and off the court, describing her as a person of “exceptionally high personal culture.”

Rybakina thanked President Tokayev for his personal support and attention to the development of tennis in Kazakhstan. She said she was proud to represent Kazakhstan on the international stage and would continue striving for high results.

Rybakina’s latest achievement caps a landmark 2026 season. She won the Australian Open and US Open, reached the finals of Indian Wells and Toronto, and became the first player representing Kazakhstan to top the WTA singles rankings. She is the 30th woman in WTA history to reach world No. 1.

World.title: Kazakhstan Women’s Chess Team Wins Silver at World Chess Olympiad
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s women’s chess team won silver at the 46th World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, finishing the 11-round tournament undefeated with 18 points. China won gold, while India took bronze.

Undefeated run

Held from Sept. 16 to 27, the Olympiad brought together nearly 400 teams. Kazakhstan finished second among 189 women’s teams, recording seven wins and four draws.

The team faced Poland in the final, and the match ended in a draw. The silver medal marks Kazakhstan’s second consecutive runner-up finish, following the team’s result at the 2024 Olympiad in Hungary.

The Kazakhstan lineup comprised Bibisara Assaubayeva, Alua Nurman, Meruyert Kamalidenova, Yelnaz Kaliakhmet and Zarina Nurgaliyeva. For 16-year-olds Kaliakhmet and Nurgaliyeva, the tournament marked their Olympic debuts, reported Kazinform.

Kazakhstan has competed in the women’s section of the Chess Olympiad since 1992. This year, the team recorded its first undefeated campaign. Assaubayeva also extended her unbeaten run across three consecutive Olympiads.

Men’s team finishes with 15 points

Kazakhstan’s men’s team drew 2-2 with Vietnam in the final round. It finished the tournament with 15 points from six wins, three draws and two losses.

Uzbekistan won the men’s competition, followed by India in second place and Germany in third. Germany secured its first Olympic medal since 2000, when it won silver.

Timur Turlov elected FIDE President

Kazakhstan Chess Federation President Timur Turlov was elected president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) on Sept. 26 during the organization’s General Assembly in Samarkand, held alongside the Olympiad.

Turlov received 110 of 196 votes.

He has headed the Kazakhstan Chess Federation since 2023. During his tenure, Kazakhstan hosted the World Chess Championship match and the FIDE World Team Rapid and Blitz Championships.

World.title: Kazakhstan Jet Fuel Production on Track to Exceed Annual Target
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects to produce 825,000 tons of jet fuel this year, exceeding its annual target of 750,000 tons and increasing output by 13% from 2025.

The country produced 591,000 tons of jet fuel in January-August. Production is expected to reach 825,000 tons by the end of the year, compared with 726,000 tons in 2025, the Energy Ministry reported.

The ministry is continuing work to increase domestic jet fuel production and ensure stable supplies to the domestic market. Domestic production fully covers the needs of Kazakhstan’s civil aviation sector, security agencies, civil protection services and the state material reserve.

Kazakhstan’s passenger aviation sector is estimated to demand 680,000 tons annually.

Jet fuel production is expected to increase further in the coming years, with output targeted to reach 1.5 million tons by 2031.

World.title: Tokayev Orders Radical Military Reform
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for a radical reform of Kazakhstan’s Armed Forces, saying the safety and lives of service officers must be an unconditional priority for commanders at all levels, following the deaths of 14 military personnel during exercises in the Mangystau Region.

Speaking at a meeting with the leadership of the Ministry of Defense on Sept. 27, Tokayev said the Caspian Sea tragedy exposed systemic shortcomings in the military and underscored the need for fundamental changes in how the Armed Forces are managed, trained and equipped. He also introduced newly appointed Defense Minister Aidos Myrzakhmetov to the ministry’s leadership, Akorda reported.

The meeting began with a minute of silence for the 14 service officers who lost their lives during the exercises on Sept. 24. Tokayev said he had sent messages of condolence to the families of all those who died and assured them that they would receive the necessary assistance.

“It is time for a radical military reform. This is an urgent task,” Tokayev said.

President orders investigation into military exercise

Tokayev gave a critical assessment of the circumstances surrounding the deaths and said the investigation must go beyond establishing what happened during the exercise.

He instructed officials to examine how the exercise was designed, whether its objectives matched modern security threats, and how the General Staff coordinated its preparation and conduct.

President Tokayev questioned why the Commander-in-Chief of the Naval Forces had not attended the exercise and raised concerns about the military’s crisis-response plans and command procedures.

According to Tokayev, service officers participating in the exercise were not provided with necessary equipment, including marine life jackets.

He instructed the Government commission investigating the incident to assess the actions of all officials responsible for planning and conducting the exercise, supplying personnel and ensuring compliance with safety requirements.

Tokayev stressed that military ranks and positions could not exempt anyone from responsibility.

Comprehensive review of Defense Ministry underway

The Ministry of Defense has also launched a comprehensive review. The inspection covers the organization of military service, supplies, and the Armed Forces’ material and financial provision.

The commission, headed by Deputy Chair of the Security Council Aida Balayeva, has been tasked with identifying violations and determining which officials should be held accountable. The President placed the issue under his personal control.

Ten-day deadline set for military reform plan

Tokayev said the shortcomings revealed by the tragedy demonstrated the need for a comprehensive transformation of the defense establishment.

“The goal of the reform is to create an army of a new type,” he said, adding that Kazakhstan’s military command system should be rebuilt in line with international best practices.

President Tokayev criticized what he described as outdated approaches and called for the Armed Forces to pursue digital transformation, with technology replacing human involvement wherever possible. He said the military needed practical solutions rather than standardized approaches, ceremonial exercises and formal reports.

The Security Council Secretariat, together with the Ministry of Defense, was instructed to submit a Military Reform Plan within 10 days. The plan is expected to be considered at a Security Council meeting in the second half of October. Tokayev also ordered the reform to be presented as a clear, concrete, phased plan rather than a broad concept or roadmap.

Priorities for the new Defense Minister

President Tokayev identified several immediate priorities for Myrzakhmetov. First, improve the efficiency of military spending.

“All funds allocated must produce the maximum possible result for ensuring the country’s defense capability,” Tokayev said, stressing that misuse of funds and embezzlement would not be tolerated.

The second priority is to reform the Armed Forces to meet modern threats. Tokayev also called for transparent criteria for selecting and evaluating military personnel. He said appointments to command positions should be based on experience and competence, not personal loyalty.

The third priority is to strengthen ideological and educational work in the Armed Forces, with an emphasis on constitutional values, military history and the achievements of Kazakh and world culture.

Service officers’ safety placed at center of reform
