World.title: Azerbaijan’s Deputy PM meets with Iranian Minister of Roads and Urban Development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 29. As part of the visit to the Islamic Republic of Iran of a delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister of Azerbaijan Shahin Mustafayev, a meeting was held between the co-chairs of the Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation between the two countries (Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev on the Azerbaijani side and Minister of Roads and Urban Development Farzaneh Sadegh on the Iranian side.)

The meeting discussed the current state of relations in the economic and trade, transport and communications, and humanitarian fields, as well as other issues of mutual interest and prospects for cooperation.

The sides also discussed the implementation status of the agreements reached, and the measures envisaged in the Memorandum of Understanding signed following the 17th meeting of the State Commission held in Baku in February this year.

The Deputy Prime Minister underlined that the active political dialogue and friendly relations between President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and President of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian have provided significant impetus to the development of relations between the two countries.

He particularly highlighted the meeting between the leaders held in Bishkek.

Shahin Mustafayev highlighted the progress made over the past period, emphasizing the importance of accelerating the implementation of agreed projects and continuing coordinated efforts among the relevant institutions.

During the discussion, the development of the North-South International Transport Corridor and the enhancement of its throughput capacity in the transport and transit sector were among the key topics.

The completion of the construction of the Aghband–Kelaleh highway bridge was hailed, and issues related to commissioning the border-crossing infrastructure were discussed.

The measures taken to complete work at the Astara cargo terminal and expand its cargo-handling capacity were also reviewed.

The sides exchanged views on promising infrastructure projects between the two countries.

The meeting concluded with an agreement to continue efforts aimed at developing mutually beneficial cooperation between Azerbaijan and Iran, ensuring the consistent implementation of the agreements reached at the 17th meeting of the State Commission, and speeding up the implementation of joint projects.

World.title: Housing developer walks away from 1,900-home SA project
World.content:
"Hundreds" of homebuyers will not be left in limbo despite a major developer walking away from a new estate in Adelaide's north, the state's housing minister has insisted.

The Eyre development near Penfield, between Edinburgh and Andrews Farm, was announced in 2010, and includes plans for 1,900 homes on a 120-hectare site.

SA government agency Renewal SA said it had entered an agreement with developer AVJennings — since bought by AVID Property Group — to build the homes, and that "about 750" had been completed, along with sporting fields and a shopping centre.

But it said that AVID had made the decision to "conclude its activities" in the South Australian market, leaving the remainder of the project back in the hands of the SA government.

Acting Housing Minister Michael Brown said the state government would seek to partner with another developer to deliver the project, and that outstanding contracts would be honoured.

"There's a few hundred contracts," he said.

"AVJennings are absolutely adamant that they will be delivered … so those who have signed deals with AVJennings need not be concerned."

Mr Brown described AVID's move as "a commercial decision".

The ABC has contacted AVID for comment — but in a statement on its website, it said it had "agreed to transition the developer role at the Eyre community" to Renewal SA.

"The decision … is a strategic business decision reflecting AVID's focus on the Australian eastern seaboard," it said.

"While Renewal SA assumes responsibility for the future direction of the community, AVID remain committed to delivering in-progress and planned stages and amenities, including a park, streetscapes and blocks.

"If you hold a contract for a lot in Stage 17 or 18, your contract remains on foot and AVID remains your point of contact for all settlement-related matters."

Renewal SA says the project will "remain on track". (YouTube: Eyre Penfield)

Master Builders Association CEO Will Frogley told 891 ABC Adelaide it was "definitely disappointing" that the company had opted against further involvement in the project.

"The main thing that Master Builders would really like to see is stability in the market — there's a lot of turbulence at the moment," he said.

"Last year we built a record number of homes, so it is quite disappointing to see a brand that size, a national developer, moving away from South Australia."

Renewal SA said the project would "remain on track" and that the "transition would not affect existing purchasers".

It said AVID had committed to finishing "outstanding work on current stages, including landscaping and delivery of a reserve, while also working with existing buyers to finalise upcoming settlements required design approvals and ensure that all commitments to existing buyers are maintained".

It said that work was expected to be completed by mid-2027.

"Eyre is a very significant development — there's already been a lot of interest from other developers over the years," Mr Brown said.

"We are extremely confident we'll find a major development partner going forward."

Housing options on defence sites

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was in Adelaide on Tuesday morning for talks on the future of the Hampstead Barracks, which was identified as a possible future housing development site following the announcement of defence site sales earlier this year.

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the Hampstead Barracks on Tuesday. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas has previously indicated interest in the residential potential of the site.

The federal government today said it was seeking to advance negotiations, "with a view to divesting the site" to the state government.

It said the site "could support about 400 homes" including apartments and townhouses "around a large public park".

World.title: Council facing hefty bill to remove whale carcass from popular beach
World.content:
Authorities are hoping to tag sharks lured to one of Perth's most popular beaches by a whale carcass, as they try to work out how to transport the 10-metre specimen to landfill.

Beaches in the Town of Cambridge remain closed after the dead whale washed up at City Beach early yesterday morning, attracting sharks within metres of the shoreline.

Mayor Gary Mack told 102.5 ABC Perth the council was getting quotes from contractors to take the stinking carcass to landfill, since it was not viable to tow it out to sea.

The decomposing whale carcass remained on the beach this morning. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Town facing huge bill

In 2014, the bill for removing a whale carcass from Scarborough Beach hit $175,000.

"I've been warned by people that were involved in the Scarborough incident ... that it is going to be expensive," Mr Mack said.

"But one thing we do know is that we can't wait, we've got to get that carcass removed as soon as possible and that's our intent."

More onlookers have been drawn to the whale carcass at City Beach. (ABC News)

Mr Mack said the council would ask the state government for financial help to remove it.

Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said she had not been briefed on the cost of removing the carcass, which was a matter for the Town of Cambridge and the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions.

"Generally local governments manage these types of things on beaches, that is part of their responsibility, but I won’t provide further comment," she said.

'Opportunistic tagging opportunity'

Ms Jarvis confirmed drum lines had been placed in the water in a bid to tag sharks circling the beach.

"We make use of opportunistic tagging opportunities," she said.

Authorities will try to tag sharks lured by the whale carcass. (ABC News)

She also shed light on why the carcass could not be simply towed out to sea.

"My understanding is if the carcass is dragged out further in these type of weather conditions, it increases the chances of the carcass being broken up and washing back onto shore and therefore causing more shark activity," she said.

Mr Mack said City Beach and Floreat Beach would remain closed until the carcass was removed.

World.title: Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals
World.content:
The family of a soccer player injured in a game believe the decision to take him by ambulance to the closest regional hospital led to unnecessary pain and delayed surgery.

After waiting hours at Victor Harbor's South Coast District Hospital for an ambulance transfer, Harry Jones made the 70-kilometre dash to a metropolitan hospital in the back seat of a car.

Mr Jones, the captain of the senior men's team at the Southern Breakers Football Club, was injured during the last game of the season.

Harry Jones is the captain of the Southern Breakers senior men's team and started playing soccer with the club at the age of five. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

He caught his right boot in the goal net while trying to stop an opposition strike and landed awkwardly, breaking both bones in his lower left leg.

He later had surgery to insert a titanium rod into one of the broken bones.

Painful wait for surgery

Club trainer Peta Haldane, an experienced registered nurse and a nurse practitioner in training, administered first aid to Mr Jones while they waited for an ambulance.

Peta Haldane says it was obvious Harry Jones needed to be a transferred to a hospital equipped for complex orthopaedic surgery. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

She said it was obvious he had a complete fracture to both bones in his lower leg and should have been taken straight to Flinders Medical Centre (FMC) since the closest hospital, Victor Harbor's Southern Fleurieu Health Service, was not equipped to deal with the level of orthopaedic surgery he needed.

Harry Jones had surgery to insert a titanium rod in his tibia the following day. (Supplied: Anna Jones)

Instead, she believed SA Ambulance policies meant he had to be taken to the nearest hospital.

His fiancee, Victoria Briggs said Mr Jones was in "excruciating pain" as he was X-rayed. He then waited for a transfer to FMC.

She said staff advised them they could be waiting another four to five hours for an ambulance and there was "no guarantee" he would be transferred that day.

According to Ms Briggs, a staff member told them "if it was them" they would use a private car to move him.

She took this advice and transferred Mr Jones herself, with the help of his mother, so he could undergo surgery that same day as his leg was continuing to swell.

Despite their efforts, Mr Jones still had to wait until the next day for surgery.

Tori Briggs transported Harry Jones to the Flinders Medical Centre in the back seat of this car with the help of his mother. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Call for change

Ms Briggs and Ms Haldane have urged the health minister to consider Mr Jones's experience and the delays and pain he experienced.

They have also raised concern for others on the Fleurieu needing orthopaedic surgery, questioning if they could be sent straight to a metropolitan hospital.

Do you know more? Contact Caroline Horn on horn.caroline@abc.net.au

Ms Briggs stressed they had no issues with the care he had received.

"The paramedics were fabulous. All the hospital staff have been wonderful … but something needs to change," she said.

Gordon Scott says most people would have made the same decision to drive a loved one themselves. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Mr Jones's coach, former police officer Gordon Scott, backed Ms Briggs and Ms Haldane's call for a review.

He said someone undertaking a car transfer themselves for an injured loved one could emotionally compromise their driving.

"If you're being told there's no patient transport available to transport your loved one for several hours and a better option is to take them in your private car then you're probably going to take that option," he said.

Destination policy

A spokesperson from SA Ambulance said the ambulance crew had made the decision to take Mr Jones to the Victor Harbor hospital to "ensure the patient would receive the quickest medical care and quick access to appropriate pain relief options".

"The SA Health ambulance destination policy looks at a range of considerations, one of which is transport to an 'appropriate and geographically closest' hospital, as well as other considerations such as the patient's immediate health care needs, demand on individual hospitals etc," they said in a statement.

"These decisions are made by appropriate healthcare professionals, depending on the patient's individual needs."

World.title: A would-be surrogate gave us a gift. It wasn't the one we were expecting
World.content:
I started sharing my failures in fertility five years ago.

Mostly because I have a big mouth. And I couldn't dodge the constant question: "Do you have kids?" Everyone asks it. Colleagues, acquaintances, that person I bumped into on the way to the bin.

I expected sharing my miscarriages and failed IVF transfers to bring in a barrage of advice: "Sashi, have you tried [insert doctor, product, test, treatment or magic spell]?"

It was so well-intentioned that I fast learnt to politely nod while internally howling into a canyon.

I also expected strangers to short-circuit in response to my breaking of the social contract to only share good news.

Once, after hearing of my miscarriages, a woman put her hands on my stomach and said, "I do declare your womb will bear, by the will of God."

I politely nodded so the barbecue could continue. Unfortunately, whichever god she contacted was busy.

What I never expected was the outpouring of support, and to hear from so many in the same situation.

What I also didn't expect was a stranger to volunteer as a surrogate.

Last spring, I shared the stranger's message with my husband, Charlie. After firmly deciding to take a break from IVF, I had researched other options with the zeal of an Olympic sprinter hurtling towards the finish line.

The waters of international adoption and commercial surrogacy appeared murky and expensive. Now, here was a surrogate in our own city. Someone who seemed far too altruistic for the cynical world shouted about on the nightly news.

Finding out her fertility struggles weren't about her body being unable to carry a child gave Sashi a sense of freedom she had not felt in a long time. (Supplied: Sashi Perera)

Charlie said: "That's got to be a weirdo, love," and I said: "Almost definitely, but it's worth a phone call."

That call led to meeting a kind and lovely human at a cafe a few months later. She was married with two kids and felt compelled by our story to contact me. There are good people doing good things constantly, they're just not featured in the news too often.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

I looked into the state of Victoria's surrogacy process, which requires counselling, legal advice and medical approvals. Even with two law degrees, it was a lot to decipher.

We decided to walk the path lined with endless paperwork. The first step was to get approval from my IVF clinic. I thought that would be the easiest one. I didn't expect the answer I got.

"You can do this," they said over the phone, "but it's unlikely to make a difference in your case."

It was the first time I was told the problem likely wasn't my body, it was the embryos. For whatever reason the tests couldn't pinpoint, they weren't keepers.

I'd spent so long feeling guilty. It was why I'd researched every other path, to the exasperation of Charlie, who said we'd be fine without kids.

I'd taken every pill and potion available, consulted with a UK-based naturopath I've never seen or met, used a hormone tracking device to monitor my daily pee, and watched what I ate, drank and how I slept.

I thought that if I did enough, I could shake the guilt that screamed it was my defective body's fault that we couldn't grow a family.

And now, I'd found a whole other, clearly functioning body. And that still wasn't enough?!

I should've felt fury but all I felt was relief.

My shoulders dropped from the level of my ears. I didn't even know they were up there. Or how long they'd been like that for.

Years ago, I tried wakeboarding for the first time. I was really struggling to stay on the board and was distracted by the thought that waterboarding was a far more sensible term for boarding on the water — why did we use that term for a terrible form of torture instead?

My friend shouted from the boat, you're fighting with the rope for control instead of letting it guide you, you've got to relax your hold.

I've been told to relax my whole life and would you believe, it's never helped me to relax. But the moment I slackened my hold on the rope that tethered me to the boat, I flew over the water on a board.

I thought about that moment after my call with the IVF clinic.

Being told to relax her whole life never helped Sashi relax, except that one time wakeboarding. Letting go of her need to solve infertility felt a little like that. (Supplied: Sashi Perera)

For the first time, I believed that it was not my fault and there was nothing more I could do. I threw every pill and test into the bin along with the hormone monitoring device. I fished that last one back out because it was quite expensive and might come in handy for menopause.

With no finish line for me to sprint towards, I discovered the ability to relax my hold and enjoy whatever's ahead, without trying to control it.

I'm now on the biggest tour of my comedy career with Charlie. The surrogate gave us a gift, just not in the way we expected.

World.title: Crossland expected to miss grand final with guilty plea over Cleary tackle
World.content:
Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland will plead guilty at the judiciary over the tackle that left Nathan Cleary with a compound fracture.

Crossland was sent off for the hip-drop tackle in the 36th minute of Newcastle's preliminary final win over Penrith on Sunday and the match review committee sent him straight to the judiciary with a dangerous contact charge.

A hearing is set for 6pm AEST tonight to decide the punishment, with Crossland's plea all but guaranteeing he will miss Sunday's grand final, barring an 11th-hour miracle.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

Dragons forward Ryan Couchman was referred straight to the judiciary in round three for a hip drop that ended the season of Parramatta's J'Maine Hopgood.

Couchman pleaded guilty and was suspended for four games after being sin-binned for the tackle that left Hopgood with a torn ACL.

"Whilst the panel accepted that this did not incorporate any element of intention or recklessness, it took the view that the player's level of culpability was significant, a factor reflected in the serious injury sustained by the ball carrier," judiciary chair Geoff Bellew said during a 90-minute hearing.

Crossland has apologised to Cleary, who urged people to stop abusing the Knights number nine online.

"It was a complete accident, and he doesn't deserve the unwarranted hate. He reached out to apologise, and I have nothing but respect for him," Cleary posted on social media after surgery on his broken left leg.

Phoenix Crossland was sent off as Nathan Cleary left on a medicab. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"He's a competitor, and our game is made up of split-second moments that sometimes lead to unfortunate circumstances.

"Comments like this are so unfair. Spread love, not hate."

Newcastle football director Chris James on Monday described it as "a horrible accident at speed under fatigue".

"Phoenix Crossland has made more tackles in the NRL than any other player and he got one wrong," he told ABC Sport.

"He got one wrong and it was a horrible injury for Nathan, but that's not Phoenix's go. If you've ever met Phoenix Crossland, he's one of the great men of rugby league.

"Horrible for Nathan, the thoughts of our club go out to Nathan.

"He'll go down as one of the greats of the game and we hope he has a speedy recovery, but we'll also wrap our arms around Phoenix and make sure we look after him this week too."

World.title: Sydney-based senior counsel to prosecute case against federal MP Luke Gosling
World.content:
The Northern Territory Director of Public Prosecutions (NTDPP) has engaged an interstate lawyer to take on the assault case against federal MP Luke Gosling, to avoid a perceived conflict of interest.

High-profile Sydney-based senior counsel Sophie Callan will prosecute the charges against the Member for Solomon, who is alleged to have assaulted NT Administrator David Connolly at the NT Thai Grand Festival in July.

Sophie Callan SC has been appointed by the NT Director of Public Prosecutions to lead the case against Luke Gosling. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

The administrator is the Crown's representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.

Mr Gosling denies the allegations and said he would contest the two assault charges, relating to two separate incidents.

In discussing the allegations during Mr Gosling's first court appearance in July, the MP's lawyer Marty Aust SC said the first alleged incident had occurred "in a manner in which the administrator was unable to see the approach".

David Connolly was sworn into the role of NT administrator in February. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The court heard the second charge pertained to an alleged hip-and-shoulder collision between the two men, during which Mr Gosling allegedly drew back his left elbow and struck Mr Connolly in his upper rib.

Since his first court appearance, Mr Gosling has also been charged with breaching his bail on August 14.

He subsequently stepped aside as special envoy for defence, veterans' affairs and northern Australia due to the "distraction" his matter was causing the Albanese government.

Commonwealth declined to take on case

Ms Callan's appointment comes a month after the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions declined to take on the case.

An NTDPP spokesperson said it was outsourcing the prosecution case to Ms Callan "to avoid any conflict of interest arising for the NTDPP".

CDPP declines to take on Labor MP assault charges An assault charge brought against Luke Gosling is up in the air.

"The prosecution will continue in the ordinary course before the courts," they said.

Ms Callan's website says she has previously appeared for the Crown in the corruption prosecution of former NSW politicians Ian Macdonald and Eddie Obeid.

She has also appeared as counsel assisting in the Lindt Cafe siege inquest.

Gosling to defend breach of bail charge

Mr Gosling's bail conditions mean he is banned from coming within 50 metres of NT Government House, where Mr Connolly resides.

Mr Gosling also has to give Mr Connolly's office 48 hours' notice before attending any event where both men would be in attendance.

Luke Gosling announced in August that he would "temporarily" stand aside from his special envoy role. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

If the two do attend the same event, Mr Gosling is required to stay 15 metres away from the administrator at all times.

A spokesperson for Mr Gosling has previously said despite the breach of bail charge, the MP "did not attend any events at the same time as the administrator" on August 14.

"Mr Gosling is discussing the matter with his legal team, and will be defending the charge," they said.

Mr Gosling's matter is expected to return to Darwin Local Court tomorrow.

World.title: Chinese-owned firm takes over one of Australia's largest cannabis farms
World.content:
One of Australia's largest cannabis cultivators is now almost entirely owned by Chinese-owned firm Yongji Health.

Company documents show Yongji, a subsidiary of a Guizhou-based company, has taken full control of Pijen, which owns more than 95 per cent of the shares in Tasmanian Botanics.

Yongji was already a part-owner in Pijen but purchased the remaining shares from Australian shareholders in a deal worth about $31 million, according to industry publication Cannabiz.

Tasmanian Botanics cultivates, manufactures and packages medicinal cannabis products from a farm and processing facility at Pontville in southern Tasmania.

Craig Knight says the business operations and staffing will remain the same. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The company's chief executive, Craig Knight, told 936 ABC Hobart that while foreign investment could "sound ominous", there was no indication there would be any significant changes for staff or customers.

"It's been one of the things that has been crystal clear throughout the whole process," Mr Knight said.

" They want the company as it is, if not bigger than it is, so there are no issues around job security or changes to operations. "

The farm is one of Australia's biggest cannabis producers. (ABC News: Scout Wallen)

More than 150 people work at the Tasmanian Botanics site, which includes a greenhouse and an outdoor crop of about 2.5 hectares, as well as packaging and manufacturing facilities.

The takeover comes at a time when the Australian medicinal cannabis industry grapples with increased competition from overseas manufacturers, particularly in Thailand.

Mr Knight said Yongji had made a "significant investment", which showed the firm's confidence in the Australian sector.

"People don't invest this type of money into something they don't have confidence in — that's very much how I viewed it," he said.

"We're now part of a bigger company … which also has other assets in the medicinal cannabis industry in Australia, so it's a pretty good synergy."

There are more than 150 workers at Tasmanian Botanics. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The cannabis farm boss said that while some might be concerned about foreign ownership, it was simply one of the realities of the business world.

"I can understand there's a world we would like to think everything that's in Tasmania is owned by Tasmanians," Mr Knight said.

"But we're part of a bigger landscape, a bigger world, and sometimes people are interested in things here and it happens all over the world."

Australia's cannabis industry is facing increased competition from overseas. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Yongji is a subsidiary of Guizhou Yongji Printing, a cigarette packaging company listed on the Shanghai stock exchange.

The ABC has contacted the federal government's Foreign Investment Review Board for comment.

World.title: Three people escape suspicious house fire south of Brisbane
World.content:
Three people have escaped a suspicious blaze that gutted a home at Logan, south of Brisbane, overnight.

Emergency services were called shortly after 9pm, with reports a house at Woodridge was engulfed in fire.

The blaze was extinguished within an hour of firefighters arriving, but the two-storey home was extensively damaged.

Neighbouring homes were also damaged.

The people inside got out before firefighters arrived and no injuries were reported.

Investigators are at the house and have declared a crime scene. (ABC News)

Investigators are still at the house and have declared a crime scene.

Hane White lives a few doors down and was home with her family when the blaze began.

She said she was afraid the fire would jump to the property next door.

"We all came out and the fire just, was too much so I just ran back in, picked up my granddaughter, and just ran," she said.

Neighbour Hane White was home with her family when the blaze began. (ABC News: Lottie Twyford)

Police are appealing for anyone who was in the area between 9pm and 9:30pm and has dash cam footage or CCTV to come forward.

World.title: ‘Working till 67, hoping for the best’
World.content:
Sponsored MoneySuper & retirementAMP ‘Working till 67, hoping for the best’ Sponsored by AMP Super Franki Hobson September 29, 2026 — 12:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The shift can be cancelled two minutes before it starts. That is the arithmetic Antony* has lived on for a decade as a casual community-sector support worker, transporting and supervising children in care, some days a 150-kilometre round trip. “If my shift gets cancelled, I don’t get paid,” the 59-year-old says. “And that can be anywhere up to two minutes before I start.” Three shifts one week brings in about $400, exactly his weekly mortgage payment and nothing else. A flat-out week of 10 brings $1600. School holidays thin the shifts; the six weeks over Christmas might hold two or three shifts. His working rule: “Do it while I can get it, and while I can do it.” Steering your own path to a secure retirement takes confidence. The plan he made alone Antony has about $98,000 in super and about $100,000 left on his mortgage for his modest three-bedroom home. His plan: work to 67, use the super to pay out whatever remains of the mortgage, live on the Government Age Pension. He turns 60 in January, the age from which Australians can generally begin accessing super, and nobody has walked him through what that means; 67 is the only number in his plan. Eight years as a stay-at-home dad meant his first super contribution landed when he was around 30. Paying fees on three separate super accounts eventually prompted him to roll them all into one.



Fewer than half of Australians aged 50 to 64 feel confident about retirement, according to AMP’s 2026 Retirement Confidence Pulse. At his age, the gap between those who worry about running out of money in retirement and those who don’t is a chasm: 26 per cent feel confident, against 82 per cent who don’t. He knows which side he is on. “I’m eventually going to run out of money after I retire, and there’s nothing I can physically do to make it any better,” he says. “So I’ve just accepted it.” A friend, retired before 60, is off to Canada, then Hawaii. “I’m happy for them. I’d like to go to Hawaii, but I don’t think that’ll ever happen for me.” When the plan met a fever Then pneumonia arrived. Six weeks, no shifts, no sick pay, no income. He had gone guarantor on one of his children’s homes, his own house as security, so the redraw on his mortgage, his usual backup, was unavailable. Suddenly, he was asking his kids for money. “I felt really vulnerable.” AMP director of growth and customer solutions Julie Slapp hears the same across the research. “The size of a super balance is important, but on its own it doesn’t tell someone what their retirement will look like,” she says. “People tend to feel more confident when they can translate that balance into a realistic income and understand where their money will come from month to month once their pay cheque stops.”



The sum he has never done It’s a step Antony has never taken. He guesses the full Government Age Pension at “about a thousand a fortnight”. He hasn’t done the sums, or registered that the $400 a week he sends to the mortgage, double the required payment, will vanish from his living costs the day the house is paid out. “I’m a bit of an ostrich sometimes. Put my head in the sand and figure it out later.” Starting is simpler than it feels, says AMP general manager of guidance and advice Andrea Boss: “List your super, savings, investments, property and debts, then estimate your spending. A simple snapshot is far more valuable than putting it off because it feels overwhelming. If you changed nothing from today, how much retirement income would you have, and how does that compare to what you want to live on?” Antony has done more right than he credits himself: the doubled mortgage payments, the extra super contributions made early on, a decade of hard, necessary work. What he has never had is the picture. His advice to his 40-year-old self suggests as much: “Put more money in your superannuation. Only because I know how important it is now.” And after the last shift? “What am I going to do to keep myself occupied all day?” he asks. “I might have to take up salsa dancing!”



Retirement can come with big questions. When the answers aren’t clear, fear can often fill the gaps. AMP Super’s Retire the Fear hub offers practical tools, guidance and support to help you understand where you stand, explore your options and take the next step with greater confidence. Visit amp.com.au/retirethefear. *Name and some identifying details have been changed at the interviewee’s request. Disclaimer: This information is general in nature and does not constitute financial product advice. Readers should consider their own circumstances, consider seeking independent professional advice, and consult the relevant PDS and TMD before making decisions. World.title: AFL considering changes to free agency system
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 AFL considering changes to free agency system Jake Niall September 29, 2026 — 12:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL will consider changes to free agency in the interests of ensuring that the system does not skew the competitive balance of the competition in favour of the teams in premiership contention. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon confirmed that the league would discuss potential changes to the free agency rules to make sure that the competitive balance of the 18 clubs was not distorted. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has flagged potential changes to free agency. Eddie Jim “Look, I think it’s been in place for now probably 12 or 14 years,” the AFL boss told this masthead in grand final week. “I think what we’re seeing in the last couple of years is what everyone thought would happen at the start, and it didn’t necessarily. “But it’s something that we’ll talk with the players association about because competitive balance is really important. That you know, we do a lot of work around the draft, we do a lot of work around the salary cap, a lot of work around the soft cap.”



Asked if the AFL would consider changes to free agency, Dillon said: “Yeah, with the agreement [with the players], just to make sure that the competitive balance isn’t distorted.” The potential to reform free agency – which was introduced for 2012 and has been the subject of minor changes and ongoing debate – comes as the Brisbane Lions, once stragglers, won their third flag on end in their fourth consecutive grand final. They attracted both Sam Draper and Oscar Allen from lowly Essendon and West Coast, respectively, as free agents, albeit the Eagles received a generous pick No.2 for their ex-skipper. The AFL wanted to change the compensation system at the end of last year to remove compensation picks inside the top 10, and thus not compromise the draft for teams who weren’t finalists (not counting the new wildcards). But the AFL Players Association resisted that change, and the status quo remained. As a result, Port Adelaide can receive pick No.5 in return for exciting superstar free agent Zak Butters and Gold Coast can gain pick No.7 for key forward Ben King, who is crossing to Hawthorn.



These deals give the clubs losing the star arguably superior compensation compared to what they could gain in a trade if they choose to match the free agent offers. The AFL is closely watching the side deals that those clubs – the Western Bulldogs and Port, Hawthorn and Gold Coast – propose, to make sure that they are “commercial” and reflect market value. Related Article Opinion

AFL grand final Why three-peat Hawks and another super side have Fagan’s Heroes covered Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age One potential reform, which is likely to be canvassed, is a rule that forces the top teams to give up a draft pick, such as their first pick, for a high-value free agent. Under that reform, Hawthorn, as a top four team, would lose their first draft pick for King, and still land him as a free agent. This could potentially apply to the top four, top six or top eight teams from that season. Most of the most prized free agents have gone to teams that had been in premiership contention. These include Lance Franklin (Sydney), Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong), Tom Lynch (Richmond), Jeremy Cameron (Geelong) and Joe Daniher (Brisbane Lions). It is rare for a restricted free agent to opt for a team in the bottom six or eight. The position on free agency varies among clubs. Some would argue that it should be less restricted, others that the system is skewed towards teams in premiership contention.



AFL free agency is enshrined in the players’ collective bargaining agreement and needs the players’ union’s consent to be altered in that agreement. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Gold’s rollercoaster ride shows the messy state of the global economy
World.content:
BusinessMarketsGold Opinion Gold’s rollercoaster ride shows the messy state of the global economy Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 29, 2026 — 12:08pm

September 29, 2026 — 12:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you were looking for an illustrated view of what’s been happening in the global economy and markets over the course of this year, you’d have to look no further than a chart of the gold price. The precious metal has had a volatile 2026 so far, hitting a record high of $US5595 ($7970) an ounce in late January, falling to a year low below $US4000 an ounce in July, recovering to just under $US4700 an ounce in late August before tumbling back to about $US4160 this week. The price has been buffeted by the cross-currents being generated by the war in the Middle East, the fiscal stress in developed economies, particularly in the US, stubborn inflation rates, the turmoil in bond markets, and turbulent currency markets. 2026 has been a rollercoaster for gold investors so far. Bloomberg Many of those influences are centred in the US and flow from the impact of the war with Iran on the markets for oil and its derivative products, although the boom in artificial intelligence-related investment is also playing a role. There are also some longer-term elements to the shifting tides in the price.



The gold rush that pushed the metal to record highs in January was sparked by the three rate cuts the US Federal Reserve made last year as it shifted its focus from inflation to growth. Gold has historically been regarded as a hedge against inflation but it also has an inverse correlation with interest rates. Gold generates no income from interest but has holding and opportunity costs, so a lower rate environment makes it more attractive. As an indicator of how troubled, messy and confusing the emerging new world order and the debt-laden global economy are, the gold price is providing some appropriately volatile signals. With the US flirting with stagflation last year – low growth but relatively high levels of inflation – and unsettling discussions about how the Trump administration might respond to public finances that are spiralling out of control, gold’s “safe haven” status was another factor in the price surge. China’s record buying activity last year, when it purchased more than 1000 tonnes of gold – a 60 per cent-plus increase on its 2024 purchases – also helped.



After the 2023 freezing of Russia’s dollar-denominated offshore reserves in the wake of its invasion of Ukraine, China’s central bank has, along with other central banks, increasingly shifted its reserves out of the US Treasuries market and into gold. Related Article Opinion

Gold What the price of gold tells us about Trump and the future Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Donald Trump’s trade wars with the rest of the world may have provided an extra incentive for China – and even America’s traditional allies – to reduce their exposures to the US. Aided at the margin by a stronger yuan, China has bought gold almost regardless of the price, so the sharp fall in the price over the past few weeks should create an appealing buying opportunity. It’s not only the central bank that’s plunged into the precious metal.



With China’s property market five years into a seemingly endless downwards spiral, households have, in the absence of property as a viable investment, also been heavy buyers of gold. Although with China’s domestic economy seemingly stressed, that source of buying seems to have shrunk somewhat in recent months. What changed from the bull market in gold early in the year to its steady price decline as the year progressed, including the steep fall from just under $US4700 in late August to about $US4160 an ounce today, and about $US4135 an ounce on the spot market? The war and an oil price that has soared from about $US70 a barrel to more than $US100 a barrel, forcing petrol and diesel prices up by far greater amounts, is the obvious culprit. It is feeding into higher inflation and interest rates and slower growth in most of the world. The US, the key economy for global financial markets, doesn’t have that slower growth, thanks to the extraordinary levels of AI investment and the wealth effects of a sharemarket at near-record levels.



It does, however, have the same challenge, with high levels of inflation that have forced the Fed to reluctantly start raising US interest rates for the first time in more than three years. America, along with much of the developed world, also has deteriorating public finances, with a deficit of close to 6 per cent, gross government debt of more than $US40 trillion and an annual interest bill of about $US1 trillion that rises every time a longer-dated bond matures. The combination of continuing high inflation, the competition for capital between the government and AI companies, and the fear that the Trump administration might try to inflate its way out of the fiscal trap that its profligacy has built, has prompted bond investors to take matters into their own hands, forcing yields up to levels not seen for nearly two decades. Donald Trump’s assault on the post-WWII order and his “America First” approach to geopolitics and geoeconomics have rocked the gold price. AP America’s unsustainable public finances and the turbulence in the world’s most important financial market might make the concept of holding more gold appealing. But the surge in yields has increased both the cost of holding gold and the opportunity cost associated with it. Hence the recent tumble in the price.



That inverse relationship between the price of gold and US interest rates is unlikely to disappear for some time. Having defied those who were sceptical that the Trump-appointed Fed chair Kevin Warsh would risk infuriating Trump with a rate rise, the markets are now pricing in a 70 per cent probability that this month’s 25 basis point increase in the federal funds rate will be followed up with a similar move next month. Indeed, 100 basis points of increases – a full percentage point – is expected over the next 12 months. That probably adds more pessimism to the outlook for the gold price but it may also accelerate the decline of the US bond market as the most important market in the world. China, which has cut its holdings of US Treasuries from a peak of $US1.3 trillion in 2013 to $US618 billion, even as it built its gold holdings, isn’t the only country that will see the cheaper gold price as an opportunity. That is, provided the US dollar’s relative strength (it has gained more than 2 per cent against its major trading partners’ currencies this month) doesn’t offset the price decline. Gold is now the biggest store of central bank reserves. At the end of last year it accounted for about 27 per cent of all central bank reserve assets, up from 20 per cent a year earlier. That proportion has almost certainly increased through this year, widening the lead over US Treasuries, where the holdings fell from 25 per cent of reserves to 22 per cent last year.



Related Article Global economy AI’s hidden $4.3 trillion bill could wreck world economy, warns Big Short investor The volatile path the gold price has traced this year reflects the messy and risky macro environment, with the US at the epicentre of most of the major issues and factors impacting the price. Debt, inflation, the war in the Middle East, the Trump-led assault on the post-WWII order and his “America First” approach to geopolitics and geoeconomics, rising interest rates and the diversion of global savings into the risky but potentially transformative AI sector are all reflected in the shifting movements in the price of the shiny metal. As an indicator of how troubled, messy and confusing the emerging new world order and the debt-laden global economy are, the gold price is providing some appropriately volatile and, at times, paradoxical signals. World.title: Greens leader showdown to occur at Sydney retreat
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Greens leader showdown to occur at Sydney retreat Nick Newling September 29, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens MPs will elect a new federal leader at a two-day retreat in Sydney this week, as possible contenders go quiet on who will lead the party to the next election. The party’s leadership was unexpectedly thrown into contention when current leader Larissa Waters announced her resignation on Monday night, citing worsening chronic kidney disease. Outgoing Greens leader Larissa Waters (centre) with colleagues Mehreen Faruqi (left) and Sarah Hanson-Young. Penny Stephens Waters has yet to speak publicly but is expected to address a press conference alongside the newly elected leader following a pre-planned party room meeting on Wednesday or Thursday. None of the party’s possible contenders have publicly pitched themselves for the leadership, though NSW senators Mehreen Faruqi and David Shoebridge, South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young and Tasmanian senator Nick McKim appear to be frontrunners for the top job.



Those close to the leadership deliberations anticipate that contenders will seek to come to a consensus position before this week’s meeting, as some seek an uncontested ballot. After former leader Adam Bandt’s loss at the 2025 election, Waters took the leadership unopposed. Related Article Political leadership Larissa Waters quits as Greens leader due to illness A spokesperson for Faruqi said the senator, who currently serves as the party’s deputy leader, was considering her options. First appointed to the Senate in 2018, Faruqi has expressed frustration that the party has not tapped into the same populist-left wave that has boosted the careers of New York City’s socialist Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdani and UK Greens leader Zack Polanski. Hanson-Young, the party’s longest-serving senator and another key contender, has become the main negotiator for the passage of legislation, particularly in the communications space, where she is pushing for a toughening of Labor’s digital duty-of-care laws. Some in the party consider the senator, who has served the federal Greens for 18 years, too moderate. Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May’s office said she had no comment to make on the leadership but the senator has increasingly been pushed into the spotlight with an extensive traditional and social media presence over the past year.



Other senators Penny Allman-Payne and Jordon Steele-John, alongside lower house MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown, are unlikely to challenge for the leadership, though the former two could be considered for deputy depending on who becomes leader. South Australian senator Barbara Pocock has already announced her retirement at the next election, expected in early 2028, making her and Waters the only MPs ruled out of contention. In a post to Instagram on Tuesday, Pocock said she was “deeply saddened” that Waters had to step down, saying the leader had shown “tremendous leadership” over her tenure. Loading Newly appointed Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer has yet to determine whether she would challenge for the leadership but is unlikely to make a tilt, having sat in the Senate for just over two months. The offices of all sitting Greens MPs have been contacted for comment.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday said he had spoken to Waters and “wished her well”, saying the senator was attending further health checks on Tuesday. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: RBA expected to announce fourth rate rise this year; Greens leader Larissa Waters steps down due to illness; Trump denies asking Xi about potential US arms sales “I just wish her all the very best on a personal level. I obviously have differences with the Greens political party but this is a human issue and I can also have compassion, and I have a good relationship with Larissa,” Albanese said. “I thank her for the constructive engagement that I’ve had with her. I work with people across the parliament. We have to do that in order to secure any legislation through our Senate. We haven’t always agreed, and we won’t always agree going forward, but I wish her all the very best.” Waters took on the job just over 15 months ago at a tumultuous time for the Greens. At the last election the party’s then-leader Adam Bandt lost his previously safe seat of Melbourne to Labor. The Greens also lost Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates’ seats in Brisbane, leaving the party with only one lower house seat and devoid of Chandler-Mather’s firebrand energy.



Waters, 49, plans to return to the Senate after time away dealing with her health, so her resignation as leader does not open an upper house vacancy. She said the minor party had achieved significant wins, including protecting native forests in a deal with Labor to reform Australia’s 25-year-old environmental laws. World.title: Nassif’s Toplace paid $134,000 for surveillance of Strathfield mayor
World.content:
Follow the hearings live A private investigator invoiced Jean Nassif’s development company $134,000 for surveillance of the former Strathfield mayor, with then-Labor councillor Sharangan Maheswaran convincing Toplace to pay the bill. Maheswaran, who was also the lawyer for Toplace, said the surveillance work had a “tangential” connection to Nassif because then-mayor Matthew Blackmore had “linked up” with another individual who Maheswaran believed was targeting him because of his connection to the disgraced developer. Sharangan Maheswaran arrives at the ICAC on Tuesday. Sam Mooy The Independent Commission Against Corruption is investigating whether Maheswaran and his fellow Labor councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in blackmail and/or offences under the Surveillance Devices Act while waging a pressure campaign to force Blackmore to resign as mayor.



The commission heard on Tuesday Nassif’s daughter Ashlyn raised the payment to private investigator Shane De Kauwe as a personal expense for Maheswaran to cover but he convinced her Toplace should pay the invoices because he was already owed money. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Former Strathfield councillor Sharangan Maheswaran returns for likely final day of public hearings “I believe that Toplace paid it on the basis that I was insisting that I need to get this paid, and I will offset it against other liabilities you owe me because I regard the targeting of me by this individual to be linked to Toplace Pty Ltd,” Maheswaran said. Maheswaran told the commission he only became aware De Kauwe was making covert audio recordings after the lawyer was provided with highly detailed notes. He said when he asked De Kauwe to explain something in his surveillance notes, the private investigator said he would “go back and check”.



“That’s when it became apparent that he’d taken a recording. Now, Mr De Kauwe also said to me that he might record if there was obvious criminality involved and he said he was entitled to do so,” Maheswaran said. Maheswaran told the commission he then sought legal advice for himself about the legality of making these recordings, which he passed on to De Kauwe. He has been ordered to provide that advice to the commission. However, last week De Kauwe told the commission he only began to make audio recordings of Blackmore after receiving legal advice from Maheswaran, and his understanding was if he suspected criminality, he could record the conversation. Maheswaran also offered to “stir up” Blackmore to try and capture damaging comments on a covert audio recording, the ICAC has heard. De Kauwe texted Maheswaran to let him know Blackmore was at a cafe. “Have you got a good audio on him? If so I’ll stir him up,” Maheswaran said.



Maheswaran told the commission he thought he could prompt Blackmore into talking about council-related matters, and “things I thought he was orchestrating on the council at that point”. Maheswaran later texted Pensabene that he thought Blackmore realised he was “being watched”. “Did we get caught?” Pensabene asked. “Nah, but he was highly suss,” Maheswaran replied. Maheswaran told the ICAC that Pensabene was aware of the surveillance but may not have been aware of the covert recordings.

World.title: Wallabies sweat on stars for Bledisloe as RA chases answers on ‘phone-gate’
World.content:
The Wallabies’ hopes of following up their Optus Stadium heroics with a drought-breaking victory over the All Blacks in Auckland next week have been given a boost, with Len Ikitau’s ankle injury not as serious as first feared. Ikitau’s potential availability for the first Bledisloe Cup Test came as Rugby Australia confirmed that they are investigating the cause of the communications breakdown that led to the bizarre scene of referee Andrea Piardi speaking to the television match official on a mobile phone on Sunday night. Len Ikitau passes the ball against the Springboks. Getty Images The referee communications problem was one of many elements of high drama in Perth, in which the Wallabies held on for an unbelievable victory despite being reduced to 11 men in the last 10 minutes. Ikitau hobbled off with an ankle injury in the second half – and was later seen in a moon boot – and centre partner Hunter Paisami was later cited for a high tackle that earned him one of four yellow cards. Paisami’s case will be initially heard before the SANZAAR foul play review committee on Tuesday night.



If found guilty the No.12 faces a suspension that could keep him out of the first Bledisloe Cup clash at Eden Park on October 10. Australia hasn’t won at the venue since 1986, and the All Blacks haven’t lost there to anyone since 1994. Along with Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper returning to their clubs in Paris and Exeter respectively, and in-form lock Josh Canham also in doubt with a hamstring injury, the Wallabies face the prospect of five stars missing from the opening Bledisloe clash. Ahead of Les Kiss confirming his squad on Wednesday, however, the news on Ikitau appears more positive than first feared. There was concern the star centre – who scored two tries against the Springboks – had suffered a syndesmosis injury, which usually has a six-to-12 week recovery period and can require surgery. Loading Ikitau has scans on Monday but sources with knowledge of the situation say the John Eales medallist is confident the injury is not a worst-case scenario and he may be able to play against the All Blacks. Ikitau missed the Japan Tests in August after having clean-up surgery on the same ankle.



The contingency planning for the Wallabies’ midfield would mean Isaac Henry and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii returning to the centres, and Jordan Petaia may also be an option after joining the squad last week in Perth. But Kiss will be crossing his fingers that Ikitau is available, given his importance on a range of fronts: as a ball-player, game manager, defensive bulwark and open-field attacker. He crossed the gain line against the vaunted Springbok defence in 80 per cent of his carries in Perth. Loading Tupou and Hooper are also big losses. Tupou helped lock down the Wallabies scrum against the Boks, and Hooper was a work-rate machine in the crazy final minutes. Meanwhile, Rugby Australia are seeking answers after Piardi was forced to speak to his television match official on a mobile phone due to issues with his communications device during the closing stages of Sunday’s Test victory against South Africa.



The issue comes just over a year before Australia host the Rugby World Cup. As host nation, RA utilised its regular supplier of referee communications for one-off home Tests, Gravity Media. RA has used the company to supply this technology for more than 10 years without incident. Gravity Media is also listed as one of five companies approved to provide referee communications services at its tournaments, including next year’s World Cup. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii of the Wallabies offloads. Getty Images In a statement provided to this masthead, RA acknowledged the technological difficulties for the match officials on Sunday. “Rugby Australia acknowledges that match officials’ communications were affected by a technical issue during Sunday’s Test between the Wallabies and South Africa in Perth.



“Further information is currently being sought from the relevant third-party service provider to understand the cause of the issue and ensure appropriate measures are taken to prevent a recurrence.” Related Article Australian rugby Booming global interest in 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia as one-year countdown begins Piardi was forced to use a mobile phone after 69 minutes to speak to television match official Matteo Liparini to confirm that Wallabies captain Harry Wilson had made a high tackle and would receive a yellow card. After 73 minutes, Piardi explained to Wallabies stand-in captain Jeremy Williams and South Africa skipper Andre Esterhuizen that he was finding it challenging to officiate without his normal technology to talk to his television match official. Referee communication issues had also plagued the Springboks’ last Test against New Zealand in Baltimore.



Referee Karl Dickson was forced to stop the game for eight minutes and 53 minutes midway through the first half, with officials unable to communicate with each other. World Rugby and Gravity Media were contacted for comment. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Ben Simmons is back in the NBA. One topic at media day had him swearing
World.content:
SportBasketballBen Simmons Ben Simmons is back in the NBA. One topic at media day had him swearing Jon Pierik September 29, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A rejuvenated Ben Simmons has declared basketball is his art and he is ready to dominate and prove to the world how much he missed the sport in a year away from the game. Simmons was a top draft pick with the Philadelphia 76ers and one of the great hopes for that team’s turnaround in fortunes. But the relationship soured and when his five-year, $250 million deal expired after the 2024-25 season, he was traded to the Brooklyn Nets – then waived. Back in the big league: Three-time All Star Ben Simmons says he is a happy and healthy and ready to make a splash with the Sacramento Kings. Getty He spent his last season with the Los Angeles Clippers, and then turned his attention to professional sport fishing. Simmons, 30, who has struggled with physical and mental health issues throughout his career, is back and ready to make a splash in his return to the NBA.



Related Article Exclusive

NBA How Josh Giddey helps others get better, on and off the court He has worked hard on shedding a back issue which had long plagued his game and, in some ways, took the pure joy away from playing. “I think that was more so just my body. It wasn’t about if I wanted to play. All these people talk about, I don’t love the game. That’s bullshit – I love this game,” the Australian guard said. “If I didn’t, I wouldn’t have taken that year to focus on myself and get back to where I’m at.” Former NBA player Patrick Beverley recently claimed Simmons quit when things got hard, and questioned his respect and love for the game.



“What do I love about the game? Everything. It’s my art,” Simmons said. Related Article NBA The secret Ben Simmons training session that has tongues wagging “You know, I get to come out here and be creative and play hard and compete against, you know, a numerous amount of talented guys. So for me, it’s just, it’s in my blood. I’ve been doing it since I was a baby.” Simmons impressed Australian Boomers coaches and players at an unofficial squad camp in Melbourne last month, sources close to the pass-first playmaker confirming to this masthead he is keen to represent his country at the FIBA World Cup in Qatar next year. Fellow Australian Josh Giddey, the star Chicago Bulls’ playmaker, said there was no reason why Simmons could not again be a force.



“It was awesome to see him back fit and firing in Melbourne, and I think it was awesome for him to be amongst that national team program,” Giddey told this masthead ahead of the Bulls’ media day. “He knows how much, you know, we want him to be a part of it, and I think it’s an awesome place for him to rejuvenate his career and get back to where he belongs in the NBA. So, super excited to see him. “He looks good. He looks really healthy and fit. And, yeah, I’m excited to watch him this year and see how he goes in Sacramento.” Simmons averaged 13.1 points, 7.4 rebounds and 7.2 assists per game through his career, but outside shooting was an issue.



Related Article Exclusive

NBA Grudge matches, trash talk and sharp shooting: Dash Daniels on his path to the NBA “I’m right where I need to be. I took a lot of time to focus on my body over the season. I think it was the best thing I’ve done and decision I’ve made for my career,” Simmons, on a one-year, $3.5 million contract, said. “I’m looking forward to getting going. I feel great and I’m ready to go. No limitations, so ready. “I miss playing the game a lot. But when you’re not physically right, it’s hard to want to be out there and do what you love. “So the fact that I’m healthy, and I’m able to compete every day and play every day, I love it.”



It shapes as a tough season for an undermanned Kings’ unit in a loaded western conference. But Simmons has a goal: “Every time I step on the floor, to dominate,” he said. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Working till 67, hoping for the best’
World.content:
Sponsored MoneySuper & retirementAMP ‘Working till 67, hoping for the best’ Sponsored by AMP Super Franki Hobson September 29, 2026 — 12:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The shift can be cancelled two minutes before it starts. That is the arithmetic Antony* has lived on for a decade as a casual community-sector support worker, transporting and supervising children in care, some days a 150-kilometre round trip. “If my shift gets cancelled, I don’t get paid,” the 59-year-old says. “And that can be anywhere up to two minutes before I start.” Three shifts one week brings in about $400, exactly his weekly mortgage payment and nothing else. A flat-out week of 10 brings $1600. School holidays thin the shifts; the six weeks over Christmas might hold two or three shifts. His working rule: “Do it while I can get it, and while I can do it.” Steering your own path to a secure retirement takes confidence. The plan he made alone Antony has about $98,000 in super and about $100,000 left on his mortgage for his modest three-bedroom home. His plan: work to 67, use the super to pay out whatever remains of the mortgage, live on the Government Age Pension. He turns 60 in January, the age from which Australians can generally begin accessing super, and nobody has walked him through what that means; 67 is the only number in his plan. Eight years as a stay-at-home dad meant his first super contribution landed when he was around 30. Paying fees on three separate super accounts eventually prompted him to roll them all into one.



Fewer than half of Australians aged 50 to 64 feel confident about retirement, according to AMP’s 2026 Retirement Confidence Pulse. At his age, the gap between those who worry about running out of money in retirement and those who don’t is a chasm: 26 per cent feel confident, against 82 per cent who don’t. He knows which side he is on. “I’m eventually going to run out of money after I retire, and there’s nothing I can physically do to make it any better,” he says. “So I’ve just accepted it.” A friend, retired before 60, is off to Canada, then Hawaii. “I’m happy for them. I’d like to go to Hawaii, but I don’t think that’ll ever happen for me.” When the plan met a fever Then pneumonia arrived. Six weeks, no shifts, no sick pay, no income. He had gone guarantor on one of his children’s homes, his own house as security, so the redraw on his mortgage, his usual backup, was unavailable. Suddenly, he was asking his kids for money. “I felt really vulnerable.” AMP director of growth and customer solutions Julie Slapp hears the same across the research. “The size of a super balance is important, but on its own it doesn’t tell someone what their retirement will look like,” she says. “People tend to feel more confident when they can translate that balance into a realistic income and understand where their money will come from month to month once their pay cheque stops.”



The sum he has never done It’s a step Antony has never taken. He guesses the full Government Age Pension at “about a thousand a fortnight”. He hasn’t done the sums, or registered that the $400 a week he sends to the mortgage, double the required payment, will vanish from his living costs the day the house is paid out. “I’m a bit of an ostrich sometimes. Put my head in the sand and figure it out later.” Starting is simpler than it feels, says AMP general manager of guidance and advice Andrea Boss: “List your super, savings, investments, property and debts, then estimate your spending. A simple snapshot is far more valuable than putting it off because it feels overwhelming. If you changed nothing from today, how much retirement income would you have, and how does that compare to what you want to live on?” Antony has done more right than he credits himself: the doubled mortgage payments, the extra super contributions made early on, a decade of hard, necessary work. What he has never had is the picture. His advice to his 40-year-old self suggests as much: “Put more money in your superannuation. Only because I know how important it is now.” And after the last shift? “What am I going to do to keep myself occupied all day?” he asks. “I might have to take up salsa dancing!”



Retirement can come with big questions. When the answers aren’t clear, fear can often fill the gaps. AMP Super’s Retire the Fear hub offers practical tools, guidance and support to help you understand where you stand, explore your options and take the next step with greater confidence. Visit amp.com.au/retirethefear. *Name and some identifying details have been changed at the interviewee’s request. Disclaimer: This information is general in nature and does not constitute financial product advice. Readers should consider their own circumstances, consider seeking independent professional advice, and consult the relevant PDS and TMD before making decisions.
