World.title: AFL considering changes to free agency system
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 AFL considering changes to free agency system Jake Niall September 29, 2026 — 12:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL will consider changes to free agency in the interests of ensuring that the system does not skew the competitive balance of the competition in favour of the teams in premiership contention. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon confirmed that the league would discuss potential changes to the free agency rules to make sure that the competitive balance of the 18 clubs was not distorted. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has flagged potential changes to free agency. Eddie Jim “Look, I think it’s been in place for now probably 12 or 14 years,” the AFL boss told this masthead in grand final week. “I think what we’re seeing in the last couple of years is what everyone thought would happen at the start, and it didn’t necessarily. “But it’s something that we’ll talk with the players association about because competitive balance is really important. That you know, we do a lot of work around the draft, we do a lot of work around the salary cap, a lot of work around the soft cap.”



Asked if the AFL would consider changes to free agency, Dillon said: “Yeah, with the agreement [with the players], just to make sure that the competitive balance isn’t distorted.” The potential to reform free agency – which was introduced for 2012 and has been the subject of minor changes and ongoing debate – comes as the Brisbane Lions, once stragglers, won their third flag on end in their fourth consecutive grand final. They attracted both Sam Draper and Oscar Allen from lowly Essendon and West Coast, respectively, as free agents, albeit the Eagles received a generous pick No.2 for their ex-skipper. The AFL wanted to change the compensation system at the end of last year to remove compensation picks inside the top 10, and thus not compromise the draft for teams who weren’t finalists (not counting the new wildcards). But the AFL Players Association resisted that change, and the status quo remained. As a result, Port Adelaide can receive pick No.5 in return for exciting superstar free agent Zak Butters and Gold Coast can gain pick No.7 for key forward Ben King, who is crossing to Hawthorn.



These deals give the clubs losing the star arguably superior compensation compared to what they could gain in a trade if they choose to match the free agent offers. The AFL is closely watching the side deals that those clubs – the Western Bulldogs and Port, Hawthorn and Gold Coast – propose, to make sure that they are “commercial” and reflect market value. Related Article Opinion

AFL grand final Why three-peat Hawks and another super side have Fagan’s Heroes covered Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age One potential reform, which is likely to be canvassed, is a rule that forces the top teams to give up a draft pick, such as their first pick, for a high-value free agent. Under that reform, Hawthorn, as a top four team, would lose their first draft pick for King, and still land him as a free agent. This could potentially apply to the top four, top six or top eight teams from that season. Most of the most prized free agents have gone to teams that had been in premiership contention. These include Lance Franklin (Sydney), Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong), Tom Lynch (Richmond), Jeremy Cameron (Geelong) and Joe Daniher (Brisbane Lions). It is rare for a restricted free agent to opt for a team in the bottom six or eight. The position on free agency varies among clubs. Some would argue that it should be less restricted, others that the system is skewed towards teams in premiership contention.



AFL free agency is enshrined in the players’ collective bargaining agreement and needs the players’ union’s consent to be altered in that agreement. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Gold’s rollercoaster ride shows the messy state of the global economy
World.content:
BusinessMarketsGold Opinion Gold’s rollercoaster ride shows the messy state of the global economy Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 29, 2026 — 12:08pm

September 29, 2026 — 12:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you were looking for an illustrated view of what’s been happening in the global economy and markets over the course of this year, you’d have to look no further than a chart of the gold price. The precious metal has had a volatile 2026 so far, hitting a record high of $US5595 ($7970) an ounce in late January, falling to a year low below $US4000 an ounce in July, recovering to just under $US4700 an ounce in late August before tumbling back to about $US4160 this week. The price has been buffeted by the cross-currents being generated by the war in the Middle East, the fiscal stress in developed economies, particularly in the US, stubborn inflation rates, the turmoil in bond markets, and turbulent currency markets. 2026 has been a rollercoaster for gold investors so far. Bloomberg Many of those influences are centred in the US and flow from the impact of the war with Iran on the markets for oil and its derivative products, although the boom in artificial intelligence-related investment is also playing a role. There are also some longer-term elements to the shifting tides in the price.



The gold rush that pushed the metal to record highs in January was sparked by the three rate cuts the US Federal Reserve made last year as it shifted its focus from inflation to growth. Gold has historically been regarded as a hedge against inflation but it also has an inverse correlation with interest rates. Gold generates no income from interest but has holding and opportunity costs, so a lower rate environment makes it more attractive. As an indicator of how troubled, messy and confusing the emerging new world order and the debt-laden global economy are, the gold price is providing some appropriately volatile signals. With the US flirting with stagflation last year – low growth but relatively high levels of inflation – and unsettling discussions about how the Trump administration might respond to public finances that are spiralling out of control, gold’s “safe haven” status was another factor in the price surge. China’s record buying activity last year, when it purchased more than 1000 tonnes of gold – a 60 per cent-plus increase on its 2024 purchases – also helped.



After the 2023 freezing of Russia’s dollar-denominated offshore reserves in the wake of its invasion of Ukraine, China’s central bank has, along with other central banks, increasingly shifted its reserves out of the US Treasuries market and into gold. Related Article Opinion

Gold What the price of gold tells us about Trump and the future Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Donald Trump’s trade wars with the rest of the world may have provided an extra incentive for China – and even America’s traditional allies – to reduce their exposures to the US. Aided at the margin by a stronger yuan, China has bought gold almost regardless of the price, so the sharp fall in the price over the past few weeks should create an appealing buying opportunity. It’s not only the central bank that’s plunged into the precious metal.



With China’s property market five years into a seemingly endless downwards spiral, households have, in the absence of property as a viable investment, also been heavy buyers of gold. Although with China’s domestic economy seemingly stressed, that source of buying seems to have shrunk somewhat in recent months. What changed from the bull market in gold early in the year to its steady price decline as the year progressed, including the steep fall from just under $US4700 in late August to about $US4160 an ounce today, and about $US4135 an ounce on the spot market? The war and an oil price that has soared from about $US70 a barrel to more than $US100 a barrel, forcing petrol and diesel prices up by far greater amounts, is the obvious culprit. It is feeding into higher inflation and interest rates and slower growth in most of the world. The US, the key economy for global financial markets, doesn’t have that slower growth, thanks to the extraordinary levels of AI investment and the wealth effects of a sharemarket at near-record levels.



It does, however, have the same challenge, with high levels of inflation that have forced the Fed to reluctantly start raising US interest rates for the first time in more than three years. America, along with much of the developed world, also has deteriorating public finances, with a deficit of close to 6 per cent, gross government debt of more than $US40 trillion and an annual interest bill of about $US1 trillion that rises every time a longer-dated bond matures. The combination of continuing high inflation, the competition for capital between the government and AI companies, and the fear that the Trump administration might try to inflate its way out of the fiscal trap that its profligacy has built, has prompted bond investors to take matters into their own hands, forcing yields up to levels not seen for nearly two decades. Donald Trump’s assault on the post-WWII order and his “America First” approach to geopolitics and geoeconomics have rocked the gold price. AP America’s unsustainable public finances and the turbulence in the world’s most important financial market might make the concept of holding more gold appealing. But the surge in yields has increased both the cost of holding gold and the opportunity cost associated with it. Hence the recent tumble in the price.



That inverse relationship between the price of gold and US interest rates is unlikely to disappear for some time. Having defied those who were sceptical that the Trump-appointed Fed chair Kevin Warsh would risk infuriating Trump with a rate rise, the markets are now pricing in a 70 per cent probability that this month’s 25 basis point increase in the federal funds rate will be followed up with a similar move next month. Indeed, 100 basis points of increases – a full percentage point – is expected over the next 12 months. That probably adds more pessimism to the outlook for the gold price but it may also accelerate the decline of the US bond market as the most important market in the world. China, which has cut its holdings of US Treasuries from a peak of $US1.3 trillion in 2013 to $US618 billion, even as it built its gold holdings, isn’t the only country that will see the cheaper gold price as an opportunity. That is, provided the US dollar’s relative strength (it has gained more than 2 per cent against its major trading partners’ currencies this month) doesn’t offset the price decline. Gold is now the biggest store of central bank reserves. At the end of last year it accounted for about 27 per cent of all central bank reserve assets, up from 20 per cent a year earlier. That proportion has almost certainly increased through this year, widening the lead over US Treasuries, where the holdings fell from 25 per cent of reserves to 22 per cent last year.



Related Article Global economy AI’s hidden $4.3 trillion bill could wreck world economy, warns Big Short investor The volatile path the gold price has traced this year reflects the messy and risky macro environment, with the US at the epicentre of most of the major issues and factors impacting the price. Debt, inflation, the war in the Middle East, the Trump-led assault on the post-WWII order and his “America First” approach to geopolitics and geoeconomics, rising interest rates and the diversion of global savings into the risky but potentially transformative AI sector are all reflected in the shifting movements in the price of the shiny metal. As an indicator of how troubled, messy and confusing the emerging new world order and the debt-laden global economy are, the gold price is providing some appropriately volatile and, at times, paradoxical signals. World.title: Greens leader showdown to occur at Sydney retreat
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Greens leader showdown to occur at Sydney retreat Nick Newling September 29, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens MPs will elect a new federal leader at a two-day retreat in Sydney this week, as possible contenders go quiet on who will lead the party to the next election. The party’s leadership was unexpectedly thrown into contention when current leader Larissa Waters announced her resignation on Monday night, citing worsening chronic kidney disease. Outgoing Greens leader Larissa Waters (centre) with colleagues Mehreen Faruqi (left) and Sarah Hanson-Young. Penny Stephens Waters has yet to speak publicly but is expected to address a press conference alongside the newly elected leader following a pre-planned party room meeting on Wednesday or Thursday. None of the party’s possible contenders have publicly pitched themselves for the leadership, though NSW senators Mehreen Faruqi and David Shoebridge, South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young and Tasmanian senator Nick McKim appear to be frontrunners for the top job.



Those close to the leadership deliberations anticipate that contenders will seek to come to a consensus position before this week’s meeting, as some seek an uncontested ballot. After former leader Adam Bandt’s loss at the 2025 election, Waters took the leadership unopposed. Related Article Political leadership Larissa Waters quits as Greens leader due to illness A spokesperson for Faruqi said the senator, who currently serves as the party’s deputy leader, was considering her options. First appointed to the Senate in 2018, Faruqi has expressed frustration that the party has not tapped into the same populist-left wave that has boosted the careers of New York City’s socialist Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdani and UK Greens leader Zack Polanski. Hanson-Young, the party’s longest-serving senator and another key contender, has become the main negotiator for the passage of legislation, particularly in the communications space, where she is pushing for a toughening of Labor’s digital duty-of-care laws. Some in the party consider the senator, who has served the federal Greens for 18 years, too moderate. Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May’s office said she had no comment to make on the leadership but the senator has increasingly been pushed into the spotlight with an extensive traditional and social media presence over the past year.



Other senators Penny Allman-Payne and Jordon Steele-John, alongside lower house MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown, are unlikely to challenge for the leadership, though the former two could be considered for deputy depending on who becomes leader. South Australian senator Barbara Pocock has already announced her retirement at the next election, expected in early 2028, making her and Waters the only MPs ruled out of contention. In a post to Instagram on Tuesday, Pocock said she was “deeply saddened” that Waters had to step down, saying the leader had shown “tremendous leadership” over her tenure. Loading Newly appointed Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer has yet to determine whether she would challenge for the leadership but is unlikely to make a tilt, having sat in the Senate for just over two months. The offices of all sitting Greens MPs have been contacted for comment.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday said he had spoken to Waters and “wished her well”, saying the senator was attending further health checks on Tuesday. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: RBA expected to announce fourth rate rise this year; Greens leader Larissa Waters steps down due to illness; Trump denies asking Xi about potential US arms sales “I just wish her all the very best on a personal level. I obviously have differences with the Greens political party but this is a human issue and I can also have compassion, and I have a good relationship with Larissa,” Albanese said. “I thank her for the constructive engagement that I’ve had with her. I work with people across the parliament. We have to do that in order to secure any legislation through our Senate. We haven’t always agreed, and we won’t always agree going forward, but I wish her all the very best.” Waters took on the job just over 15 months ago at a tumultuous time for the Greens. At the last election the party’s then-leader Adam Bandt lost his previously safe seat of Melbourne to Labor. The Greens also lost Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates’ seats in Brisbane, leaving the party with only one lower house seat and devoid of Chandler-Mather’s firebrand energy.



Waters, 49, plans to return to the Senate after time away dealing with her health, so her resignation as leader does not open an upper house vacancy. She said the minor party had achieved significant wins, including protecting native forests in a deal with Labor to reform Australia’s 25-year-old environmental laws. World.title: Nassif’s Toplace paid $134,000 for surveillance of Strathfield mayor
World.content:
Follow the hearings live A private investigator invoiced Jean Nassif’s development company $134,000 for surveillance of the former Strathfield mayor, with then-Labor councillor Sharangan Maheswaran convincing Toplace to pay the bill. Maheswaran, who was also the lawyer for Toplace, said the surveillance work had a “tangential” connection to Nassif because then-mayor Matthew Blackmore had “linked up” with another individual who Maheswaran believed was targeting him because of his connection to the disgraced developer. Sharangan Maheswaran arrives at the ICAC on Tuesday. Sam Mooy The Independent Commission Against Corruption is investigating whether Maheswaran and his fellow Labor councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in blackmail and/or offences under the Surveillance Devices Act while waging a pressure campaign to force Blackmore to resign as mayor.



The commission heard on Tuesday Nassif’s daughter Ashlyn raised the payment to private investigator Shane De Kauwe as a personal expense for Maheswaran to cover but he convinced her Toplace should pay the invoices because he was already owed money. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Former Strathfield councillor Sharangan Maheswaran returns for likely final day of public hearings “I believe that Toplace paid it on the basis that I was insisting that I need to get this paid, and I will offset it against other liabilities you owe me because I regard the targeting of me by this individual to be linked to Toplace Pty Ltd,” Maheswaran said. Maheswaran told the commission he only became aware De Kauwe was making covert audio recordings after the lawyer was provided with highly detailed notes. He said when he asked De Kauwe to explain something in his surveillance notes, the private investigator said he would “go back and check”.



“That’s when it became apparent that he’d taken a recording. Now, Mr De Kauwe also said to me that he might record if there was obvious criminality involved and he said he was entitled to do so,” Maheswaran said. Maheswaran told the commission he then sought legal advice for himself about the legality of making these recordings, which he passed on to De Kauwe. He has been ordered to provide that advice to the commission. However, last week De Kauwe told the commission he only began to make audio recordings of Blackmore after receiving legal advice from Maheswaran, and his understanding was if he suspected criminality, he could record the conversation. Maheswaran also offered to “stir up” Blackmore to try and capture damaging comments on a covert audio recording, the ICAC has heard. De Kauwe texted Maheswaran to let him know Blackmore was at a cafe. “Have you got a good audio on him? If so I’ll stir him up,” Maheswaran said.



Maheswaran told the commission he thought he could prompt Blackmore into talking about council-related matters, and “things I thought he was orchestrating on the council at that point”. Maheswaran later texted Pensabene that he thought Blackmore realised he was “being watched”. “Did we get caught?” Pensabene asked. “Nah, but he was highly suss,” Maheswaran replied. Maheswaran told the ICAC that Pensabene was aware of the surveillance but may not have been aware of the covert recordings.

World.title: Wallabies sweat on stars for Bledisloe as RA chases answers on ‘phone-gate’
World.content:
The Wallabies’ hopes of following up their Optus Stadium heroics with a drought-breaking victory over the All Blacks in Auckland next week have been given a boost, with Len Ikitau’s ankle injury not as serious as first feared. Ikitau’s potential availability for the first Bledisloe Cup Test came as Rugby Australia confirmed that they are investigating the cause of the communications breakdown that led to the bizarre scene of referee Andrea Piardi speaking to the television match official on a mobile phone on Sunday night. Len Ikitau passes the ball against the Springboks. Getty Images The referee communications problem was one of many elements of high drama in Perth, in which the Wallabies held on for an unbelievable victory despite being reduced to 11 men in the last 10 minutes. Ikitau hobbled off with an ankle injury in the second half – and was later seen in a moon boot – and centre partner Hunter Paisami was later cited for a high tackle that earned him one of four yellow cards. Paisami’s case will be initially heard before the SANZAAR foul play review committee on Tuesday night.



If found guilty the No.12 faces a suspension that could keep him out of the first Bledisloe Cup clash at Eden Park on October 10. Australia hasn’t won at the venue since 1986, and the All Blacks haven’t lost there to anyone since 1994. Along with Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper returning to their clubs in Paris and Exeter respectively, and in-form lock Josh Canham also in doubt with a hamstring injury, the Wallabies face the prospect of five stars missing from the opening Bledisloe clash. Ahead of Les Kiss confirming his squad on Wednesday, however, the news on Ikitau appears more positive than first feared. There was concern the star centre – who scored two tries against the Springboks – had suffered a syndesmosis injury, which usually has a six-to-12 week recovery period and can require surgery. Loading Ikitau has scans on Monday but sources with knowledge of the situation say the John Eales medallist is confident the injury is not a worst-case scenario and he may be able to play against the All Blacks. Ikitau missed the Japan Tests in August after having clean-up surgery on the same ankle.



The contingency planning for the Wallabies’ midfield would mean Isaac Henry and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii returning to the centres, and Jordan Petaia may also be an option after joining the squad last week in Perth. But Kiss will be crossing his fingers that Ikitau is available, given his importance on a range of fronts: as a ball-player, game manager, defensive bulwark and open-field attacker. He crossed the gain line against the vaunted Springbok defence in 80 per cent of his carries in Perth. Loading Tupou and Hooper are also big losses. Tupou helped lock down the Wallabies scrum against the Boks, and Hooper was a work-rate machine in the crazy final minutes. Meanwhile, Rugby Australia are seeking answers after Piardi was forced to speak to his television match official on a mobile phone due to issues with his communications device during the closing stages of Sunday’s Test victory against South Africa.



The issue comes just over a year before Australia host the Rugby World Cup. As host nation, RA utilised its regular supplier of referee communications for one-off home Tests, Gravity Media. RA has used the company to supply this technology for more than 10 years without incident. Gravity Media is also listed as one of five companies approved to provide referee communications services at its tournaments, including next year’s World Cup. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii of the Wallabies offloads. Getty Images In a statement provided to this masthead, RA acknowledged the technological difficulties for the match officials on Sunday. “Rugby Australia acknowledges that match officials’ communications were affected by a technical issue during Sunday’s Test between the Wallabies and South Africa in Perth.



“Further information is currently being sought from the relevant third-party service provider to understand the cause of the issue and ensure appropriate measures are taken to prevent a recurrence.” Related Article Australian rugby Booming global interest in 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia as one-year countdown begins Piardi was forced to use a mobile phone after 69 minutes to speak to television match official Matteo Liparini to confirm that Wallabies captain Harry Wilson had made a high tackle and would receive a yellow card. After 73 minutes, Piardi explained to Wallabies stand-in captain Jeremy Williams and South Africa skipper Andre Esterhuizen that he was finding it challenging to officiate without his normal technology to talk to his television match official. Referee communication issues had also plagued the Springboks’ last Test against New Zealand in Baltimore.



Referee Karl Dickson was forced to stop the game for eight minutes and 53 minutes midway through the first half, with officials unable to communicate with each other. World Rugby and Gravity Media were contacted for comment. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: NRL appoints grand final referees as Klein and 2025 incumbent miss out
World.content:

Adam Gee has been appointed to referee his second NRL grand final with Chris Butler to work as the bunker official in Sunday’s Roosters-Knights decider.

Gee was in charge of the Roosters’ 36-20 preliminary final defeat of the Dolphins on Friday, in which he referred contentious tries to Jamayne Isaako and Rob Toia to the bunker, which were subsequently awarded by video official Ashley Klein, who deemed to not have sufficient evidence to overturn the on-field decision.

World.title: Ben Simmons is back in the NBA. One topic at media day had him swearing
World.content:
SportBasketballBen Simmons Ben Simmons is back in the NBA. One topic at media day had him swearing Jon Pierik September 29, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A rejuvenated Ben Simmons has declared basketball is his art and he is ready to dominate and prove to the world how much he missed the sport in a year away from the game. Simmons was a top draft pick with the Philadelphia 76ers and one of the great hopes for that team’s turnaround in fortunes. But the relationship soured and when his five-year, $250 million deal expired after the 2024-25 season, he was traded to the Brooklyn Nets – then waived. Back in the big league: Three-time All Star Ben Simmons says he is a happy and healthy and ready to make a splash with the Sacramento Kings. Getty He spent his last season with the Los Angeles Clippers, and then turned his attention to professional sport fishing. Simmons, 30, who has struggled with physical and mental health issues throughout his career, is back and ready to make a splash in his return to the NBA.



Related Article Exclusive

NBA How Josh Giddey helps others get better, on and off the court He has worked hard on shedding a back issue which had long plagued his game and, in some ways, took the pure joy away from playing. “I think that was more so just my body. It wasn’t about if I wanted to play. All these people talk about, I don’t love the game. That’s bullshit – I love this game,” the Australian guard said. “If I didn’t, I wouldn’t have taken that year to focus on myself and get back to where I’m at.” Former NBA player Patrick Beverley recently claimed Simmons quit when things got hard, and questioned his respect and love for the game.



“What do I love about the game? Everything. It’s my art,” Simmons said. Related Article NBA The secret Ben Simmons training session that has tongues wagging “You know, I get to come out here and be creative and play hard and compete against, you know, a numerous amount of talented guys. So for me, it’s just, it’s in my blood. I’ve been doing it since I was a baby.” Simmons impressed Australian Boomers coaches and players at an unofficial squad camp in Melbourne last month, sources close to the pass-first playmaker confirming to this masthead he is keen to represent his country at the FIBA World Cup in Qatar next year. Fellow Australian Josh Giddey, the star Chicago Bulls’ playmaker, said there was no reason why Simmons could not again be a force.



“It was awesome to see him back fit and firing in Melbourne, and I think it was awesome for him to be amongst that national team program,” Giddey told this masthead ahead of the Bulls’ media day. “He knows how much, you know, we want him to be a part of it, and I think it’s an awesome place for him to rejuvenate his career and get back to where he belongs in the NBA. So, super excited to see him. “He looks good. He looks really healthy and fit. And, yeah, I’m excited to watch him this year and see how he goes in Sacramento.” Simmons averaged 13.1 points, 7.4 rebounds and 7.2 assists per game through his career, but outside shooting was an issue.



Related Article Exclusive

NBA Grudge matches, trash talk and sharp shooting: Dash Daniels on his path to the NBA “I’m right where I need to be. I took a lot of time to focus on my body over the season. I think it was the best thing I’ve done and decision I’ve made for my career,” Simmons, on a one-year, $3.5 million contract, said. “I’m looking forward to getting going. I feel great and I’m ready to go. No limitations, so ready. “I miss playing the game a lot. But when you’re not physically right, it’s hard to want to be out there and do what you love. “So the fact that I’m healthy, and I’m able to compete every day and play every day, I love it.”



It shapes as a tough season for an undermanned Kings’ unit in a loaded western conference. But Simmons has a goal: “Every time I step on the floor, to dominate,” he said. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Auckland Council's governing body votes to move to in-person booth voting in 2028
World.content:
Auckland Council's governing body has voted to move to in-person booth voting for the next local elections in 2028.

The decision came after a morning of debates on the cost and benefits of the various options of postal voting, booth voting, or a combination of both.

The last local elections in 2025 had historically low voter turnout and growing concerns about the security and integrity of postal voting - after 79 votes were fraudulently cast in Papatoetoe.

The majority of councillors have voted to support looking at ways to acheive booth voting for a cost of under $20 million.

Auckland Council esimates that a 10-day booth voting election would cost between $31 million and $40 million, compared with approximately $16 million for a postal election, however and amendment directing staff to look at ways of lowering this cost to $20 million, was accepted.

Three councillors were not present, two abstained due to conflict of interests.

Those opposing include mayor Wayne Brown, Councillor Greg Sayers and Councillor Andy Baker.

Several councillors hit out at the current postal voting system as "broken" and undermining democracy.

Councillor Julie Fairey said having a system with integrity was worth the additional cost of running booth voting.

She said a lack of integrity in the system would discourage people from voting in the first place, adding that the current system was "breaking", if not broken already.

Fairey said moving to booth voting would at least demonstrate that there was willingness to fix the system.

Councillor Lotu Fuli who also supported booth voting asked the room: "What price are we willing to pay to protect our democracy?"

She said if nothing was done to fix the current system, then that was like rewarding fraudsters.

Councillor Ken Turner, who also supported booth voting, likened the current postal voting system to a broken vehicle, and said it needed a major overhaul.

Opposing councillor Andy Baker said investing about $9 million extra into booth voting (more than the approximate $11m for an enhanced postal voting system) was like "gambling".

He said he would prefer to enhance the current system at a lesser cost.

Ōtara-Papatoetoe local board chair Apulu Reece Autagavaia. LDR / Mary Afemata

Ahead of the vote, Ōtara-Papatoetoe local board chair Apulu Reece Autagavaia hit out at Auckland's mayor, questioning how much he valued democracy.

Autagavaia supported changing systems, after the board's last election was voided due to claims that voting papers were stolen and used without consent.

But Auckland mayor Wayne Brown questioned the cost of changing systems.

"We're talking about possibly spending 2 percent of our rates, just to solve a couple of postal things?"

Autagavaia interrupted, asking the mayor "is that how much you value our democratic right to vote for our representatives?"

Brown pointed to concerns about the cost of living, to which Autagavaia accused the mayor of being "willing to allow fraud".

World.title: Two-year home loan fix might be worth considering - ANZ
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1650799%2Ftwo-year-home-loan-fix-might-be-worth-considering-anz

A two-year home loan fix might not be a bad option right now, ANZ's economists say.

The bank has released its latest Property Focus report, which notes that it expects further small declines in house prices through the rest of this year, and growth of about 2 percent next year.

It said rising interest rates, both locally and offshore, were the main driver of a slowdown in activity this year. ANZ expects three more 25 basis point increases to the official cash rate, to take it to 3.5 percent.

Banks have been increasing many of their fixed home loan rates, but have often left their two-year rates unchanged, or even reduced them.

ANZ's economists said some borrowers might be tempted to fix for longer in an environment where rates were rising, but there would be trade-offs in that decision.

They said a two-year fix might seem a good option to some borrowers.

"Given where we expect floating and shorter-term mortgage rates to go over the next few years, the two-year rate has some appeal. It is long enough that it provides some certainty but is not significantly more expensive.

"Breakevens show that fixing for two years at 5.39 percent will be cheaper than fixing for one year at 5.15 percent and re-fixing for another year as long as the one-year rate is above 5.63 percent in a year's time.

"Given that our projections, based on our wholesale interest rate forecasts, have the one-year mortgage rate rising to 5.6 percent in a year's time, the certainty of fixing for longer may appeal. Fixing for three years or longer may also appeal, but the step up into those longer terms is more than it was a month ago and some borrowers may not want to be locked in for that long if they see mortgage rates coming down in a couple of years, if oil prices fall and inflation is tamed. A mix of terms may also appeal given heightened uncertainty."

ANZ said there was a mixed picture around the country. In Wellington, declines in house prices have accelerated since March while in the South Island there were signs that the previous upward trend in prices had lost steam in the last few months.

On Tuesday, Treasury updated its forecasts and said housing prices were expected to be weaker than previously thought, with growth of just 0.6 percent in 2027 compared with 4 percent forecast in the Budget.

It put that down to higher interest rates, growth in housing supply and lower net migration.

ANZ senior economist Matthew Galt said Treasury had pulled back from what had previously been a stronger view than many other forecasters.

He said a weaker housing market would have an impact on the economy.

"It makes households less likely to spend… those wealth effects, even though they're not always nice for different groups, particularly renters, they do have a real impact on the economy as a whole, with homeowners tending to spend more when the housing market's stronger.

"But they're not the whole economy by any stretch of the imagination. The export sector's really strong at the moment, and there are other drivers of growth working through with the economy showing good signs of recovering. So we can still have a very decent economic recovery without house prices rising."

He said it was notable how much the global situation as affecting New Zealand.

"With persistent inflation pressures in a lot of countries overseas and higher oil prices all pressuring central banks around the world to hike interest rates. And we can't avoid those pressures either, and so those global forces are really transmitting to our housing market and contributing to some of the weakness."

World.title: New human waste-dumping plan to be considered by Otago council
World.content:
Central Otago District Council could backtrack on plans to truck treated human effluent onto farmland after discovering the proposed site near Lauder might not be able to handle all of its sludge.

The council will decide on Wednesday on how to deal with a growing volume of treated wastewater sludge, with staff warning that Cromwell's ponds urgently need de-sludging and geobags containing thousands of cubic metres of dried sludge - dating back a decade - need moving.

The original recommendation was to dump the waste on land near Lauder, using a non-notified consent that already allows Wānaka's sludge to be disposed of at the property.

The move was expected to save at least $600,000, compared with the estimated $1.6 million cost of carting the sludge to Southland's Winton landfill.

The proposal had angered Federated Farmers, but in a late addition to the agenda on Tuesday, staff recommended sending the stored sludge to Winton landfill instead, because the Lauder site might only be able to take half of Cromwell's sludge.

The total cost of transport to Winton and de-sludging the ponds was now estimated to be more than $3 million including contingencies.

The report said sludge from the Alexandra wastewater treatment plant might still go to the Lauder site, because it could be accommodated within the consent conditions.

The updated report said the council had received three tenders to remove the geobags and de-sludge the Cromwell ponds.

"Given the recently raised concerns by the consent-holder at Lauder, there is an increased risk that there could be interruptions to the program of work for removal of the geobag material. Delays in transporting this material will result in a variation to the contract being required and contract cost increases," the report said.

"Following assessment of the tender prices, staff believe the cost impacts of potential delays outweigh the cost efficiency of transporting the material a shorter distance to Lauder."

If personal hygiene products were found in the geobags, it would affect the ability to spread sludge at Lauder, the report said.

The Otago Regional Council, which granted the original non-notified consent to the Queenstown Lakes District Council in January, said it was taking community concerns seriously and there was a regular compliance and monitoring programme in place.

Speaking before the agenda item was updated, Federated Farmers Otago president Anna Gillespie said the plan had annoyed local farmers who had copped flak about water quality in the area and had worked hard to make improvements.

"They're angry that it could have gone through non-notified and there wasn't any consultation and they're angry that it's happening," she said.

"The feeling is that if it had been a notified consent then we could have stopped it rather than it going ahead."

Federated Farmers wanted the original consent reconsidered, Gillespie said.

"It's absolutely staggering that the council is even discussing this after the recent outcry over Wānaka trucking its treated excrement to a Lauder farm," she said.

Gillespie said the practice of spreading treated effluent on land was not new but the Lauder site was highly unsuitable.

"Experienced local farmers know what a farm like this - with porous gravely soils and low rainfall - can realistically produce by way of crops to soak up effluent nutrients," she said.

"We all understand the desire to save ratepayers' money but this shouldn't be at the expense of water quality in a sensitive catchment upstream of public water intakes."

The decision to dump treated human effluent from Wānaka on the Lauder property has prompted outage from locals worried about the potential impact on their water and health.

In the initial staff report to councillors, Three Waters group manager Julie Muir said testing of the sludge from the Alexandra site and geobags stored at Cromwell met the consent requirements for disposal in Lauder.

The report initially recommended councillors approve plans to transport the sludge to Lauder because it was the most cost-effective and legally compliant option for Central Otago ratepayers despite community unhappiness about the consent.

Earlier this year, Beca reviewed the capacity and ability of the Cromwell treatment plant to cope with increased demand because of growth, finding that it needed immediate and ongoing treatment upgrades to ensure the nitrogen limits were not triggered.

The Cromwell wastewater ponds were de-sludged a decade ago into geobags that allow the sludge to dry over time and reduce transport costs.

About 20,000 cubic metres of sludge was identified in the ponds, which would cost an estimated $2.8-$3.2 million to remove.

"Dried sludge contained in geobags on this site needs to be moved and the ponds de-sludged again as a matter of urgency," Muir said.

"This work is required to ensure that a consent condition which will require a reduction in nitrogen loading is not triggered.

"Once this trigger is reached then the nitrogen and ammonia limits on the consent reduce significantly which will require alternative more costly treatment methods."

Otago Regional Council chief executive Richard Saunders said the consent was non-notified based on an assessment of information supplied as part of the application process.

Council staff had since spoken with local residents and interested parties about their concerns, he said.

"The issues raised have primarily related to water quality, odour, human health and the consent process. The consent was processed in accordance with the Resource Management Act and is now subject to regular compliance audits," Saunders said.

Saunders said the concerns included any impact on the sensitive Manuherekia catchment area.

"We are aware through our engagement with the Manuherekia community that there are a number of concerns about the potential for adverse effects," he said.

"We are taking these concerns seriously and will continue to engage with the community on them."

The council had a regular compliance and monitoring programme underway for the site but Saunders did not rule out a potential review of the resource consent and said information from the community was helping to inform the council's response.

"It is too early to say what if any changes may be sought through this process," he said.

World.title: Man charged with drink driving causing death after double-fatality crash in Rotorua
World.content:
A man faces two charges of driving with excess breath alcohol causing death, following a double-fatality crash in Rotorua last month.

Emergency services were called to the crash between a car and a motorbike at the intersection of Te Ngae Road and Rotokawa Road on 14 August. The rider and passenger on the motorbike died.

Senior Sergeant John Stapleford said in a statement to RNZ on Tuesday that the investigation was ongoing, but a 72-year-old man had been charged with two charges of driving with excess breath alcohol causing death.

World.title: All Blacks named for Bledisloe: Codie Taylor captain, Scott Barrett and Shannon Frizell back
World.content:
The All Blacks squad to take on the Wallabies has been named with a pair of veterans earning their international recall.

Dave Rennie has named his 34-man squad for the Bledisloe Cup, with former captain Scott Barrett included to complete his comeback.

Barrett has not been cited in black in 2026 but made a return to rugby last weekend with Taranaki in a big win over Hawke's Bay.

Rennie saw enough to recall the 88-test stalwart, along with Tasman's Shannon Frizell, back in the country after three years in Japan.

Codie Taylor will captain the side for the two tests against the Wallabies, with several key players sidelined with injury.

Ruben Love will sit out the series with an ankle injury, Richie Mo'unga and Josh Jacomb named as the only first fives.

Beauden Barrett retains his spot in the outside backs, with no room for Emoni Narawa.

Others to have missed the cut include lock Sam Darry, props Siale Lauaki and Saula Ma'u, number eight Semisi Tupou Ta'eiloa and the versatile Leicester Faingaʻanuku, just back from a long lay-off.

In total, the squad includes 31 of the players who were named in the original 44-man squad which travelled to South Africa.

Jacomb, who played two franchise games during Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour, is the only member of the squad yet to earn a Test cap.

Rennie said the season so far had given a large number of players valuable experience that would be vital for upcoming the Bledisloe Cup.

"Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour was great for us. We've learnt a lot about our game and about ourselves, and it gave a lot of guys valuable time in the jersey. Plenty of them put their hands up, and every player selected fully deserves their place."

Rennie welcomed back both Barrett and Frizell.

"Scott has had a challenging stretch on the sidelines, and we're thrilled to have his experience and leadership back in the group. Shannon brings plenty of Test experience and physical impact to our loose forwards."

Having held the trophy for 23 years, Rennie said the history means a lot to the All Blacks.

"We've held it since 2003 and we don't take that for granted. Australia will be a real challenge. It's now a very experienced Wallabies side who have played a lot of Test footy together. After eight games on the road, we're excited to start this series in front of our home crowd at Eden Park," Rennie said.

Taylor said he was humbled to be asked to captain the All Blacks for the Bledisloe Cup.

"To lead this team is a massive honour, and I know I'm lucky to have a lot of good leaders around me who make that job easier. A special thank you also to my whānau for their support, none of this would be possible without them. Ardie has done an outstanding job for us this year and we're all gutted he's not with us. We'll be doing everything we can to make him proud.

The All Blacks squad will assemble in Auckland on Sunday ahead of the first Bledisloe Cup Test.

All Blacks Bledisloe Cup squad:

Forwards: Codie Taylor (captain), Asafo Aumua, Samisoni Taukei'aho, Ethan de Groot, George Bower, Xavier Numia, Tyrel Lomax, Fletcher Newell, Pasilio Tosi, Scott Barrett, Josh Lord, Fabian Holland, Tupou Vaa'i, Simon Parker, Shannon Frizell, Anton Segner, Ethan Blackadder, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi.

Backs: Cam Roigard, Cortez Ratima, Kyle Preston, Richie Mo'unga, Josh Jacomb, Jordie Barrett, Quinn Tupaea, Timoci Tavatavanawai, Rieko Ioane, Fehi Fineanganofo, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby, Will Jordan, Beauden Barrett, Damian McKenzie.

Unavailable due to injury: Ruben Love (ankle), Patrick Tuipulotu (calf), Ardie Savea (shoulder), Luke Jacobson (elbow), Anton Lienert-Brown, Billy Proctor, Caleb Clarke, (shoulder), Ollie Norris (knee).

2026 Bledisloe Cup:

7.10pm October 10 at Eden Park, Auckland

World.title: 'We're coming to get you': A rural town tackling its meth problem
World.content:
Audio player for " Meth Toll: Waipukurau community tackles issue of addiction " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1637931%2Fwe-re-coming-to-get-you-a-rural-town-tackling-its-meth-problem

Meth Toll: Waipukurau community tackles issue of addiction Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A rural town in Central Hawke's Bay has one of the highest levels of meth in the country, and its community is trying to tackle the issue together.

With a population of just 5000, Waipukurau is a friendly and quiet town, but its reputation as a close knit, hard working community is tainted by meth.

In 2024, wastewater testing in the town found meth consumption had soared 333 percent in 12 months, to more than 4.8 grams per day, per thousand people.

Results have remained consistently high ever since, despite a covert police operation that ended in three people being arrested in December 2025 for supplying methamphetamine.

Waipukurau's wastewater ponds, where testing has revealed some of NZ's highest levels of methamphetamine. RNZ / Alexa Cook

A Waipukurau social support worker, who wants to be known only as Bob, told RNZ that meth is everywhere in the town.

"I'm tired of working with this s***, it is draining and it will suck the life out of you.

"Who isn't on it?" he said.

Bob is a former addict, and through his work helping others with their addictions, he feels meth is becoming normalised - like alcohol.

"There are so many people accepting it as is, it's just their day-to-day norm... their routine along with having a cup of tea in the morning.

"This isn't to say it's accepted - but in pockets, and there are a variety of pockets, it is not limited to one pocket of society - this is just normal," Bob said.

Hawke's Bay police area prevention manager, Inspector Caroline Martin and Central Hawke's Bay officer in charge Sergeant Neil Baker. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The local police officer, sergeant Neil Baker, is trying to understand why Waipukurau's meth rates are so high.

"It definitely appears to be more acceptable in people's lives now and the number of people that you come across who... would have cannabis in their pocket, now they have a meth pipe and utensils or something along those lines.

"So yes, I think it is becoming more and more common, which is very sad," Baker said.

He told RNZ the issue is hard to get his head around, but he does have a theory.

"I believe that we potentially have a number of functioning users who are able to use methamphetamine on a daily basis, go about their business, go about their employment, and still function as every day members of the community, but have a habit. We're certainly hearing more and more stories like that.

"We're seeing more people being affected by methamphetamine. And the number of those contacts is certainly increasing, those who are regular users of methamphetamine," Baker said.

He said while there is a definite gang link to the distribution and sale of meth in Central Hawke's Bay, it's a much broader demographic who are actually using it.

"The more I learn into the distribution of it, it's certainly a lot wider. And I think that what we see on the ground is just one portion of a very big problem for the country."

Baker's vowing to keep fighting back against the rise of meth in his community.

"I certainly hope that we haven't lost the battle just yet. We're going to continue the good fight and keep coming to work every day to try and catch as many as we can."

His message to those supplying methamphetamine is clear: "Get ready, we're coming to get you."

RNZ / Alexa Cook

Wastewater testing can't tell police who is consuming meth or how much they are taking, that's why they rely on information from the public.

Hawke's Bay police area prevention manager Inspector Caroline Martin said last year's arrests were thanks to people helping police, and they're urging others with any information to do the same.

"Seeing any consumption levels high in a community is concerning. To try and understand that, we need the community support. We do know that there are users in the community.

"We rely on information from the public to help us with this issue. We need people to come forward. We need people to tell us what's happening in our local community here in Central Hawke's Bay," she said.

In response to the spike of meth in the wastewater, the Central Hawke's Bay Methamphetamine Harm Reduction Group was formed in 2024, which includes local leaders, organisations, health services and police.

It's funded by the Resilience to Organised Crime in Communities (ROCC) programme. The programme's manager Hannah O'Leary said that support has led to the community group developing a localised strategy.

"Subsequent to that, there has been a road map that has been developed on actually how to implement that strategy. It's very much community based ... I think there were about 30 different people in the room discussing what works for their community.

"Making sure we've got the right people sitting around that table from all the different walks of life is really important," she said.

The ROCC programme is now in 13 communities across New Zealand.

"What we do know is that organised groups exploit vulnerability such as disconnection, trauma, economic hardship, addiction, where there's limited access to opportunities and weakened protective factors," O'Leary said.

Central Hawke's Bay mayor Will Foley. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The Central Hawke's Bay Methamphetamine Harm Reduction Group has created a strategy to try and drive down Waipukurau's high meth consumption. Mayor Will Foley said that includes education and awareness around the impacts of meth, and where to go for help.

"The good thing about a plan is then it shows what we do need when we ask for further support.

"Being a small community, we don't necessarily have good facilities and services for things like that, as opposed to some of the bigger cities. So seeing what we could do to set up and just have people and services available for those people that need help."

The mayor said it's a community-wide effort to tackle the town's meth problem, but he's also being realistic.

"We hope to reverse that trend, but we know it's going to be an ongoing issue," Foley said.

Bob said he was sceptical about the group's strategy.

"So far nothing has worked. America's 'war on drugs', it's not unique to them... the only winner is drugs," he said.

When asked if there is anything that could help reduce meth use in Central Hawke's Bay, Bob said there needs to be more facilities for addicts to "dry out".

"There's a real lack of detox centres. I've always bitched and moaned about that - only one detox bed for the whole of Hawke's Bay," he said.

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey told RNZ the government is investing more in Hawke's Bay to help people access faster drug addiction support.

"Through the Government's Reducing Demand for Methamphetamine plan, we have committed $2.32 million over four years to Hawke's Bay, including Central Hawke's Bay and Wairoa.

"This investment will provide community-based, peer-led support as well as additional specialist addiction practitioners and registered nurses, with a specific focus on reducing meth harm and supporting people through withdrawal," Doocey said.

World.title: Election 2026 live: A look inside the books as the campaign continues
World.content:
Nicola Willis has received an economic reprieve with the PREFU, but it's not all good news for voters.

World.title: Woolworths confirms plan to move 130 jobs to Australia
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1646794%2Fwoolworths-confirms-plan-to-move-130-jobs-to-australia

Woolworths New Zealand is going ahead with plans to cut 130 jobs in New Zealand and move them to Australia.

The supermarket chain has confirmed that, after a consultation process, it will integrate its Auckland customer care team into the customer support network in Sydney.

"This has been a difficult decision, and we recognise the significant impact it has on our customer care team members who have served our Kiwi customers with dedication for many years," Mark Wolfenden, director of digital and ecommerce said.

"We have taken on feedback received during the consultation process, and adjusted our approach accordingly, however we will progress with the core elements of the proposal.

"Our absolute priority right now is supporting every impacted team member with dignity, care, and clarity. We are working one-on-one with each team member to explore genuine redeployment opportunities across our supermarket network, supply chain, and broader business, including ring-fencing vacant roles.

"We have engaged specialist career transition partners and are proactively connecting with local employers who are actively recruiting for customer support talent. Comprehensive support packages also include employee counselling for impacted team and their families, as well as redundancy compensation."

Workers First union said affected workers were locked out by Woolworths at Christmas after refusing worse terms and conditions.

Deputy secretary Rudd Hughes said the decision was short-sighted and an insult to workers and customers alike.

"Woolworths has just banked $163 million in earnings from Kiwi shoppers, and its response is to put 130 New Zealanders out of work to save pocket change," he said.

"It's short-sighted, it's greedy, and it's a company turning its back on a country it has extracted mega-profits from."

He said it was a slap in the face for "workers who provide a world-class service. They don't understand the rationalte behind it apart from the fact they want to save money".

"One of the things that comes out of Woolworths is that they're really concerned about customer service. This is one of the best customer service centres in the country. It's world-class and now they're closing it."

Earlier, the union said it was concerned that these staff had knowledge that it would not be possible to replicate offshore.

Many were people who had taken the roles because they offered flexibility and the ability to work remotely. Some, once employed, had shifted to other parts of the country where it would be harder for them to find replacement roles.

"There are quite a few single parents who are doing this kind of work and being able to do it from home means they can give proper care for their children. They picked up these jobs on the basis that they would be able to do them from home, they could move out of Auckland, which is incredibly expensive, they could maintain a decent lifestyle on the wages they've got."

He said many workers had had their jobs extended until November 30. "What that means is that these people will be going out on to the job market, becoming unemployed right around Christmas time."

He said he did not have high hopes for redeployment.

World.title: This iron Rooster has been the NRL's best forward in 2026
World.content:
The end of a footy season isn't just for finals; it's also prime territory for end-of-season awards.

Every team has them: the best and fairest for the star, the most improved for the biggest riser and the coach's award for the battler who came good.

Other than the top prize, there's nothing better than winning best forward or best back, and if you were giving out a trophy for the former for the entire NRL in 2026 it would have to end up in the mighty hands of Naufahu Whyte.

The iron Rooster enters Sunday's grand final after a season in which he's confirmed his place as one of rugby league's top players and certainly its premier front-rower of the year.

Whyte will lead the Roosters from the front in Sunday's grand final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Given Whyte leads all forwards in metres gained and post-contact metres averages over 16 runs per game, it's hard to find a better battering ram through the middle of the field.

He's also fifth among all forwards for tackle busts and just outside the top 10 for offloads, proving he's far from an empty calories stat-chaser.

Simply put, in all aspects of play, he's had the best year of any forward in the NRL and if he doesn't make the Dally M team of the year on Wednesday night we may as well call the whole thing off.

Other forwards might be his equal, but this year none of them have been better.

After two weeks on the leash, Whyte's performance in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins was his latest blunt-force masterpiece as he finished with 18 runs for 207 metres, more than all three opposition starting middles combined.

"All I remember is the start. I was getting ready to take the kick-off carry to start the game and the crowd was just roaring, the trumpets were playing and everything was just going off," Whyte said.

"I remember taking about the first carry and starting the game off and then I remember us winning it at the end and that is all I need. That's all that matters to me."

More than once Whyte took more than one run per set, something that has become his trademark this season as he's established himself as one of the NRL's apex predators.

If history is any guide, the 24-year-old will repeat the dose against Newcastle in Sunday's grand final, where he will once again be tasked with being the lead horse of the Roosters pack.

A sensational work rate in attack has driven Whyte to new heights in 2026. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts )

It's a job Whyte feels like he is built to do, which allows him to deliver the gifts he feels made to give.

"It's just what I want to do for my brothers and that's a superpower of mine, to carry that ball and I can create opportunities off the back of that for Sammy [Walker], Teddy [James Tedesco], Chez [Daly Cherry-Evans], all of those boys to really express themselves," he said.

"I just feel like every time I can get my hands on that ball I can create something special for them.

"I've got to make sure that's there for my teammates and brothers on that field every time I'm doing something, whether it's running the ball, tackling or whatever.

Whyte was one of the Roosters' best against the Dolphins on Friday night. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

"That's not gonna change coming into this week. If I need to take three, four carries a set, I'll do it.

"As long as it's to help my team and help them play off the back of it, then that's me."

Whyte has made his name by running through whatever ends up in front of him but he's only been able to do so by running away from a year he never wants to revisit.

The 24-year old made his NRL debut in 2021 but spent all of the following season outside the big league, failing to play a single first grade game.

Hard lessons from his debut NRL year still fuel Whyte. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Even now, years later and with a reputation as one of the best forwards in the league, that season in the wilderness still haunts him in the best way possible.

"I just had a sit back for myself personally, I got a bit too comfortable being in you know NRL. I thought I made it," Whyte said.

"It was a good reality check for myself and it was good that I got to start early on in my career because now I stick with that forever.

"I don't ever want to experience that feeling ever again. I stuck with those lessons, I took it on the chin and I bounced back.

"That's a big driving force for myself and motivation having that thought of what happened to me in 2022. I know for sure.

"I'm never gonna go back to that situation again."

Sunday will mark Whyte's grand final debut but he is well acquainted with the lore the Roosters carry into the decider.

Where some players downplay their club's recent history, Whyte revels in it. He admits to being a regular viewer of replays of the Tricolours' 2018 and 2019 grand final wins, taking them as a source of inspiration.

"I remember everything about them, I still watch YouTube videos of those games all the time," Whyte said.

"I've actually watched it lately and tried to envision myself in that moment and stuff. Seeing all their hard work pay off. It's something I've always wanted to experience.

"The boys still talk about it every now and then and now it's my time to hopefully enjoy a moment like that for myself."

Of special attention is the opening exchanges of the 2018 decider, when the Roosters forwards stampeded over Melbourne in the opening quarter like a herd of wildebeest.

The Roosters are searching for their first grand final win since 2018-19. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Whyte has too much respect for Newcastle to promise a repeat but it's an effort he knows his side has in them.

"They started pumping them straight away and after that you already knew Roosters were gonna dominate and win," Whyte said.

"That's a strength of ours as well.

"They [Newcastle] deserve the flowers for making grand final, but it's not gonna change anything for us, it doesn't matter if you make grand final or not — us, as a team, are going to come after you."

The New Zealand international is too humble to ever say that he is the greatest part of that howling fury that may be unleashed but then again he doesn't need to.

Whyte has reached a point where he can move in silence and violence because by now everyone knows what he's got.

If he dominates on Sunday it won't be a surprise. When you're the best forward of the season you can't sneak up on anybody.

World.title: Cleary defends Crossland after gruesome injury as hearing locked in
World.content:
Nathan Cleary has leapt to the defence of Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland, pleading with fans to stop peppering the embattled Knight with social media abuse as he prepares to plead his case to the NRL judiciary tonight.

Cleary confirmed on Monday night that Crossland had apologised for the hip-drop tackle that left him needing emergency surgery for a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle.

But less than 24 hours before Crossland was due to launch a desperate bid to play in the grand final, Cleary posted on Instagram from his hospital bed to offer support to the Knights number nine.

"Please don't be one of those people writing comments like this to Phoenix," Cleary posted alongside a graphic of some of the abuse Crossland had received.

Cleary vows 'I'll be back' Nathan Cleary says "I'll be back" in an upbeat Instagram post after successful surgery on his badly broken leg.

"It was a complete accident, and he doesn't deserve the unwarranted hate. He reached out to apologise, and I have nothing but respect for him.

"He's a competitor, and our game is made up of split-second moments that sometimes lead to unfortunate circumstances.

"Comments like this are so unfair. Spread love, not hate."

The comments against Crossland included accusations the tackle was deliberate and threats to maim the Knights dummy-half. Several are not suitable for print.

Crossland had almost appeared close to tears as Cleary was stretchered off Stadium Australia after the tackle and appeared to have accepted his fate even before referee Gerard Sutton sent him off.

He cut a dejected figure in the dressing room after being dismissed, before the Knights held on for a famous 22-14 win to qualify for the grand final.

Crossland seemed to accept his fate before it was even decided. (Supplied: Fox League)

Crossland was referred straight to the judiciary over the incident, with a hearing set for 6pm AEST tonight.

"We need to go down there and present a case to them, but it is a horrible accident at speed under fatigue," Knights director of football Chris James told ABC Sport.

"Phoenix Crossland has made more tackles in the NRL than any other player and he got one wrong.

"He got one wrong and it was a horrible injury for Nathan but that's not Phoenix's go. If you've ever met Phoenix Crossland, he's one of the great men of rugby league.

"Horrible for Nathan, the thoughts of our club go out to Nathan.

"He'll go down as one of the greats of the game and we hope he has a speedy recovery, but we'll also wrap our arms around Phoenix and make sure we look after him this week too."

The New Zealander will almost certainly be rubbed out of Sunday's grand final against the Sydney Roosters, with a question of how much of a ban extends to the World Cup.

The longest suspension handed down for a hip-drop tackle is five weeks. That would keep Crossland out of the World Cup final, if they qualify.

"He was disappointed, we've got to try and get him upbeat," Knights coach Justin Holbrook said after Sunday's game.

"He's an emotional guy. He's been so great for us every week this year. Hopefully Nathan's OK."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Bombers poach former Swans premiership coach John Longmire
World.content:
Essendon have poached former Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new general manager of performance in a huge recruiting coup.

Longmire departs Sydney after 25 years in various roles to reunite with his former assistant, new Bombers coach Mark McVeigh, in a new role.

"I'm really excited to be joining the Essendon Football Club," Longmire said in a statement.

"I've known Mark for a long time and have worked with him as well. He is passionate about the Bombers and has a clear vision for the team.

"I look forward to supporting both him and the staff as the club looks to take the necessary steps back towards being a consistent team who challenge the opposition every week."

The Bombers have effectively split the football boss role in two, with Longmire to oversee game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group, performance analytics and strength and conditioning.

The 55-year-old, most recently Sydney's executive director of club performance, will start this week ahead of the trade period.

John Longmire won the 2012 AFL premiership with the Swans in a 14-season spell as head coach. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Landing Longmire, who did not pursue any vacant head coach roles, is a huge result for the battling Bombers, who finished last on the ladder and needed to put support around first-year coach McVeigh.

"John's football experience and leadership are exactly what we have been looking for in this role," Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said in a statement.

"We have made no secret of our ambition to build a football program capable of delivering sustained success, and bringing in someone of John's calibre is a significant investment in that goal.

"Over 14 seasons as senior coach of the Sydney Swans, John built a program that consistently competed at the pointy end, including the 2012 premiership and four further grand final appearances.

"He knows what a winning program looks like from the inside and how to sustain it year after year.

"Just as importantly, John will be an enormous asset to Mark McVeigh.

"Very few people understand the demands of the senior coach role like John does and having someone of his experience alongside Mark to provide support, guidance and a sounding board will allow Mark to focus on coaching and developing our players."

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham hailed Longmire as a "much-loved and respected figure" and "legend".

Longmire joined Sydney as an assistant coach in 2002 and was involved in the drought-breaking 2005 premiership, later succeeding Paul Roos.

Across 333 games, Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach had a 63 per cent winning record, won the 2012 premiership and led Sydney to five grand finals and 12 finals campaigns.

He stepped down after the 2024 grand final loss to Brisbane.

"Having arrived at the Swans 25 years ago this club has meant so much to me and my family," Longmire said in a Swans statement.

"I will look back with extreme fondness of my time in Sydney and always be proud of what we achieved as a football club."

AAP

World.title: 'I'll be back': Cleary vows to return after surgery
World.content:
Penrith Panthers star Nathan Cleary has vowed to return after his 2026 season was brutally cut short on Sunday, thanking fans for their support from his hospital bed.

The 28-year-old suffered a horrific compound fracture of his left ankle in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final defeat against Newcastle, ruling him out of the Kangaroos' World Cup campaign.

The Panthers, who led 14-6 at half-time, ultimately fell apart to lose to the 12-man Knights, 22-14.

On Monday, the star halfback posted a photo from hospital, with his left leg bandaged following surgery.

"Surgery done," he wrote on Instagram, with a photo of him smiling and giving thumbs up to the camera.

"Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable.

"Yesterday sucked but it's all part of the journey and it's made me even more grateful for the people I have around me.

"I'll be back."

Nathan Cleary was taken from the field in agony. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gruesome injury cast a pall over the Sydney Olympic Stadium, with Panthers players visibly distressed on field while their star was being treated by medical staff.

"He's one of my best mates," Panthers captain Isaah Yeo said post-match.

"He's your brother out there. You don't like seeing anyone like that. You just want to be there for him.

"It's a lonely little place out there when you've got something like that going on."

Cleary's father, coach Ivan Cleary, also revealed that seeing his son in such a state at half-time was "emotional".

It was later revealed that Cleary, who started the game from the bench, was already playing with a broken bone in his right foot as the Panthers hoped to manage his involvement in the prelim with half an eye looking forward to next weekend's grand final against the Sydney Roosters.

Cleary came onto the field 25 minutes into the first half, but only lasted 10 minutes before Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland fell onto his ankle in a tackle.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop and was sent straight to the NRL judiciary by the match review committee, where a lengthy suspension could not only rule him out of Newcastle's first NRL grand final in 25 years, but also impact the Kiwi's World Cup campaign.

Slater calls for change

Phoenix Crossland is unlikely to play in the grand final. (Getty Images)

Crossland is likely to face a lengthy ban, but has been given support from former Maroons coach Billy Slater.

Speaking on The Billy Slater Podcast, Slater said the current rules were leaving players unsure as to how to tackle players effectively without giving away a penalty.

"It has to come down to the responsibility of the tackler," Slater said.

"[But] I honestly feel the game has a little bit of a responsibility in this as well. When you change interpretations and change rules, you always have a flow-on effect.

"If you think about the protection of kickers and ball players and not being able to tackle them even fractionally after they pass the ball … 10 years ago this wouldn't have happened. Fifteen years ago that tackle would not have happened because Phoenix Crossland would've had more speed and force going into that tackle.

"But because he was worried about tackling Nathan after he passed the ball he was actually in a passive position.

"He was on his inside, which is normally when you put pressure on the ball player and you go out and you make tackles on that ball player, even after they pass the ball slightly.

"Phoenix wasn't in that mindset. He was in a passive mindset thinking Nathan was going to pass, then all of a sudden Nathan threw a dummy and he had to make a tackle and he didn't have that force behind him.

"I've got no doubt that has contributed to why Phoenix Crossland is in this grabbing and sitting down position, because he doesn't have that momentum and force and mindset of making a tackle."

The NRL judiciary will sit on Tuesday, with Crossland needing to argue his case to have any chance of playing in the 2026 grand final.

World.title: Socceroos expect Brazil backlash in Brisbane
World.content:
Ageless Socceroo Aziz Behich has no plans to pull the pin with the side on the rise, buoyed by a performance against Brazil they are keen to do better than in Brisbane.

Australia conceded a goal with the final play of their Townsville clash on Friday to walk away with a 1-1 draw that, tellingly, left them disappointed.

A Brazilian backlash is expected at Lang Park on Tuesday night, and the A-League's only player in the 26-man squad is primed to counter it.

"We've set the bar high for ourselves … it was good, but we need to be better," the 35-year-old said.

"How brave we were on the ball … we trusted each other and took the game on.

"When you do that against an opponent like that, you earn their respect and we need to do that again, that's for sure."

Incredibly Behich's 88th national appearance was his first game since the World Cup, but the veteran was able to display his trademark pace and work rate despite being in preseason mode with Melbourne City.

There is optimism the next generation of talent will take the Socceroos to new heights and, with the Asian Cup on the horizon in January, Behich plans to do more than stick around.

"I wouldn't call it hanging on … I'm still playing at a high level … it's exciting times," he said.

"I feel great. I'm a player that's always honest with myself. I know when I'm not at a level I should be. But I have a lot in the tank to give."

The Socceroos took the lead against Brazil, and deserved it as well. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Coach Tony Popovic echoed Behich's sentiment ahead of the Brisbane rematch.

"Being confident, being brave … we've clearly seen a difference in the players' demeanour since the World Cup," he said.

He said the challenge would be to back-up that performance on a short-turnaround.

"We don't have players playing regular Champions League, or in the top leagues, 60 games a year," he said.

"It's a great test."

The Brisbane fixture serves as a homecoming for rising defender Lucas Herrington.

The 19-year-old played his last game for the Roar in January this year, before using the World Cup to springboard from Colorado in the MLS to Hull in the Premier League.

"We've seen against Brazil a confident young man, defending against the very best," Popovic said.

"Now he's got the challenge of doing something he maybe hasn't done in a while, against that calibre, backing up three, four days later.

"Can the body do it and are you ready to play at that level once more?"

AAP

World.title: Matthews claims world championship silver after life-threatening crash
World.content:
Michael Matthews felt that his career was probably over at the start of the season.

Having missed a large portion of the 2025 season after a pulmonary embolism was discovered in his lung, a horrific collision with a fire truck while training in March could have cost him an awful lot more than just his career.
